0.title: The God Who Redeems: The Book of Exodus
0.overview:
Exodus is the great drama of redemption. If Genesis tells us how the world was made and how it fell, Exodus tells us how God comes down to rescue a people for himself. "I have surely seen the affliction of my people," he says, "and I have come down to deliver them" (Ex. 3:7-8). That sentence holds the gospel in seed form: a holy God who sees, hears and comes down.

The book unfolds in three movements. First, redemption accomplished (chs. 1-18), from slavery through the Passover to the sea. Second, the covenant given (chs. 19-24): at Sinai the redeemed people receive the law, not as a ladder to climb to God but as the shape of life with the God who has already saved them. Third, the presence secured (chs. 25-40): the golden calf nearly undoes everything, mercy triumphs, and the book that opens with a people enslaved ends with God himself dwelling in their midst.

Exodus is about God from start to finish. Israel does almost nothing to save itself; it cries out, grumbles and sins, and salvation is the LORD's from beginning to end. When Moses asks to see his glory, God answers by proclaiming his name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (34:6).

And every page points to Christ. The Passover lamb without blemish is fulfilled when Paul writes, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor. 5:7). Israel was "baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea" (1 Cor. 10:2); the manna is the bread of life (John 6); the rock struck in the desert is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4); the tabernacle anticipates the Word made flesh who "tabernacled among us" (John 1:14). Moses, the mediator who stands in the breach and offers his own life for the people, is a shadow of the one Mediator who actually gave his.

When did the exodus happen? Two dates are argued. The early date, about 1446 BC, comes from Scripture’s own count of 480 years from the exodus to the fourth year of Solomon (1 Kgs 6:1) and from Jephthah’s 300 years in the land (Judg 11:26). The late date, about 1260 BC under Rameses II, rests on the store city of Raamses (1:11) and on the archaeology of Canaan. Those who hold the early date take the Bible’s figures as given and “Raamses” as the later name for the place, as in Genesis 47:11; those who hold the late date read the 480 years as a round figure for twelve generations. Faithful scholars hold both dates; this commentary leaves the question open, since nothing in the book’s message hangs on it. On the early date the pharaoh of the exodus was probably Amenhotep II; on the late date, Rameses II. Scripture never names him: the king who claimed to be a god is simply “Pharaoh”, while two slave midwives are named (1:15). Egypt left no record of the exodus, which is not surprising, since its monuments did not record defeats. But Semites did live in the eastern delta, and by about 1210 BC an Egyptian inscription, the Merneptah stele, names Israel as a people in Canaan.

Who wrote it? Exodus says Moses wrote down events and laws (17:14; 24:4; 34:27), and Jesus calls it the book of Moses (Mark 12:26). Many modern scholars think the five books of Moses were compiled from later sources; others answer that this remains a theory, and that the substance can come from Moses with later touches such as updated place-names. This commentary takes that second view, though the question is still debated.

Were there really 600,000 men (12:37), perhaps two million people? Some read the word for “thousand” as “clan” or “unit”, making a far smaller company. But the totals are consistent throughout, and the census silver of 38:25–26 matches 603,550 men at half a shekel each exactly; that sum cannot be read as clans. The numbers are best taken as written: the fruit of the multiplication Exodus opens with (1:7), and a vast people kept by God in the wilderness for forty years.

1.title: A People Multiplied in the Furnace
1.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household:<sup>2</sup>Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah,<sup>3</sup>Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,<sup>4</sup>Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.<sup>5</sup>All the descendants of Jacob were seventy persons; Joseph was already in Egypt.<sup>6</sup>Then Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation.<sup>7</sup>But the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them.<sup>8</sup>Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.<sup>9</sup>And he said to his people, "Behold, the people of Israel are too many and too mighty for us.<sup>10</sup>Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, lest they multiply, and, if war breaks out, they join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land."<sup>11</sup>Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens. They built for Pharaoh store cities, Pithom and Raamses.<sup>12</sup>But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. And the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel.<sup>13</sup>So they ruthlessly made the people of Israel work as slaves<sup>14</sup>and made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and brick, and in all kinds of work in the field. In all their work they ruthlessly made them work as slaves.<sup>15</sup>Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah,<sup>16</sup>"When you serve as midwife to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him, but if it is a daughter, she shall live."<sup>17</sup>But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live.<sup>18</sup>So the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this, and let the male children live?"<sup>19</sup>The midwives said to Pharaoh, "Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them."<sup>20</sup>So God dealt well with the midwives. And the people multiplied and grew very strong.<sup>21</sup>And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.<sup>22</sup>Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, "Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall cast into the Nile, but you shall let every daughter live."
1.overview:
Exodus opens by tying itself back to Genesis: the names of the sons of Israel who came down to Egypt. The family of seventy has become a people. The command of Eden and the promise to Abraham are quietly being fulfilled, even under the lash.

Then comes the ominous sentence: "there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph." Pharaoh launches the first attempt in Scripture to destroy a whole people, and yet the more Egypt presses down, the more Israel spreads. Into this furnace step two unlikely heroes, the midwives Shiphrah and Puah, who fear God more than Pharaoh and quietly defy the empire.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-7: The book opens mid-sentence, tied by a conjunction to the end of Genesis. A whole generation is buried in a sentence, and then the language of Genesis 1:28 returns: in the soil of a foreign empire, God is growing a garden.
verseByVerse.theology:
From Family to Nation

The people multiply after every protector is in a tomb.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the promise to Abraham kept itself underground through generations when nothing seemed to happen.

Now: God deals in names, and his kingdom advances by ordinary generations more often than by dramatic intervention.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. All the descendants of Jacob were seventy persons; Joseph was already in Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exodus begins as the next chapter of Genesis: the God who promised Abraham a nation now knows each of Jacob’s sons by name. The Hebrew opens with “and”, joining the book to the end of Genesis, and its Hebrew title is Shemot, “Names”.

Seventy persons was the whole family (Genesis 46:27). Seventy is also the number of the nations in Genesis 10: here is a small household that will carry blessing to the world (Genesis 12:3).

Textual note. Stephen says seventy-five (Acts 7:14), following the Greek Old Testament, which counts five more descendants of Joseph. The Hebrew counts seventy. Different ways of counting, not a contradiction.

A list of names is not filler. God deals with people one by one, not as statistics (Isaiah 43:1).

In everyday life. God knows your name and your family’s story. You are not lost in the crowd.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus means “going out.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation. But the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph dies, and with him every witness to God’s providence in Genesis. The new generation has only the promise, yet God makes Israel grow so fast that they fill the land: his promise does not depend on any one protector.

The five verbs of verse 7 (fruitful, increased, multiplied, grew strong, filled) echo creation (Genesis 1:28) and the promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:2; 15:5). God is keeping his word in a foreign land, in Goshen in the eastern Nile delta, where Jacob’s family settled (Genesis 47:27).

What it does not mean. Not that numbers prove God’s blessing; Israel will soon be enslaved while still growing. Blessing and suffering run side by side.

For worship. Thank God whose promises grow quietly over centuries, even when the people who held them up are gone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-14 — The Pharaoh Who Did Not Know Joseph
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-14: One sentence swings the chapter from blessing to bondage. Pharaoh looks straight at the blessing of God and calls it a security problem, and his policy fails on the spot.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pharaoh Who Did Not Know Joseph

A new king refuses Egypt's debt to Joseph and calls God's blessing a security problem. Forced labour follows, and fails.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the bitter herbs of Passover would recall this labour every year (12:8). Now: pressure has never yet wiped out the people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new king rises, perhaps from a new dynasty, and blessing turns to bondage. The narrator never names him: the most powerful man on earth stays anonymous, while two slave midwives are named (v. 15).

Did not know Joseph. The Hebrew verb “know” means to acknowledge, to recognise a relationship, not merely to have heard of. He refused the debt: Egypt had survived the famine through a Hebrew (Genesis 41).

Where Christians differ: the date of the exodus. Some date it about 1446 BC, from 1 Kings 6:1 (480 years before Solomon’s temple). Others date it about 1260 BC, from the city name Raamses (v. 11) and archaeology. This commentary’s view: both views are held by faithful scholars. The exodus was a real event; its exact date is less certain than the fact.

In everyday life. Where gratitude is forgotten, hostility often follows. Remember what you owe to God, who has done far more for you than Joseph did for Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his people, "Behold, the people of Israel are too many and too mighty for us. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, lest they multiply, and, if war breaks out, they join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh looks at God’s blessing on Israel and sees only a threat to be managed: the fruitfulness that fulfils God’s promise looks, to unbelief, like a security problem.

To “deal shrewdly” is to act with calculating, self-protecting cunning. It echoes the crafty serpent (Genesis 3:1), and “Come, let us” echoes the builders of Babel (Genesis 11:3–4): human schemes against God’s purposes.

The fear that Israel might join Egypt’s enemies made sense to him, for Goshen lay on Egypt’s eastern frontier, the route of any invader from Canaan. And he wants their labour, not their absence; yet his fear that they will “escape from the land” foretells exactly what God will do.

Wise planning is not the sin here. The sin is planning against God and against the weak (Psalm 2:1–4).

In everyday life. When the world treats Christian growth as a threat, do not be surprised. Pray, and keep living faithfully.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens. They built for Pharaoh store cities, Pithom and Raamses. But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. And the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh sets taskmasters, overseers of forced labour gangs, over Israel to “afflict” them: to humble and crush them, the very word God used when he foretold this (Genesis 15:13). They build store cities, supply depots for grain and military stores.

But the more they are oppressed, the more they multiply. God turns the whip into the means of growth; Pharaoh is fighting God’s word, and every measure backfires. The Egyptians come to feel a sickened dread of Israel: the powerful empire is afraid of its powerless slaves.

What it does not mean. Not that suffering is good in itself, nor that God sends it without care. He uses it, as he will later use persecution to spread the church (Acts 8:1–4).

For worship. Praise God who can make opposition the very means of his people’s growth.
verseByVerse.note: Pithom and Raamses were store cities in the eastern Nile delta.

verseByVerse.quote: So they ruthlessly made the people of Israel work as slaves and made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and brick, and in all kinds of work in the field. In all their work they ruthlessly made them work as slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt makes Israel’s life bitter with crushing labour, and Scripture records the suffering in full rather than hurrying past it.

Ruthlessly. The Hebrew word (perek) means harsh, crushing severity, work meant to break a person, and it opens and closes the description. The law later forbids Israel to rule anyone this way (Leviticus 25:43, 46).

The work was in mortar and brick, mud bricks mixed with straw, the basic building material of Egypt. God does not treat his people’s pain as unimportant; he sees it and records it (3:7).

In everyday life. If your work feels crushing, tell God honestly. He sees. And if you manage others, never rule them harshly; you too have a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-22 — The Fear of God Versus the Fear of Pharaoh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 15-22: Oppression has failed, so Pharaoh turns to murder. When the midwives' fear of God defeats his secret plan, the mask comes off in a public decree.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Fear of God Versus the Fear of Pharaoh

Two midwives who fear God undo the king's plan, and God deals well with them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: two women with no power undid the king's plan. Now: "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29); the fear of God is where courage comes from.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah, "When you serve as midwife to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him, but if it is a daughter, she shall live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When labour fails, Pharaoh turns to murder, ordering the Hebrew midwives to kill every newborn boy.

Midwives helped at childbirth, a respected profession, and the two named may have led a larger group. “Hebrew midwives” may mean midwives who were Hebrews or midwives to the Hebrews; their names, “Beauty” and perhaps “Splendour”, are Semitic, so most take them as Hebrews.

The “birthstool” is literally “the two stones” on which a woman crouched to give birth: the point of greatest vulnerability.

Pharaoh wants the sons killed, not the daughters, because boys would grow into fighters and girls could be absorbed into Egypt. Behind Pharaoh, as behind Herod (Matthew 2:16), stands the enemy who tries to destroy the promised offspring (Genesis 3:15; Revelation 12:4).

The text treats the killing of infants as monstrous, and gives no support to the idea that unborn or newborn lives are less valuable.

verseByVerse.quote: But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The midwives fear God more than the king, and refuse to kill the boys. This fear is not terror but reverent awe that takes God more seriously than anyone else: the root of wisdom (Proverbs 1:7).

Their refusal is the first recorded act of civil disobedience in Scripture, and God honours it.

What it does not mean. Not a licence to disobey authorities whenever we disagree. Christians are to be subject to rulers (Romans 13:1). But when a ruler commands sin, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

In everyday life. Is there a command at work or in your culture that would require you to do wrong? The fear of God sets you free from the fear of people, and it grows not from willpower but from knowing the God who forgives (Psalm 130:4).

verseByVerse.quote: So the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this, and let the male children live?" The midwives said to Pharaoh, "Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Summoned before Pharaoh, the midwives explain that Hebrew women give birth before they arrive.

Why have you done this? Two slave women answer to the king of Egypt, knowing what failure usually costs.

“Vigorous” is literally “lively”, full of life. Their answer may have been partly true, but it was meant to mislead.

Where Christians differ: did they lie, and was it right? Some (Augustine, Calvin) hold it was a lie, a real sin that God forgave while rewarding their faith. Others argue that deceiving a murderer to save life is not the sin of lying, since he had no right to the truth. This commentary’s view: God rewards their fear of him and their protection of life (v. 20), and the second view is the more likely: deceiving those bent on murder is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids. Rahab stood in the same place, and is honoured for her faith (Hebrews 11:31). Ordinary lying is still sin (Colossians 3:9).

In everyday life. Courage under pressure matters. Pray for wisdom to protect the vulnerable without needing to deceive.

verseByVerse.quote: So God dealt well with the midwives. And the people multiplied and grew very strong. And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God does not remove the danger, but he deals well with the midwives in it, and “gave them families”: literally “made them houses”, households and descendants. Those who protected Israel’s families are given families of their own. Meanwhile Israel multiplies, and Pharaoh’s second plan fails like the first.

This is not a promise that obedience always brings children or material reward, which would wound many faithful people. It shows that God sees and honours those who fear him (Hebrews 6:10).

For worship. Thank God that no act of costly faithfulness goes unnoticed by him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, "Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall cast into the Nile, but you shall let every daughter live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh now orders all his people to throw every Hebrew baby boy into the Nile. Murder is no longer secret but public policy, a whole nation enlisted in killing.

The Nile was Egypt’s source of water, food and life, worshipped as a god (Hapi). Later the Nile will turn to blood (7:20), and Egypt’s army will drown (14:28). And Pharaoh, who lets every daughter live, underestimates women: it is women who will save Moses (2:1–10).

The chapter ends in darkness, but not in defeat. In the next verses the same river will carry the deliverer in a basket (2:3).

In everyday life. When evil seems to have the last word, keep reading. God is already at work. Pray for children at risk today, and for those who protect them.

1.theology:
The faithfulness of God to his promises. Israel's growth is God keeping his covenant with Abraham (Gen. 12, 15). No empire can cancel what God has sworn. The whole book rests on this: God remembers.

The fear of God. Shiphrah and Puah show that reverence for God is the root of moral courage. To fear God is to be set free from the tyranny of the fear of man.

Suffering and providence. God's people are not promised ease but his presence. Their affliction is real, yet it is woven into a providence that advances, not defeats, God's purposes.
1.examples:
Then: A favoured immigrant people became despised slaves under a regime that feared their numbers and sought their destruction, and was met by the quiet defiance of God-fearing women.

Now: Christians under pressure should not be surprised; the church has often grown where it is persecuted. We are called, like the midwives, to a higher allegiance, and the Spirit who lives in believers is the one who loosens the grip of the powerful's threats (2 Timothy 1:7).

2.title: Drawn Out of the Water
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Now a man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman.<sup>2</sup>The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.<sup>3</sup>When she could hide him no longer, she took for him a basket made of bulrushes and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds by the river bank.<sup>4</sup>And his sister stood at a distance to know what would be done to him.<sup>5</sup>Now the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, while her young women walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant woman, and she took it.<sup>6</sup>When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the baby was crying. She took pity on him and said, "This is one of the Hebrews' children."<sup>7</sup>Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?"<sup>8</sup>And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Go." So the girl went and called the child's mother.<sup>9</sup>And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages." So the woman took the child and nursed him.<sup>10</sup>When the child grew older, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, "Because," she said, "I drew him out of the water."<sup>11</sup>One day, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his people and looked on their burdens, and he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his people.<sup>12</sup>He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.<sup>13</sup>When he went out the next day, behold, two Hebrews were struggling together. And he said to the man in the wrong, "Why do you strike your companion?"<sup>14</sup>He answered, "Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Then Moses was afraid, and thought, "Surely the thing is known."<sup>15</sup>When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian. And he sat down by a well.<sup>16</sup>Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock.<sup>17</sup>The shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses stood up and saved them, and watered their flock.<sup>18</sup>When they came home to their father Reuel, he said, "How is it that you have come home so soon today?"<sup>19</sup>They said, "An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds and even drew water for us and watered the flock."<sup>20</sup>He said to his daughters, "Then where is he? Why have you left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread."<sup>21</sup>And Moses was content to dwell with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah.<sup>22</sup>She gave birth to a son, and he called his name Gershom, for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land."<sup>23</sup>During those many days the king of Egypt died, and the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God.<sup>24</sup>And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.<sup>25</sup>God saw the people of Israel—and God knew.
2.overview:
Against Pharaoh's death decree, God begins his rescue not with armies but with a baby in a basket. A Levite woman hides her son, then entrusts him to the very river meant to drown him, and he is drawn out of it by the daughter of the tyrant who ordered his death. God's providence is full of irony, and his hand is sovereign.

Moses grows up in two worlds, nursed by his Hebrew mother and raised in Pharaoh's palace. Then comes his own attempt to deliver Israel by force: he kills an Egyptian, is exposed, and flees to Midian. The man who tried to save Israel in his own strength must spend forty years in the wilderness learning that salvation belongs to the LORD.

The chapter closes with four of the most tender verbs in Scripture: God heard, God remembered, God saw, God knew. The silence of heaven is about to break.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — The Basket on the Nile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-10: Against a death decree, God begins his rescue with a baby. A basket, a watching sister and a princess's pity end with the child's own mother paid Egyptian wages to nurse her son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Basket on the Nile

The deliverer is saved through the waters meant for his death, in an ark like Noah's, by the tyrant's own daughter.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Hebrews calls the parents' hiding faith (Heb. 11:23). Now: God's rescues are often built out of small, ordinary things: a basket, a sister, a crying baby, every one of them bearing weight.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman. The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s answer to Pharaoh’s death decree begins quietly, with a Levite marriage and a baby. The parents come from the tribe that will later carry the priesthood, but they are not yet named: at this point they are ordinary slaves.

“A fine child” is literally “good” (tov), the word of Genesis 1 (“God saw that it was good”). Stephen calls him “beautiful in God’s sight” (Acts 7:20). His beauty is the occasion of his parents’ faith, not the reason for his worth: every child bears God’s image (Genesis 9:6).

She hid him. Hebrews 11:23 calls this faith: his parents were not afraid of the king’s edict. They trusted God and defied the order to kill.

In everyday life. God’s great works often begin in ordinary homes, with faithful parents protecting a child.
verseByVerse.note: Moses’ parents are named later as Amram and Jochebed.

verseByVerse.quote: When she could hide him no longer, she took for him a basket made of bulrushes and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds by the river bank. And his sister stood at a distance to know what would be done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When she can hide him no longer, his mother puts him in a little waterproofed ark among the reeds, and his sister watches.

The word for the basket (tevah) is used elsewhere only of Noah’s ark. Both carried God’s chosen safely through waters meant for death. And the reeds (suph) look ahead: Israel will later cross the yam suph, the “Sea of Reeds” (13:18).

The sister is probably Miriam (15:20). Faith does what it can, then watches and waits. The mother has not given up: she obeys the letter of Pharaoh’s decree, putting her son in the river, while trusting God with the outcome.

In everyday life. When you have done what you can for someone you love, entrust them to God and keep watching in hope.
verseByVerse.note: The basket was made of papyrus reeds (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, while her young women walked beside the river. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant woman, and she took it. When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the baby was crying. She took pity on him and said, "This is one of the Hebrews' children."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Of all people in Egypt, it is the daughter of the man who ordered the killing who finds the crying baby. This is providence: God’s quiet direction of ordinary events, and nothing in the account calls it coincidence. At this moment God’s weapon against Egypt is a crying baby (1 Corinthians 1:27).

She knows the decree, recognises him as one of the Hebrews’ children, and takes pity on him: she chooses mercy. God can move any heart (Proverbs 21:1).

For worship. Thank God for the times he arranged events for your good before you knew him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you?" And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Go." So the girl went and called the child's mother. And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this child away and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages." So the woman took the child and nursed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Miriam offers to find a Hebrew nurse and brings the baby’s own mother. Wet-nurses were common for royal children, and babies were nursed for two or three years.

So Pharaoh’s household pays Moses’ mother to raise her own son: God turns the death decree upside down (Psalm 2:4). In those early years she could teach him that he was a Hebrew and who Israel’s God was. Egypt would give him his education; his mother gave him his identity (Hebrews 11:24–25).

What it does not mean. Not that Miriam and Jochebed deceived the princess. The princess knew he was Hebrew (v. 6); Scripture does not say she knew who the nurse was.

In everyday life. Parents and grandparents: the early years matter. Teach children who God is, trusting him, not your skill, to give them faith.

verseByVerse.quote: When the child grew older, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, "Because," she said, "I drew him out of the water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After weaning, Jochebed keeps her word and brings him to the princess: a second, harder surrender. Adopted into the royal household, he was “instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Acts 7:22), yet privilege did not erase his identity.

“Moses” is an Egyptian name meaning “son” or “born of” (as in Thutmose), which sounds like the Hebrew mashah, “draw out”. The one drawn out of water will draw Israel out through water.

Christ in view. Another infant spared from a king who killed boys, called out of Egypt (Matthew 2:13–15). Moses is a shadow; Christ is the true deliverer.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses” sounds like the Hebrew for “draw out” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-22 — The Failed Deliverer in Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 11-22: Moses tries to deliver Israel with his own fist, is rejected, and flees. At a well in Midian he rescues again, this time without violence, and settles as a sojourner.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Failed Deliverer in Exile

Moses' own attempt at deliverance ends in rejection and exile, where God will make a shepherd of him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Stephen saw the rejected one as the appointed one. Now: seeing what God sees does not authorise acting in God's place, and long obscurity is where God makes a man.

verseByVerse.quote: One day, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his people and looked on their burdens, and he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his people. He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grown up (Stephen says forty years old, Acts 7:23), Moses goes out to his people and sees their burdens with sympathy, as God himself will “see” their affliction (3:7). Hebrews 11:24–26 calls it faith: he chose to suffer with God’s people rather than enjoy “the fleeting pleasures of sin”.

Before he strikes, he looks this way and that: he checks for witnesses but not for God’s direction, and he hides the body.

Where Christians differ: murder or justice? Some see a justified rescue: Stephen says Moses supposed his brothers would see that God was saving them by his hand (Acts 7:25). Others see a sinful killing. This commentary’s view: his compassion and his calling were real, but his method and timing were his own. The secrecy shows he knew it was not lawful. God would later deliver Israel by his power, not Moses’ fist.

In everyday life. Zeal for justice is not wrong, but good causes can tempt us to wrong methods. Ask not only “Is this right?” but “Is this God’s way?”

verseByVerse.quote: When he went out the next day, behold, two Hebrews were struggling together. And he said to the man in the wrong, "Why do you strike your companion?" He answered, "Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Then Moses was afraid, and thought, "Surely the thing is known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Next day Moses tries words, not force, rebuking the man in the wrong, and is rejected. “Who made you a prince and a judge over us?” mocks him, yet God will in fact make him Israel’s ruler and judge (18:13; Acts 7:35). Like Joseph before him and Christ after him, Moses is rejected first by his own people (John 1:11).

The child whose parents were not afraid of the king is now afraid for his life. The fear of man is a snare (Proverbs 29:25).

In everyday life. If you are rejected when you try to make peace, you walk the road of Moses and of Christ. Keep loving.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh heard of it, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian. And he sat down by a well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses flees to Midian, a desert region east of the Gulf of Aqaba, beyond Egypt’s reach. In one day he loses position, home and plans. (Hebrews 11:27 says he left Egypt “not being afraid of the anger of the king”, probably looking ahead to the exodus itself.)

He sits down by a well. In Genesis, wells are where God’s story turns, as with Rebekah (Genesis 24) and Rachel (Genesis 29): something new is about to begin.

In everyday life. When your plans collapse, God has not lost track of you. The wilderness can be his school.
verseByVerse.note: The Midianites descended from Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock. The shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses stood up and saved them, and watered their flock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priest of Midian is Reuel, also called Jethro (3:1), who will later bless Israel’s God (18:10–11). When shepherds bully his daughters, Moses “saved them”: the verb yasha is the root of the names Joshua and Jesus. This time he rescues without violence, and then serves, watering their flock. His instinct for justice is God-given; it is being trained.

In everyday life. Who is being pushed aside near you? Stand up for them, and then help practically, as the God who saw Israel’s affliction came down for you.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came home to their father Reuel, he said, "How is it that you have come home so soon today?" They said, "An Egyptian delivered us out of the hand of the shepherds and even drew water for us and watered the flock." He said to his daughters, "Then where is he? Why have you left the man? Call him, that he may eat bread."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejected by his own people, Moses is now taken for “an Egyptian” by strangers. He belongs nowhere. Yet Reuel says, “Call him, that he may eat bread”: sharing a meal meant welcome and protection, and God feeds his fugitive servant through an ordinary act of kindness.

In everyday life. Invite someone to eat. You may be God’s provision for a lonely stranger (Hebrews 13:2).
verseByVerse.note: Moses’ father-in-law is called Reuel here and Jethro elsewhere; men often had more than one name or title.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses was content to dwell with the man, and he gave Moses his daughter Zipporah. She gave birth to a son, and he called his name Gershom, for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is content to settle. The man who left a palace now lives quietly as a shepherd for about forty years (Acts 7:29–30). He marries Zipporah (“bird”), a Midianite, a detail that will matter later (Numbers 12:1), and names his son for his homelessness: “I have been a sojourner in a foreign land.”

These were not wasted years. God was preparing a shepherd to lead his flock through the wilderness (Psalm 77:20).

In everyday life. If you are in a long, quiet season, God is not idle. Believers are sojourners too, looking for a better country (Hebrews 11:13–16).
verseByVerse.note: “Gershom” sounds like the Hebrew for “sojourner” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-25 — God Heard, Remembered, Saw, Knew
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 23-25: The king dies, and nothing improves; Israel's cry rises to God, and four verbs answer that are the hinge of the entire book.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Heard, Remembered, Saw, Knew

God answers groaning out of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the rescue rests on a promise to men long dead, not on Israel's worth. Now: God counts even wordless groaning as prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: During those many days the king of Egypt died, and the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Years pass, and the king dies, but slavery goes on: tyrants die, and tyranny continues. Hope does not lie in a change of ruler.

Israel’s groaning is not polished prayer but the cry of pain. The text does not say they called on God by name, yet the cry “came up to God”. God does not answer only eloquent or theologically correct prayers; he hears wordless groans (Romans 8:26).

In everyday life. If all you can manage today is a groan, bring it to God. He hears.

verseByVerse.quote: And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. God saw the people of Israel—and God knew.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After two chapters of silence, God himself becomes the subject of every verb: he heard, remembered, saw and knew. These four verbs turn the book.

For God to “remember” does not mean he had forgotten; in Scripture it means he acts on his promise (Genesis 8:1; Luke 1:72). His covenant is a binding relationship sealed by his oath: he had promised Abraham that his offspring would be enslaved four hundred years and then brought out with great possessions (Genesis 15:13–14). Rescue rests on God’s promise, not Israel’s merit.

“God knew” has no object in the Hebrew: he knew everything about them, personally and with care.

What it does not mean. Not that God was absent before. He was at work in midwives, a basket and a princess. Now he acts openly.

For worship. Thank God that he hears, remembers, sees and knows you, because of his covenant in Christ.

2.theology:
Providence. An unseen hand governs every detail, bending Pharaoh's own household toward Israel's rescue.

The weakness of the flesh. Moses' violent attempt at deliverance, made too soon, must fail so that God's deliverance may stand. Salvation is the LORD's, not the deliverer's.

Covenant remembrance. God's saving acts flow from his faithfulness to his covenant, not from Israel's worthiness.
2.examples: Now: God still uses long, hidden seasons to empty us of self-confidence and fit us for his service. And he still hears the cry of his afflicted people; our groaning is never lost in the silence.

3.title: I AM WHO I AM
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Moses was keeping the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, the priest of Midian, and he led his flock to the west side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.<sup>2</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed.<sup>3</sup>And Moses said, "I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned."<sup>4</sup>When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, "Moses, Moses!" And he said, "Here I am."<sup>5</sup>Then he said, "Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground."<sup>6</sup>And he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.<sup>7</sup>Then the LORD said, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings,<sup>8</sup>and I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>9</sup>And now, behold, the cry of the people of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them.<sup>10</sup>Come, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt."<sup>11</sup>But Moses said to God, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?"<sup>12</sup>He said, "But I will be with you, and this shall be the sign for you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain."<sup>13</sup>Then Moses said to God, "If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?"<sup>14</sup>God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"<sup>15</sup>God also said to Moses, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations.<sup>16</sup>Go and gather the elders of Israel together and say to them, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, has appeared to me, saying, "I have observed you and what has been done to you in Egypt,<sup>17</sup>and I promise that I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey."'<sup>18</sup>And they will listen to your voice, and you and the elders of Israel shall go to the king of Egypt and say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us; and now, please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.'<sup>19</sup>But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand.<sup>20</sup>So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders that I will do in it; after that he will let you go.<sup>21</sup>And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians; and when you go, you shall not go empty,<sup>22</sup>but each woman shall ask of her neighbor, and any woman who lives in her house, for silver and gold jewelry, and for clothing. You shall put them on your sons and on your daughters. So you shall plunder the Egyptians."
3.overview:
An eighty-year-old shepherd, long since written off, turns aside to see a bush that burns but is not consumed, and meets the living God. The fire is a parable of God himself: blazing in holiness, yet not destroying; full of glory, yet stooping to speak with a fugitive at the far edge of the desert.

God reveals his compassion before he reveals his name: "I have surely seen... I have heard... I have come down to deliver." The God of the burning bush is also the God who bends to the cries of slaves. Then comes the name above all names, "I AM WHO I AM": the eternal, unchanging God who depends on nothing and on whom all things depend.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-6: Forty years into obscurity, keeping another man's sheep, Moses stops to look at a bush that burns without being consumed. God's first instruction is not an errand but a boundary, and his first word after four centuries of silence ties Moses to the fathers.
verseByVerse.theology:
Holy Ground

The God who calls Moses by name is holy, and he is the God of the fathers.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jesus proved the resurrection from the present tense of verse 6 (Matt. 22:32). Now: God found Moses at ordinary work, and asked first not for competence but for reverence.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses was keeping the flock of his father-in-law, Jethro, the priest of Midian, and he led his flock to the west side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great commission begins with a shepherd minding his father-in-law’s sheep. The former prince is now a hired hand for a foreigner: forty years in Egypt, forty in Midian (Acts 7:23, 30). Jethro is another name or title for Reuel (2:18).

“The west side of the wilderness” is literally “behind the wilderness”, the far side, where shepherds went when nearer grazing ran out. Moses is not seeking God; God comes to him at Horeb, another name for Sinai. The Midian years were not wasted: God was training a shepherd for his people (Psalm 77:20).

In everyday life. If you think your useful years are behind you, God meets people in the middle of ordinary work.
verseByVerse.note: Jethro’s name probably means “excellence.”

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed. And Moses said, "I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The angel of the LORD appears in a fire in a thornbush that burns without burning up, and Moses turns aside to look.

In Scripture fire is a sign of God’s holy presence: the torch at Abraham’s covenant (Genesis 15:17), the pillar of fire (13:21), Sinai (19:18), Pentecost (Acts 2:3). Ordinary fire needs fuel; this fire needs nothing, a picture of the God who depends on nothing, whose name will be given in v. 14. Some also see Israel in the bush, afflicted but not destroyed. And the bush (seneh) is a worthless thorny shrub: God chose the humblest pulpit.

“Angel” means “messenger”, but here the one in the bush speaks as God himself (vv. 4–6).

Where Christians differ: who is the angel? Some take him as a created angel speaking for God. Many from the early church fathers to the Reformers have seen the Son of God appearing before his incarnation. This commentary’s view: he is identified with God, and speaks as God, so he is no ordinary angel. Seeing an appearance of the Son is a reasonable reading, though the text does not say so directly.

In everyday life. Turn aside when God catches your attention, in his word above all.
verseByVerse.note: Horeb is another name for Mount Sinai.

verseByVerse.quote: When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, "Moses, Moses!" And he said, "Here I am." Then he said, "Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God calls Moses by name, doubled, as he called Abraham (Genesis 22:11) and Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10): personal and urgent. Moses answers hinneni, “Here I am”, which speaks not of location but of readiness to serve.

Yet God invites and restrains in the same breath: “Do not come near.” He is near but not casual. Holy means set apart, belonging to God, pure; the dirt is ordinary, but it is holy because God is present. Removing sandals showed reverence and humility (Joshua 5:15).

What it does not mean. Not that some places today are holier for worship. In Christ, God meets his people anywhere in Spirit and truth (John 4:21–24), yet reverence is still due (Hebrews 12:28–29).

For worship. Come to God both boldly and humbly: called by name, aware of his holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God introduces himself by his covenant relationship: the God of Moses’ father, and of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who made promises to these men and keeps them.

Jesus’ use. Jesus quoted this to the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection (Matthew 22:31–32). His argument rests on the covenant: the faithful God binds himself to these men as their God, so death cannot be the end of them. He is not the God of the dead but of the living.

Moses hides his face, afraid to look at God, for sinful people cannot see God’s face and live (33:20). This is not cringing terror of a cruel God but the right awe of a creature before the Holy One (Isaiah 6:5). Later Moses will ask to see God’s glory (33:18), and on another mountain he will stand with Jesus in glory (Luke 9:30–31).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-12 — I Have Come Down to Deliver
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 7-12: God states the movement that governs everything he does about human ruin: he has come down to deliver. And he does it by sending a man, answering Moses' honest objection with his presence and with a sign that can only be checked at the far end.
verseByVerse.theology:
I Have Come Down to Deliver

The God who has come down sends Moses, and answers his inadequacy with his presence.
verseByVerse.examples: Now: Christ sends his people as the Father sent him, and goes with them (Matt. 28:20; John 20:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings, and I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and broad land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the place of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seen, heard, know, come down: four verbs that answer 2:24–25. God is not distant from suffering.

Why so long? God had foretold four hundred years of affliction (Genesis 15:13), partly to wait until “the iniquity of the Amorites” was full (Genesis 15:16). His timing joins patience with the Canaanites and faithfulness to Israel.

“I have come down” is God’s pattern: he came down at Babel (Genesis 11:5), at Sinai (19:20), and finally in the incarnation (John 1:14).

“Milk and honey” means rich pasture for herds and wildflowers for bees: a fertile land of plenty. Its peoples, the Canaanites and the rest, are those whose land God will judge for their sin (Leviticus 18:24–25).

Suffering does not mean God approves of it or has forgotten. He sees, and acts in his time.

For worship. Thank the God who came down in Christ to deliver you.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, behold, the cry of the people of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them. Come, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s coming down (v. 8) and his sending of Moses belong together: God works through the people he sends. And Israel is “my people”, belonging to God, not to Pharaoh. That claim is the whole contest of the plagues.

God does not depend on Moses, nor will Moses do it in his own strength. God is the deliverer; Moses is his instrument.

In everyday life. When you pray for God to act in a situation, be ready for him to send you.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to God, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the children of Israel out of Egypt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who am I? An honest question from a fugitive whose last attempt at rescue failed. Forty years earlier he went in his own strength; now he has no confidence at all.

God does not tell Moses how capable he is. He says, “I will be with you” (v. 12). The question is not who Moses is but who God is.

Humility is not wrong, but self-doubt can become an excuse for disobedience (4:13–14). Gideon (Judges 6:15) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:6) raised the same objection.

In everyday life. When you feel inadequate for what God asks, do not try to talk yourself up. Look to his presence (2 Corinthians 3:5).

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "But I will be with you, and this shall be the sign for you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“I will be with you” is ehyeh immak in Hebrew, and “I will be” (ehyeh) is the verb God will use for his name in v. 14.

A sign confirms God’s word, but strangely this one comes after the mission: Israel will worship on this mountain. Faith must go first and see later. God does give Moses signs beforehand in chapter 4, but the deepest confirmation comes through obedience.

To “serve” God is to worship him. The goal of the exodus is not only freedom from Pharaoh but service to God (4:23), fulfilled at Sinai (19:1–2).

For worship. The same promise is given to the church: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-22: God gives his name, to be spoken for ever and tied to three men with biographies. Then he tells Moses the end before the beginning: the elders will listen, Pharaoh will refuse until compelled, the plagues are announced before one has fallen, and Israel will not leave empty.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Name: I AM

God reveals his name, and tells Moses beforehand how the contest with Pharaoh will end.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the plunder was back wages for generations of unpaid work. Now: Jesus took the name on himself: "before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to God, "If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' what shall I say to them?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is his name? In Scripture a name expresses character. Israel had lived for centuries in Egypt among many named gods. Which God is this, and what is he like?

A lever? In the ancient world, knowing a god’s name was thought to give power over him in ritual. God will reveal his name, but not as something to control.

Israel did know the God of their fathers; they needed to know him more fully as the one who acts to save (6:2–3).

verseByVerse.quote: God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh comes from the verb “to be”.

Everything else depends on something else; God depends on nothing. He simply is, unchanging and eternal (Psalm 90:2; Malachi 3:6). This is the fire that needs no fuel. In context the name also means: I will be with you, and I will be all I have promised (v. 12). And it cannot be used to manipulate him: he will be who he will be.

Jesus. “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). His hearers took up stones, understanding the claim to be God.

This is not an abstract idea of “being”, but the name of the living, personal God who acts for his people.

For worship. Everything you have you received. Worship the one who received nothing and gives everything (Acts 17:25).
verseByVerse.note: “I AM WHO I AM” may also be rendered “I will be what I will be” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: God also said to Moses, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his personal covenant name, the LORD, as his name for ever. Small capitals in English Bibles stand for the Hebrew YHWH, probably pronounced Yahweh, formed from the verb “to be” in v. 14. Out of reverence Jews later read it aloud as Adonai, “Lord”.

The eternal God ties his name to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, flawed men with real histories: he is the God of sinners he has chosen and kept. His name is to be “remembered”, called upon in worship; he wants to be known and named. It is not a magic word, and not a name to use lightly (20:7).

In everyday life. Call on the LORD by name today. He has given it so that you may.
verseByVerse.note: Jews still often say “HaShem,” “the Name,” in place of the divine name.

verseByVerse.quote: Go and gather the elders of Israel together and say to them, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, has appeared to me, saying, "I have observed you and what has been done to you in Egypt, and I promise that I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey."'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is to gather the elders, the heads of Israel’s families and tribes. “I have observed you” translates paqad: to visit, to attend to with purpose. Joseph had promised, “God will visit you” (Genesis 50:24–25), using the same word, and it is now happening.

God repeats the promise of the land from v. 8, because discouraged people need to hear it twice. And he gives Moses the words; this is not a message Moses invents.

verseByVerse.quote: And they will listen to your voice, and you and the elders of Israel shall go to the king of Egypt and say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us; and now, please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.' But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand. So I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders that I will do in it; after that he will let you go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“The God of the Hebrews” is a name Pharaoh could understand: the God of this foreign people.

Is the request for a three days’ journey to worship deceptive, since God means to bring them out for good? An opening request is not a lie: it tests Pharaoh with a small, reasonable demand, and his refusal of even that exposes his heart (5:2).

Before any plague falls, God tells Moses the outcome: his “mighty hand” will compel Pharaoh through wonders, the plagues of chapters 7–12. The delays will not mean God is losing.

What it does not mean. Not that Pharaoh is a puppet. He refuses freely, and God also hardens him (see 4:21).

In everyday life. When opposition seems strong, remember that God has already said how the story ends.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians; and when you go, you shall not go empty, but each woman shall ask of her neighbor, and any woman who lives in her house, for silver and gold jewelry, and for clothing. You shall put them on your sons and on your daughters. So you shall plunder the Egyptians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will give Israel favour, making the Egyptians willing to give (12:36). The verb is sha’al, to ask or request; the King James “borrow” misled readers into thinking it was a trick. It was a request, freely granted.

So Israel will “plunder the Egyptians” like soldiers taking spoil, but without a battle: back wages for generations of unpaid slavery. The law later required freed slaves to be sent away generously (Deuteronomy 15:13–14), and God had promised this to Abraham (Genesis 15:14). It is not theft, nor licence to take others’ goods, but God’s justice for the oppressed.

A warning ahead. This gold will be used both for the golden calf (32:2–4) and for the tabernacle (35:22). Gifts can serve idols or God.

For worship. Use what God has given you for his worship, not for idols.

3.theology:
The holiness of God. The fire, the holy ground and the hidden face all proclaim that God is set apart, approachable only on his own terms.

God depends on nothing. "I AM WHO I AM" reveals a God who simply is: self-existent, eternal, unchanging, the source of all being. (Theologians call this his aseity.)

The compassion of God. The holy I AM is also the God who has seen, heard and come down. Holiness and mercy meet in the bush as they will meet at the cross.
3.examples: Now: The same I AM meets us in Christ. When we feel inadequate to our calling, the answer is not our record but his presence, by the Spirit he has given (John 14:16–17). The God who is enough has promised to be with us.

4.title: The Sufficiency of God in Our Weakness
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Moses answered, "But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice, for they will say, 'The LORD did not appear to you.'"<sup>2</sup>The LORD said to him, "What is that in your hand?" He said, "A staff."<sup>3</sup>And he said, "Throw it on the ground." So he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses ran from it.<sup>4</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Put out your hand and catch it by the tail"—so he put out his hand and caught it, and it became a staff in his hand—<sup>5</sup>"that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you."<sup>6</sup>Again, the LORD said to him, "Put your hand inside your cloak." And he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous like snow.<sup>7</sup>Then God said, "Put your hand back inside your cloak." So he put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, it was restored like the rest of his flesh.<sup>8</sup>"If they will not believe you," God said, "or listen to the first sign, they may believe the latter sign.<sup>9</sup>If they will not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, you shall take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground, and the water that you shall take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground."<sup>10</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent, either in the past or since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and of tongue."<sup>11</sup>Then the LORD said to him, "Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?<sup>12</sup>Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak."<sup>13</sup>But he said, "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else."<sup>14</sup>Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses and he said, "Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. Behold, he is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.<sup>15</sup>You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth and will teach you both what to do.<sup>16</sup>He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him.<sup>17</sup>And take in your hand this staff, with which you shall do the signs."<sup>18</sup>Moses went back to Jethro his father-in-law and said to him, "Please let me go back to my brothers in Egypt to see whether they are still alive." And Jethro said to Moses, "Go in peace."<sup>19</sup>And the LORD said to Moses in Midian, "Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead."<sup>20</sup>So Moses took his wife and his sons and had them ride on a donkey, and went back to the land of Egypt. And Moses took the staff of God in his hand.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "When you go back to Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the miracles that I have put in your power. But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go.<sup>22</sup>Then you shall say to Pharaoh, 'Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son,<sup>23</sup>and I say to you, "Let my son go that he may serve me." If you refuse to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.'"<sup>24</sup>At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death.<sup>25</sup>Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, "Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!"<sup>26</sup>So he let him alone. It was then that she said, "A bridegroom of blood," because of the circumcision.<sup>27</sup>The LORD said to Aaron, "Go into the wilderness to meet Moses." So he went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him.<sup>28</sup>And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him to speak, and all the signs that he had commanded him to do.<sup>29</sup>Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the people of Israel.<sup>30</sup>Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses and did the signs in the sight of the people.<sup>31</sup>And the people believed; and when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshiped.
4.overview: Moses meets God's call with excuses: they won't believe me; I'm not eloquent; send someone else. God answers each not by flattering Moses but by showing more of himself: his power over signs, his lordship over the human mouth, his promise to be present. Even his anger at Moses' refusal bends toward grace. The chapter also brings a staggering phrase, "Israel is my firstborn son": the exodus is a Father reclaiming his child so that he may worship him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — Three Signs for a Doubting Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-9: To Moses' third objection God answers with three signs: the staff, the leprous hand, and Nile water turned to blood.
verseByVerse.theology:
Three Signs for a Doubting Servant

Each sign is a credential, showing Israel that the LORD has truly appeared to Moses.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: each sign previews a front on which Egypt will fall — its power, its flesh, its river. Now: God is not stingy with a servant who is struggling to believe.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses answered, "But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice, for they will say, 'The LORD did not appear to you.'" The LORD said to him, "What is that in your hand?" He said, "A staff."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will not believe me. This is Moses' third objection, and it contradicts what God had already told him: that the elders would listen (3:18).

What is that in your hand? Only a shepherd’s staff, an ordinary stick worn by forty years of use. God begins with what Moses already has.

The staff of God. By v. 20 it bears that name. It will divide the sea (14:16), bring water from the rock (17:5–6) and be raised over Israel’s battle (17:9).

The stick itself had no power. Power belongs to God, who chooses to work through ordinary means, and so your skills, your work and your home can become instruments in his service too.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Throw it on the ground." So he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses ran from it. But the LORD said to Moses, "Put out your hand and catch it by the tail"—so he put out his hand and caught it, and it became a staff in his hand— "that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By the tail. Anyone who handles snakes knows this is the most dangerous grip. Moses has just run from the serpent; now he must reach for it in plain obedience.

Egypt’s serpent. The cobra (uraeus) on Pharaoh’s crown symbolised his royal power and divine protection. God shows that Egypt’s emblem is in his hand. When Aaron’s staff swallows the magicians’ staffs (7:12) the point is made again.

This is no model for handling snakes in worship. Signs served a particular moment of God’s revelation, and Mark 16:18 is no command to test God (Matthew 4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Again, the LORD said to him, "Put your hand inside your cloak." And he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous like snow. Then God said, "Put your hand back inside your cloak." So he put his hand back inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, it was restored like the rest of his flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Leprous like snow. The skin turned white and flaky. Such diseases made a person unclean and cut off from the community (Leviticus 13). When the hand is restored, Moses learns that God can wound and heal (Deuteronomy 32:39), and he learns it in his own flesh before he shows God’s power to anyone else.

Christ in view. Jesus touched a leper and made him clean (Mark 1:40–42): the power shown here at work in person.

Thank God, who cleanses what is unclean, including you (1 John 1:7).
verseByVerse.note: “Leprous” covers several skin diseases (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "If they will not believe you," God said, "or listen to the first sign, they may believe the latter sign. If they will not believe even these two signs or listen to your voice, you shall take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground, and the water that you shall take from the Nile will become blood on the dry ground."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers unbelief with patience: a third sign rather than a rebuke.

The Nile. Egypt’s lifeblood and a god (Hapi). Turning it to blood shows that the LORD rules what Egypt worships, and previews the first plague (7:17–21).

These are not magic tricks to impress. Signs point beyond themselves to the God who sends Moses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 10-17: Moses pleads slowness of speech, then asks God to send someone else; God's anger burns, and Aaron, already on his way, becomes Moses' mouth.
verseByVerse.theology:
"Who Made Man's Mouth?"

God's answer to weakness is his presence, and even his anger at refusal comes with a gift.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the prophet is a mouth carrying a word he did not invent. Now: God speaks at last by his Son, who needs no Aaron (Heb. 1:1-2), and the Spirit teaches his people what to say (Luke 12:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the LORD, "Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent, either in the past or since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and of tongue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not eloquent is literally “not a man of words”. Being slow of speech and of tongue may mean a speech difficulty, or rusty Egyptian after forty years in Midian.

Then and now. Stephen says that in Egypt Moses was “mighty in his words and deeds” (Acts 7:22). The confident young man is gone.

God does not use only gifted speakers. Paul too came “in weakness” and not with lofty words (1 Corinthians 2:1–5). If you feel unable to speak for Christ, you are in good company: God supplies what he asks.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to him, "Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has made man’s mouth? God is the Creator of every ability and disability. Nothing about Moses’ speech is outside his rule.

Mute, deaf, seeing, blind. God claims sovereignty even over disability. This is hard, but it is also comfort: disability is not a sign that God has looked away (John 9:1–3).

This does not mean that disability is a punishment for personal sin, nor that God is indifferent to suffering. Christ healed the blind and deaf as signs of the coming kingdom, where every body will be made whole (Isaiah 35:5–6).

I will be with your mouth. The answer is God’s presence, not Moses’ improvement. Jesus promised the same to disciples on trial (Matthew 10:19–20).

Before a hard conversation, pray: “Lord, be with my mouth.”

verseByVerse.quote: But he said, "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else." Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses and he said, "Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well. Behold, he is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you, he will be glad in his heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Please send someone else. Now there is no reason left, only reluctance; humility has become refusal. The anger of the LORD is his holy displeasure at persistent unwillingness. His patience is great, but not endless.

Aaron, your brother, the Levite, was three years older than Moses (7:7), and he was already on his way: God’s provision came before Moses' refusal.

God does not withdraw his call when we resist. Even in anger he remains merciful (Psalm 103:8–10). Is there something God has made clear which you are hoping he will give to someone else? He met Moses' reluctance with a brother at his side, and he still sends help with the task.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth and will teach you both what to do. He shall speak for you to the people, and he shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him. And take in your hand this staff, with which you shall do the signs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put the words in his mouth. The pattern of prophecy: God gives the word, the prophet passes it on unchanged (7:1; Deuteronomy 18:18; Jeremiah 1:9).

As God to him. Moses will stand to Aaron as God stands to a prophet, as the source of the message; it does not mean Moses is divine.

This was a second best. Moses refused God’s offer to be his mouth and received a middleman. Aaron will later lead Israel into idolatry (32:1–6).

Christ in view. In the last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2), with no gap between word and speaker.

Moses is to carry the staff as the sign of God’s authority.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-31 — Return to Egypt and the Firstborn Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 18-31: Moses sets out with the staff of God; God names Israel his firstborn; at a lodging place blood turns death away; Aaron meets Moses, and the people believe and worship.
verseByVerse.theology:
Return to Egypt and the Firstborn Son

The Father claims his son, and his messenger must first keep the covenant sign at home.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: blood on the household turns death away, a Passover in miniature. Now: God did not spare his own firstborn Son (Rom. 8:32), and worship, not a change of address, was always the goal.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses went back to Jethro his father-in-law and said to him, "Please let me go back to my brothers in Egypt to see whether they are still alive." And Jethro said to Moses, "Go in peace." And the LORD said to Moses in Midian, "Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life are dead." So Moses took his wife and his sons and had them ride on a donkey, and went back to the land of Egypt. And Moses took the staff of God in his hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To see whether they are still alive. Moses gives a modest reason and asks his father-in-law's leave, honouring family even while following God’s call. Jethro blesses him with shalom, wholeness and well-being.

All the men are dead. God removes the fear Moses did not voice. Matthew echoes it when the angel tells Joseph to return from Egypt because those who sought the child’s life are dead (Matthew 2:20).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "When you go back to Egypt, see that you do before Pharaoh all the miracles that I have put in your power. But I will harden his heart, so that he will not let the people go. Then you shall say to Pharaoh, 'Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son, and I say to you, "Let my son go that he may serve me." If you refuse to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Harden his heart. The heart is the centre of will and thought. To harden it is to make it stubborn and unresponsive. Exodus says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart (8:15, 32) and that God hardened it (9:12; 10:20).

Where Christians differ. Some hold that God only confirmed what Pharaoh chose. Others hold that God actively hardened him for his own purposes, while Pharaoh remained guilty. This commentary’s view: both are taught. God hands Pharaoh over to the hardness he chooses, and in his sovereignty uses it to display his power (9:16; Romans 9:17–18). Pharaoh is never a puppet; he is fully responsible.

My firstborn son. This is the first time Israel is called God’s son. The firstborn is the heir, specially loved, and God claims Israel as his own family.

I will kill your firstborn son. The judgment fits the crime, for Egypt drowned Israel’s sons (1:22).

Christ in view. “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:1) is fulfilled in Jesus, the true Son (Matthew 2:15), whose Father gave his own firstborn to save others (Romans 8:32).
verseByVerse.note: Israel is God’s firstborn son — the background to the last plague.

verseByVerse.quote: At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death. Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, "Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!" So he let him alone. It was then that she said, "A bridegroom of blood," because of the circumcision.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hard passage. The Hebrew pronouns are unclear: it may be Moses or his son who is threatened. Its centre is clear enough.

Why? Moses had failed to circumcise his son, the sign God gave Abraham of belonging to his covenant people (Genesis 17:10–14). The one sent to say “Israel is my son” had not given his own son the covenant sign.

Zipporah uses a flint, a sharp stone knife still used for circumcision in Joshua's day (Joshua 5:2). A bridegroom of blood is an obscure phrase; perhaps she means that by this blood she has her husband back from death.

Passover in view. A household under sentence of death, blood applied, and the LORD lets him alone: the pattern of chapter 12.

God is not capricious here. He takes his covenant seriously, above all with his leaders (James 3:1). Leaders must keep at home what they preach in public, and where they have failed, the covenant blood that covered Moses is still the way back.
verseByVerse.note: A hard passage: Moses had apparently failed to circumcise his son, the sign of the covenant he was about to lead.
