verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Aaron, "Go into the wilderness to meet Moses." So he went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him. And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him to speak, and all the signs that he had commanded him to do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The brothers meet at the mountain of God, Horeb, where the bush burned and where the law will be given, and greet each other warmly after forty years apart.

All the words. Moses passes on everything. The first task of God’s messengers is to hear and hand on the whole message (Acts 20:27).

Thank God for the brothers and sisters he sends to share your work.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered together all the elders of the people of Israel. Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses and did the signs in the sight of the people. And the people believed; and when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people believed, which is exactly what Moses said would not happen (v. 1). His fear was wrong; God’s word was right.

Visited. Hebrew paqad, as in 3:16: God has come to act for them, as Joseph promised (Genesis 50:24).

Bowed their heads and worshiped. They worship before deliverance: they are still slaves, but they trust God’s word and adore him. We too may worship God for what he has promised before we see it.

Their faith was not yet mature. Within a chapter they will turn on Moses when life gets harder (5:21); faith must be tested.

4.theology:
The sufficiency of God in human weakness. God's call rests on his power, not the servant's gifts, and "Who made man's mouth?" silences every excuse.

Divine sovereignty. God claims authority over speech, disability, Pharaoh's heart and the outcome of history. Nothing lies outside his rule.

Redemption for worship. "Let my son go that he may serve me." Salvation's goal is not mere liberation but the worship of God.
4.examples:
Then: A reluctant shepherd, full of excuses, was sent to confront a superpower, assured only that the God who made his mouth would go with him.

Now: When God calls us beyond our competence, the question is never "Am I able?" but "Is God able?" Our weakness is the stage for his strength. And we are redeemed not for ourselves but to serve and worship our Redeemer.

5.title: When Obedience Makes Things Worse
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'"<sup>2</sup>But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go."<sup>3</sup>Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword."<sup>4</sup>But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens."<sup>5</sup>And Pharaoh said, "Behold, the people of the land are now many, and you make them rest from their burdens!"<sup>6</sup>The same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen,<sup>7</sup>"You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves.<sup>8</sup>But the number of bricks that they made in the past you shall impose on them, you shall by no means reduce it, for they are idle. Therefore they cry, 'Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God.'<sup>9</sup>Let heavier work be laid on the men that they may labor at it and pay no regard to lying words."<sup>10</sup>So the taskmasters and the foremen of the people went out and said to the people, "Thus says Pharaoh, 'I will not give you straw.<sup>11</sup>Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least.'"<sup>12</sup>So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.<sup>13</sup>The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw."<sup>14</sup>And the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and were asked, "Why have you not done all your task of making bricks today and yesterday, as in the past?"<sup>15</sup>Then the foremen of the people of Israel came and cried to Pharaoh, "Why do you treat your servants like this?<sup>16</sup>No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people."<sup>17</sup>But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.'<sup>18</sup>Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks."<sup>19</sup>The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble when they said, "You shall by no means reduce your number of bricks, your daily task each day."<sup>20</sup>They met Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them, as they came out from Pharaoh;<sup>21</sup>and they said to them, "The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."<sup>22</sup>Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me?<sup>23</sup>For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."
5.overview:
The first confrontation goes badly. Moses and Aaron deliver God's word, and Pharaoh answers with the question that defines all rebellion: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" Then he doubles the burden: the Israelites must gather their own straw and meet the same quota of bricks.

Obedience to God makes things, for the moment, far worse. The foremen turn on Moses, and Moses turns to God: "Why did you ever send me?" Every believer walks this valley sometimes, when doing right brings not relief but trouble.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-9: The first Thus says the LORD spoken to Pharaoh, his answer Who is the LORD?, and a work order in place of theology: straw withdrawn, quota kept.
verseByVerse.theology:
"Who Is the LORD?"

Pharaoh will not bow to the God of slaves, and treats worship as idleness and God's word as lies.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the question is answered over ten chapters, until his own army cries "the LORD fights for them" (14:25). Now: the world still treats devotion as a symptom of too little work.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'" But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus says the LORD is the formula of a royal messenger, used hundreds of times by the prophets: the words carry the authority of the one who sent them.

Let my people go, because Israel belongs to God, not to Pharaoh. The feast is a pilgrimage festival, for the goal of freedom is worship (3:12).

Who is the LORD? Pharaoh, himself honoured as a god, does not recognise Israel’s God. “I do not know” uses the same verb as 1:8: it is not ignorance of facts but refusal to acknowledge.

Pharaoh’s ignorance does not excuse him. By the end he will say, “The LORD is in the right” (9:27), and Egypt will know that he is the LORD (14:4).

People still ask, “Who is God, that I should obey him?” The best answer is the story of what he has done.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword." But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens." And Pharaoh said, "Behold, the people of the land are now many, and you make them rest from their burdens!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of the Hebrews has met with us. They speak in terms Pharaoh can grasp, of a foreign people’s God. The fear of pestilence or sword shows that serving God is not optional; neglecting his worship is dangerous.

Pharaoh sees only lost labour. To him worship is wasted work time.

You make them rest. Hebrew shabat, the root of “Sabbath”. Pharaoh resents rest. God will later command Sabbath rest as a memorial of freedom from Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15).

Work is good, but life is more than production. If your employer, or your own drive, treats rest and worship as waste, remember who you belong to.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen, "You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves. But the number of bricks that they made in the past you shall impose on them, you shall by no means reduce it, for they are idle. Therefore they cry, 'Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God.' Let heavier work be laid on the men that they may labor at it and pay no regard to lying words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without straw supplied, the workers had to find their own while making the same number of bricks.

They are idle, that is, lazy. Pharaoh treats a desire to worship as laziness, and heavier work as the cure.

God’s message, confirmed by signs, is dismissed as lying words.

Why did God let this happen? Had Israel been released at once, they might have left thinking Pharaoh had been kind. Things get worse so that it will be clear who freed them (6:6–7).

Obedience does not always make things easier at first. Sometimes it makes them harder (John 16:33).
verseByVerse.note: Chopped straw mixed into the mud bound the bricks and helped them set.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 10-21: The order travels down the chain; the Israelite foremen are beaten for the impossible quota, appeal to Pharaoh in vain, and turn on Moses and Aaron.
verseByVerse.theology:
Bricks Without Straw

Oppression sets the oppressed against their deliverer.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the foremen cursed the men God sent to free them. Now: Christ too came to his own and was not received (John 1:11), and went on delivering those who shouted against him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the taskmasters and the foremen of the people went out and said to the people, "Thus says Pharaoh, 'I will not give you straw. Go and get your straw yourselves wherever you can find it, but your work will not be reduced in the least.'" So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egyptian taskmasters stood above, with Israelite foremen beneath them, responsible for the quotas.

Thus says Pharaoh. The same formula as “Thus says the LORD” (v. 1). Two kings are now speaking in Egypt; the question is whose word will stand.

Stubble, the stalks left in a field after harvest, was poorer than straw and harder to collect. The people God has just called his son are scattered and exhausted, an old tactic of oppression.

When competing voices claim your obedience, ask whose word carries final authority.

verseByVerse.quote: The taskmasters were urgent, saying, "Complete your work, your daily task each day, as when there was straw." And the foremen of the people of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and were asked, "Why have you not done all your task of making bricks today and yesterday, as in the past?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The taskmasters press hard and hurry them. The foremen were beaten. Israelites set over Israelites take the blows for the shortfall. Oppression often works by making some of the oppressed responsible for the rest.

Scripture does not approve such systems: the law will forbid ruling with harshness (Leviticus 25:43). If you are caught between demanding bosses and struggling colleagues, God sees the cost (Colossians 4:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the foremen of the people of Israel came and cried to Pharaoh, "Why do you treat your servants like this? No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And behold, your servants are beaten; but the fault is in your own people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your servants. They call themselves Pharaoh’s servants three times, appealing to his sense of fairness.

The fault is in your own people. It is honest and true, and useless before an unjust ruler.

They take their cry to Pharaoh rather than to the LORD. It is not wrong to appeal to authorities (Acts 25:11), but deliverance will come from God.

Use proper channels for justice, but pray first and trust God most.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said, "You are idle, you are idle; that is why you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.' Go now and work. No straw will be given you, but you must still deliver the same number of bricks." The foremen of the people of Israel saw that they were in trouble when they said, "You shall by no means reduce your number of bricks, your daily task each day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are idle, you are idle. Pharaoh repeats the word in contempt, linking their desire to sacrifice with laziness.

In trouble is literally “in evil”, in a bad place. Scripture records their despair honestly, yet God has not lost control: he had told Moses that Pharaoh would refuse (3:19).

verseByVerse.quote: They met Moses and Aaron, who were waiting for them, as they came out from Pharaoh; and they said to them, "The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD look on you and judge. This is more than a complaint; it is a curse, invoking God against the men he sent.

Made us stink means made us hateful to Pharaoh, and the sword in their hand is an excuse to kill us. Moses is rejected again, as he was forty years before (2:14).

Their pain is real, but their judgment is wrong: hardship is not proof that God’s messenger is false. If people blame you for trouble that came from obeying God, take it to him, not back at them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-23: Moses takes it straight to God, as an accusation rather than a question.
verseByVerse.theology:
Moses' Honest Complaint

Lament brought to God is still faith talking to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God answers with a promise, not a rebuke (6:1). Now: obedience sometimes makes things worse for a while, and the protest taken to God is itself evidence of faith (Ps. 13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses does not quit or hit back; he turns to the LORD and prays.

Why have you done evil? Literally “brought harm on”: it is an accusation, honestly spoken. “You have not delivered” is true as far as Moses can see: he obeyed exactly, and things got worse.

No rebuke follows. God answers, “Now you shall see what I will do” (6:1). Lament is a form of faith that keeps talking to God (Psalm 13; Habakkuk 1:2).

God does not do evil. Moses speaks from pain, and God will show his purpose; yet complaint is not rebellion when it is brought to God.

Christ in view. On the cross Jesus also cried “Why?” (Mark 15:34), and his cry was not answered with rescue, so that ours could be.

Bring your “why” to God. He can bear it.

5.theology:
The defiance of unbelief. "Who is the LORD?" exposes the heart of rebellion — a refusal to acknowledge God's right to rule.

The cost of obedience. Following God's word can bring immediate hardship. God's deliverances often deepen the darkness before the dawn.

Honest lament. Moses brings his bewilderment to God himself. Faith may wrestle in the dark, so long as it wrestles with God.
5.examples:
Then: The first obedience to God's command brought heavier chains, not freedom, and the deliverer was blamed by the very people he came to save.

Now: When obedience seems to make life harder and prayers seem to go unanswered, we are exactly where Moses stood, and the lowest point may be the threshold of God's mightiest work.

6.title: I Will Redeem You with an Outstretched Arm
6.text: <sup>1</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will send them out, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land."<sup>2</sup>God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD.<sup>3</sup>I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.<sup>4</sup>I also established my covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land in which they lived as sojourners.<sup>5</sup>Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.<sup>6</sup>Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.<sup>7</sup>I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who has brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.<sup>8</sup>I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you for a possession. I am the LORD.'"<sup>9</sup>Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery.<sup>10</sup>So the LORD said to Moses,<sup>11</sup>"Go in, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the people of Israel go out of his land."<sup>12</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, the people of Israel have not listened to me. How then shall Pharaoh listen to me, for I am of uncircumcised lips?"<sup>13</sup>But the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge about the people of Israel and about Pharaoh king of Egypt: to bring the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt.<sup>14</sup>These are the heads of their fathers' houses: the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi; these are the clans of Reuben.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman; these are the clans of Simeon.<sup>16</sup>These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, the years of the life of Levi being 137 years.<sup>17</sup>The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans.<sup>18</sup>The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, the years of the life of Kohath being 133 years.<sup>19</sup>The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations.<sup>20</sup>Amram took as his wife Jochebed his father's sister, and she bore him Aaron and Moses, the years of the life of Amram being 137 years.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.<sup>22</sup>The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.<sup>23</sup>Aaron took as his wife Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and the sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph; these are the clans of the Korahites.<sup>25</sup>Eleazar, Aaron's son, took as his wife one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites by their clans.<sup>26</sup>These are the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said: "Bring out the people of Israel from the land of Egypt by their hosts."<sup>27</sup>It was they who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing out the people of Israel from Egypt, this Moses and this Aaron.<sup>28</sup>On the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,<sup>29</sup>the LORD said to Moses, "I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you."<sup>30</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?"
6.overview:
To Moses' despair God answers not with a new plan but with himself. "I am the LORD" frames the passage, and between those words God recalls his covenant with the patriarchs and makes seven promises of redemption, every one in the first person: every verb of salvation belongs to him.

Here the word redeem enters in force: to buy back, to free at cost, to claim as one's own. Yet the people, broken by slavery, do not listen, and God's promises stand anyway, resting on his faithfulness rather than on their faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-5: God answers Moses' accusation with a timetable and with his name, and remembers his covenant.
verseByVerse.theology:
God Remembers His Covenant

The patriarchs had the promise; these slaves will see what the name means.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God's answer to Moses is a timetable and a name. Now: God rarely answers the "why" we ask, and gives instead a promise that can be leaned on while the trouble lasts.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to Moses, "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will send them out, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land." God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A strong hand. Pharaoh will not merely let Israel go; under God’s power he will drive them out (12:31–33).

I am the LORD is repeated four times in vv. 2–8. God’s answer to despair is himself.

God Almighty was the name of God’s power to keep promises when nature cannot (Genesis 17:1; 35:11).

Did not make myself known. The patriarchs used the name LORD (Genesis 15:7). To “know” the name is to experience what it means: God keeping his covenant in mighty acts.

Where Christians differ. Critical scholars read v. 3 as proof that Genesis came from different sources, one unaware of the name. This commentary’s view: the verse concerns knowing the name’s meaning in experience, not hearing the word; Genesis uses the name freely, and Exodus 6 itself says “my name the LORD” in that sense.
verseByVerse.note: “God Almighty” is El Shaddai (ESV note). The patriarchs knew the name LORD, but had not seen what it means in great acts of redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: I also established my covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land in which they lived as sojourners. Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God had set up and confirmed his binding promise (Genesis 17:7–8), though the patriarchs lived in the land as sojourners, resident foreigners owning only a burial plot (Genesis 23).

Remembered means to act on a promise, not to recall something forgotten (2:24). Four hundred years have passed, and the covenant still binds him. Thank God that his promises to you in Christ do not grow old.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 6-8: Seven promises, each beginning I will, sealed as they opened with I am the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Seven "I Wills"

Rescue, adoption and inheritance, all in the first person of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: these were promises to slaves who could not yet see any of them. Now: Christ shared our flesh and blood to set us free (Heb. 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment. I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who has brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Redeem. Hebrew ga’al: the act of the next-of-kin, the go’el, who bought back a relative from slavery or debt (Leviticus 25:47–49; Ruth 4). God acts as Israel’s family Redeemer.

Outstretched arm pictures God’s power reaching out to act. The great acts of judgment are the plagues, judgments on Egypt and its gods (12:12).

My people … your God. The covenant formula, repeated across Scripture (Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33) and fulfilled at the end: “they will be his people, and God himself will be with them” (Revelation 21:3).

Knowing God personally is the goal of redemption.

Christ in view. Jesus became our near kinsman to redeem us (Galatians 4:4–5), and the outstretched arm reached its fullest stretch on the cross, where the Redeemer’s arms were stretched out to purchase a people at the cost of his blood. He redeemed you as family, not as hired labour.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you for a possession. I am the LORD.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Swore is literally “lifted my hand”, the gesture of an oath: God bound himself (Genesis 22:16; Hebrews 6:13).

God brings his people out of Egypt and into a lasting inheritance, for redemption always has a destination. For the church, the inheritance is the new creation (1 Peter 1:4; Hebrews 11:16).

The section ends as it began, with “I am the LORD”: the promises rest on who God is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-30 — Unbelief, Genealogy, and a Reluctant Mediator
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 9-30: A people too crushed to listen, a genealogy rooting Moses and Aaron in Levi's line, and Moses' objection repeated.
verseByVerse.theology:
Unbelief, Genealogy, and a Reluctant Mediator

God's plan does not pause for a people too broken to hear.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: God renews the charge to Moses rather than arguing with him. Now: what God has promised never depended on our ability to feel encouraged by it.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery. So the LORD said to Moses, "Go in, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the people of Israel go out of his land." But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, the people of Israel have not listened to me. How then shall Pharaoh listen to me, for I am of uncircumcised lips?" But the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge about the people of Israel and about Pharaoh king of Egypt: to bring the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Broken spirit is literally “shortness of breath (or spirit)”: exhaustion and discouragement so deep that hope cannot get in.

This was not stubborn unbelief. They were crushed, not defiant. Some people cannot take in good news because of long pain. Be patient with them; God was (Isaiah 42:3).

Uncircumcised lips is a new way of saying “I cannot speak”: lips unfit, like something not set apart for God. God answers not with an argument but with a charge, repeating the command to Moses and Aaron.

If you are too worn out to believe the promises, let others hold them for you, and keep listening.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the heads of their fathers' houses: the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi; these are the clans of Reuben. The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman; these are the clans of Simeon. These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, the years of the life of Levi being 137 years. The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, by their clans. The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, the years of the life of Kohath being 133 years. The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations. Amram took as his wife Jochebed his father's sister, and she bore him Aaron and Moses, the years of the life of Amram being 137 years. The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri. The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri. Aaron took as his wife Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and the sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph; these are the clans of the Korahites. Eleazar, Aaron's son, took as his wife one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites by their clans. These are the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said: "Bring out the people of Israel from the land of Egypt by their hosts." It was they who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing out the people of Israel from Egypt, this Moses and this Aaron.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why a genealogy here? Before the contest with Pharaoh begins, the text roots the deliverers in Israel’s families. They are real men with real ancestors.

Reuben, Simeon, Levi were the first three sons of Jacob. Reuben slept with his father’s concubine; Simeon and Levi massacred Shechem, and Jacob cursed their anger (Genesis 34; 49:5–7). God’s deliverers come from a disgraced line.

Amram and Jochebed, Moses’ parents, are named at last (2:1). Amram married his father’s sister, which the later law forbade (Leviticus 18:12); the law had not yet been given.

The list is selective, naming key ancestors, not every generation: four hundred years are spanned by a few names.

Lineage does not earn God’s favour. Grace chooses sinners, as Matthew 1 also shows, and writes failures into his story.
verseByVerse.note: The family list traces Moses and Aaron to Levi.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt, the LORD said to Moses, "I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you." But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses’ task is to deliver God’s whole word, and again he pleads his uncircumcised lips. He is no hero, so God’s power will be the more obvious. God does not accept the excuse: in the next chapter he commissions Moses again with Aaron as his prophet (7:1–2).

You can serve God while still feeling unfit. He works through weak servants (2 Corinthians 12:9).

6.theology:
Redemption is God's work. The seven "I wills" make every verb of salvation God's own. We are brought, delivered, redeemed and taken: salvation from first to last is God's doing, not a partnership.

The covenant relationship. The goal of redemption is not just rescue from bondage but belonging to God.

God's faithfulness over our unbelief. The people cannot believe, yet God will save. His promises rest on his character, not our capacity to receive them.
6.examples:
Then: To a people too broken by slavery to listen, God pledged redemption purely on the basis of his covenant.

Now: When our spirits are too crushed to believe the gospel, the ground of our hope is not the strength of our faith but the faithfulness of our Redeemer, who has already secured the "I wills" of our salvation at the cross.

7.title: The Battle of the Gods Begins
7.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet.<sup>2</sup>You shall speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron shall tell Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go out of his land.<sup>3</sup>But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt,<sup>4</sup>Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay my hand on Egypt and bring my hosts, my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great acts of judgment.<sup>5</sup>The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them."<sup>6</sup>Moses and Aaron did so; they did just as the LORD commanded them.<sup>7</sup>Now Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.<sup>8</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron,<sup>9</sup>"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Prove yourselves by working a miracle,' then you shall say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and cast it down before Pharaoh, that it may become a serpent.'"<sup>10</sup>So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD commanded. Aaron cast down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent.<sup>11</sup>Then Pharaoh summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and they, the magicians of Egypt, also did the same by their secret arts.<sup>12</sup>For each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.<sup>13</sup>Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>14</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go.<sup>15</sup>Go to Pharaoh in the morning, as he is going out to the water, and stand on the bank of the Nile to meet him. Take in your hand the staff that turned into a serpent.<sup>16</sup>And you shall say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying, "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." But so far, you have not obeyed.<sup>17</sup>Thus says the LORD, "By this you shall know that I am the LORD: behold, with the staff that is in my hand I will strike the water that is in the Nile, and it shall turn into blood.<sup>18</sup>The fish in the Nile shall die, and the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will grow weary of drinking water from the Nile."'"<sup>19</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, and their ponds, and all their pools of water, so that they may become blood, and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.'"<sup>20</sup>Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded. In the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants he lifted up the staff and struck the water in the Nile, and all the water in the Nile turned into blood.<sup>21</sup>And the fish in the Nile died, and the Nile stank, so that the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile. There was blood throughout all the land of Egypt.<sup>22</sup>But the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart remained hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>23</sup>Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart.<sup>24</sup>And all the Egyptians dug along the Nile for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the Nile.<sup>25</sup>Seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile.
7.overview:
The plagues begin, and they are not random disasters but judgments on the gods of Egypt (12:12): the Nile Egypt worshipped, the sun, the livestock, life itself. This is cosmic warfare: the LORD against the whole pantheon of the world's greatest superpower, and it is no contest. Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs, and the river turns to blood.

Threaded through it all is Pharaoh's hardening and God's purpose: "that the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." Even in judgment God is making himself known.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Moses as God to Pharaoh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-7: Moses made like God to Pharaoh, the purpose stated before a single plague falls, and simple obedience at eighty.
verseByVerse.theology:
Moses as God to Pharaoh

Everything that follows answers Pharaoh's "Who is the LORD?"
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the deliverer's real work began at eighty. Now: God is not bound by our sense of when a life's best years are past.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet. You shall speak all that I command you, and your brother Aaron shall tell Pharaoh to let the people of Israel go out of his land. But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay my hand on Egypt and bring my hosts, my people the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great acts of judgment. The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like God to Pharaoh. The Hebrew word is elohim, “God”. Moses will speak with God’s authority over Pharaoh, who claimed to be divine. Aaron will be his prophet, his spokesman (4:16).

I will harden. As at 4:21, God’s purpose and Pharaoh’s own will are both at work, and Pharaoh’s guilt is real.

The signs and wonders are the plagues: signs point to who God is, and wonders are acts that astonish.

The Egyptians shall know. This is the answer to Pharaoh’s “Who is the LORD?” (5:2). God’s goal includes Egypt’s knowing him, not only Israel’s rescue.

Moses does not become divine. He represents God, as ambassadors represent kings.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Aaron did so; they did just as the LORD commanded them. Now Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After five objections comes simple obedience: just as the LORD commanded.

Eighty years old. Everything Moses is remembered for still lies ahead of him. Forty years in Egypt made a fugitive; forty in Midian made a shepherd; the last forty God will use to lead his people.

Age neither disqualifies anyone nor guarantees usefulness; God chooses his time. If you are older, he may not have finished using you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — Aaron's Staff Swallows the Magicians'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-13: Aaron's staff becomes a serpent; the magicians copy it, and his staff swallows theirs.
verseByVerse.theology:
Aaron's Staff Swallows the Magicians'

God lets Egypt's experts match his sign, then shows whose power prevails.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the counterfeit could copy the sign but not survive it (2 Tim. 3:8-9). Now: a thing can be supernatural and still worthless; the test is whether it stands.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "When Pharaoh says to you, 'Prove yourselves by working a miracle,' then you shall say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and cast it down before Pharaoh, that it may become a serpent.'" So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did just as the LORD commanded. Aaron cast down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Prove yourselves means “show a credential”, and God anticipates the demand.

A serpent. Hebrew tannin, not the ordinary word for snake (4:3). It can mean a great serpent, a crocodile or a sea monster, the creature that pictured Egypt and Pharaoh (Ezekiel 29:3). The sign is a picture of Pharaoh’s own power.

This is not a magic show. The point is who controls the creature.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and they, the magicians of Egypt, also did the same by their secret arts. For each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs. Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wise men, sorcerers, magicians were Egypt’s professional priests and experts in ritual, and their secret arts were their spells and techniques.

Swallowed up. Egypt can imitate God’s sign but cannot survive it. Later the earth “swallowed” Egypt’s army (15:12).

Jannes and Jambres. Jewish tradition names two of these magicians; Paul uses them as types of those who oppose the truth (2 Timothy 3:8).

Where Christians differ: what did the magicians do? Some see sleight of hand: snake-charmers can make a cobra rigid like a stick. Others see real demonic power (2 Thessalonians 2:9). This commentary’s view: the text does not say; either way, their power was real enough to deceive and too weak to win.

Not every wonder comes from God. Counterfeit signs exist; test everything by God’s word (Deuteronomy 13:1–3).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-25 — The Nile Turned to Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-25: The first plague, announced at the water's edge: every water in Egypt turns to blood, and Pharaoh does not take it to heart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Nile Turned to Blood

The first blow falls on Egypt's source of life and its god.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the river Egypt trusted for life is struck first. Now: Jesus came to bear judgment rather than pour it out (John 2:1-11 records his first sign, the joyful reverse of this one).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go. Go to Pharaoh in the morning, as he is going out to the water, and stand on the bank of the Nile to meet him. Take in your hand the staff that turned into a serpent. And you shall say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying, "Let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness." But so far, you have not obeyed. Thus says the LORD, "By this you shall know that I am the LORD: behold, with the staff that is in my hand I will strike the water that is in the Nile, and it shall turn into blood. The fish in the Nile shall die, and the Nile will stink, and the Egyptians will grow weary of drinking water from the Nile."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses meets Pharaoh in the morning, perhaps when the king went to the river for worship or inspection.

The Nile was Egypt’s life: almost no rain falls, and every crop depended on the river’s yearly flood. Egypt worshipped Hapi, god of the flood.

Pharaoh had made the Nile a grave for Hebrew boys (1:22). The river of death now turns to blood: the account is being settled.

Where Christians differ: natural or miraculous? Some explain the plagues as a natural chain: red silt or algae, then frogs, insects, disease. This commentary’s view: God can use natural processes, but here the timing, the announcement in advance, the distinction made for Goshen (8:22) and the scale make them God’s direct acts of judgment.
verseByVerse.note: The Nile was worshipped as a source of life: the plagues strike at Egypt’s gods.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their canals, and their ponds, and all their pools of water, so that they may become blood, and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and in vessels of stone.'" Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded. In the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants he lifted up the staff and struck the water in the Nile, and all the water in the Nile turned into blood. And the fish in the Nile died, and the Nile stank, so that the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile. There was blood throughout all the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The judgment is total: even water stored in vessels is struck. It is done in Pharaoh’s presence, so there is no hiding it. The fish die, a food source fails, and the stink of death fills the land.

Christ in view. Moses’ first sign brought death; Jesus’ first sign, water to wine, brought joy. Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17).

verseByVerse.quote: But the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart remained hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said. Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart. And all the Egyptians dug along the Nile for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the Nile. Seven full days passed after the LORD had struck the Nile.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The magicians could make more blood but could not turn it back to water; their power only adds to the misery.

Did not take even this to heart. Pharaoh refuses to reflect on what has happened. Hardening shows itself as indifference.

The Egyptians dig along the Nile because ground water filtered through soil was drinkable. Ordinary people suffer for their king’s pride, which is a real grief. Yet seven full days pass before the next blow, a week to reconsider: God gives time for repentance (2 Peter 3:9). When his warnings come, take them to heart rather than going back into the house.

7.theology:
The LORD over all gods. The LORD alone is God; every idol is exposed as powerless.

The hardening of the heart. Pharaoh hardens himself, and God hardens Pharaoh, a mystery Scripture holds together (Rom. 9). Human rebellion and divine sovereignty are both fully true.

Judgment as revelation. "That they may know that I am the LORD." Even God's acts of judgment serve to make his glory known.
7.examples:
Then: God began to dismantle the gods of the world's greatest empire, while Pharaoh hardened his heart.

Now: Our culture's idols — wealth, power, self — are no more able to save than Egypt's Nile. God still exposes every counterfeit and calls every heart to know that he alone is the LORD. The question is whether we will be softened or, like Pharaoh, hardened.

8.title: Escalating Judgment and a Line Drawn
8.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>2</sup>But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will plague all your country with frogs.<sup>3</sup>The Nile shall swarm with frogs that shall come up into your house and into your bedroom and on your bed and into the houses of your servants and your people, and into your ovens and your kneading bowls.<sup>4</sup>The frogs shall come up on you and on your people and on all your servants."'"<sup>5</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals and over the pools, and make frogs come up on the land of Egypt!'"<sup>6</sup>So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.<sup>7</sup>But the magicians did the same by their secret arts and made frogs come up on the land of Egypt.<sup>8</sup>Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."<sup>9</sup>Moses said to Pharaoh, "Be pleased to command me when I am to plead for you and for your servants and for your people, that the frogs be cut off from you and your houses and be left only in the Nile."<sup>10</sup>And he said, "Tomorrow." Moses said, "Be it as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.<sup>11</sup>The frogs shall go away from you and your houses and your servants and your people. They shall be left only in the Nile."<sup>12</sup>So Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the LORD about the frogs, as he had agreed with Pharaoh.<sup>13</sup>And the LORD did according to the word of Moses. The frogs died out in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields.<sup>14</sup>And they gathered them together in heaps, and the land stank.<sup>15</sup>But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart and would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>16</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, so that it may become gnats in all the land of Egypt.'"<sup>17</sup>And they did so. Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and there were gnats on man and beast. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt.<sup>18</sup>The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not. So there were gnats on man and beast.<sup>19</sup>Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself to Pharaoh, as he goes out to the water, and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>21</sup>Or else, if you will not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies on you and your servants and your people, and into your houses. And the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with swarms of flies, and also the ground on which they stand.<sup>22</sup>But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth.<sup>23</sup>Thus I will put a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign shall happen."'"<sup>24</sup>And the LORD did so. There came great swarms of flies into the house of Pharaoh and into his servants' houses. Throughout all the land of Egypt the land was ruined by the swarms of flies.<sup>25</sup>Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God within the land."<sup>26</sup>But Moses said, "It would not be right to do so, for the offerings we shall sacrifice to the LORD our God are an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice offerings abominable to the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us?<sup>27</sup>We must go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as he tells us."<sup>28</sup>So Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness; only you must not go very far away. Plead for me."<sup>29</sup>Then Moses said, "Behold, I am going out from you and I will plead with the LORD that the swarms of flies may depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people, tomorrow. Only let not Pharaoh cheat again by not letting the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."<sup>30</sup>So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD.<sup>31</sup>And the LORD did as Moses asked, and removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people; not one remained.<sup>32</sup>But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also, and did not let the people go.
8.overview: Frogs, gnats, flies: the plagues escalate, and two themes come into focus. The first is that there is no one like the LORD our God; at the gnats even the magicians reach their limit. The second is the distinction God makes between his people and Egypt: from the flies onward Goshen is spared. Meanwhile Pharaoh begins to bargain, wanting relief without surrender.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-15 — Frogs and a Hollow Repentance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-15: Frogs everywhere, Pharaoh's first request for prayer, and a hardened heart the moment there is respite.
verseByVerse.theology:
Frogs and a Hollow Repentance

Pressure produces promises; relief shows what they were worth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the test of repentance is not what is said under pressure but what is done in the respite. Now: "now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor. 6:2), not tomorrow.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. But if you refuse to let them go, behold, I will plague all your country with frogs. The Nile shall swarm with frogs that shall come up into your house and into your bedroom and on your bed and into the houses of your servants and your people, and into your ovens and your kneading bowls. The frogs shall come up on you and on your people and on all your servants."'" And the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals and over the pools, and make frogs come up on the land of Egypt!'" So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. But the magicians did the same by their secret arts and made frogs come up on the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That they may serve me. “Serve” is the Hebrew word for worship and also for slave labour. The question is whom Israel will serve: Pharaoh or the LORD.

Egyptians linked frogs with fertility and with the goddess Heqet, shown with a frog’s head. The sign of life becomes a plague.

The frogs reach the most private places of life, the bedroom and the kneading bowl, sleep and food. No one is beyond the judgment, not even the king. The magicians can add frogs, but again they cannot remove the trouble.

God is not mocking for amusement. The plagues expose powerless gods so that Egypt may know the LORD.
verseByVerse.note: Exodus 8:1–4 is 7:26–29 in the Hebrew numbering (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Plead with the LORD to take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD." Moses said to Pharaoh, "Be pleased to command me when I am to plead for you and for your servants and for your people, that the frogs be cut off from you and your houses and be left only in the Nile." And he said, "Tomorrow." Moses said, "Be it as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God. The frogs shall go away from you and your houses and your servants and your people. They shall be left only in the Nile."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who asked “Who is the LORD?” (5:2) now asks for prayer.

Moses lets Pharaoh choose the time, so that the answer cannot be called chance. Offered relief now, Pharaoh says tomorrow, choosing one more night with the frogs: pride delaying what it needs. Do not say “tomorrow” to God about what he asks today (Hebrews 3:15).

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the LORD about the frogs, as he had agreed with Pharaoh. And the LORD did according to the word of Moses. The frogs died out in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields. And they gathered them together in heaps, and the land stank. But when Pharaoh saw that there was a respite, he hardened his heart and would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses prays for his enemy, and God answers precisely. The dead frogs lie in heaps and the land stinks, so the relief itself recalls the judgment.

But as soon as there is a respite, a breathing space, the promise lifts with the pressure. Here Pharaoh hardened his heart himself; the word is literally “made heavy”, dull and insensitive.

This was not real repentance. Regret over pain is not turning from sin (2 Corinthians 7:10), and true repentance remains when the pressure goes. Keep the promises you make to God in a crisis, and if you have broken them, he still receives the one who comes back.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 16-19: Gnats from the dust, without warning, and the magicians' confession.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Finger of God

Counterfeit power reaches its limit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the magicians reached the end of their power. Now: Jesus used their words of his own work — "if it is by the finger of God that I cast out demons" (Luke 11:20).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Say to Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, so that it may become gnats in all the land of Egypt.'" And they did so. Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and there were gnats on man and beast. All the dust of the earth became gnats in all the land of Egypt. The magicians tried by their secret arts to produce gnats, but they could not. So there were gnats on man and beast. Then the magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gnats were tiny biting insects, perhaps mosquitoes or lice. They come from the dust of the ground, recalling the dust from which God formed man (Genesis 2:7).

The third plague in each set of three comes without warning (also 9:8; 10:21).

Egypt’s experts reach their limit, for creating life from dust belongs to God alone: the counterfeit power of darkness collapses before the living God. The finger of God means God’s direct power, exercised with little effort; the tablets of the law were written by it (31:18).

The magicians did not convert. Recognising God’s power is not the same as trusting him (James 2:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-32 — Flies and the Setting Apart of Goshen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 20-32: Flies, Goshen set apart, Pharaoh's first bargains, and another hardening.
verseByVerse.theology:
Flies and the Setting Apart of Goshen

God draws a line between his people and Egypt, and Pharaoh tries to redraw God's terms.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: each compromise adjusted terms that were God's to set. Now: God keeps showing mercy to those who have already shown what they do with it (Rom. 5:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself to Pharaoh, as he goes out to the water, and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. Or else, if you will not let my people go, behold, I will send swarms of flies on you and your servants and your people, and into your houses. And the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with swarms of flies, and also the ground on which they stand. But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies shall be there, that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the earth. Thus I will put a division between my people and your people. Tomorrow this sign shall happen."'" And the LORD did so. There came great swarms of flies into the house of Pharaoh and into his servants' houses. Throughout all the land of Egypt the land was ruined by the swarms of flies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The swarms of flies may have been biting dog-flies, or beetles sacred to Egypt (the scarab).

Set apart means to make a distinction, to treat differently. From now on the plagues fall on Egypt and not on Israel (9:4, 26; 10:23; 11:7).

A sign. Literally “redemption”, a ransom or division: God’s separation of his people shows that he is the LORD “in the midst of the earth”, not a local god of the Nile.

Israel was not more deserving. The distinction is grace, as the Passover will make plain (12:13). The God who pours out wrath also shelters his people from it, and beyond the Passover stands the cross, where Christ bore the judgment so that none should fall on us.
verseByVerse.note: Goshen was the region of the eastern Nile delta where Israel lived.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God within the land." But Moses said, "It would not be right to do so, for the offerings we shall sacrifice to the LORD our God are an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice offerings abominable to the Egyptians before their eyes, will they not stone us? We must go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as he tells us." So Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness; only you must not go very far away. Plead for me." Then Moses said, "Behold, I am going out from you and I will plead with the LORD that the swarms of flies may depart from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people, tomorrow. Only let not Pharaoh cheat again by not letting the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s first compromise is to worship within the land, staying in Egypt. Moses refuses: Israel’s sacrifices would include animals Egyptians held sacred or ritually offensive, and that could provoke violence. The second compromise is to go, but not very far, staying within reach.

Pharaoh will keep offering partial freedom: leave your children (10:10–11), leave your flocks (10:24). The world often allows faith if it is kept small and private.

Moses holds to God’s instruction of a three days’ journey (3:18). It was a real request, and Pharaoh never granted even that. Beware of compromises that let you keep God near but still under Pharaoh’s rule.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to the LORD. And the LORD did as Moses asked, and removed the swarms of flies from Pharaoh, from his servants, and from his people; not one remained. But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time also, and did not let the people go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers the prayer exactly: not one fly remains. Yet twice now Pharaoh has asked for prayer and broken his word, and hardening deepens with every relief.

God’s mercy is not wasted. He answers prayer even for those who will abuse it (Matthew 5:45), and their guilt grows with every mercy refused (Romans 2:4–5).

Each answered prayer is a call to keep faith, not only an escape.

8.theology:
There is no one like the LORD. The plagues expose every rival as powerless; even the magicians confess "the finger of God."

Distinguishing grace. God sets apart Goshen, sheltering his people in the day of judgment, a foreshadowing of Passover and the cross.

The hardened heart and false repentance. Pharaoh repents only of consequences, bargains for partial obedience, and hardens again when relief comes.
8.examples:
Then: As the plagues escalated, Pharaoh offered the half-repentance and compromised obedience typical of a hardened heart.

Now: The world still offers God a partial obedience — "don't go too far." But God draws a line between his people and the world, and in Christ he shelters us wholly from the judgment to come. He calls not for bargaining but for surrender.

9.title: That My Name May Be Proclaimed in All the Earth
9.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>2</sup>For if you refuse to let them go and still hold them,<sup>3</sup>behold, the hand of the LORD will fall with a very severe plague upon your livestock that are in the field, the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the herds, and the flocks.<sup>4</sup>But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that nothing of all that belongs to the people of Israel shall die."'"<sup>5</sup>And the LORD set a time, saying, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land."<sup>6</sup>And the next day the LORD did this thing. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one of the livestock of the people of Israel died.<sup>7</sup>And Pharaoh sent, and behold, not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. But the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from the kiln, and let Moses throw them in the air in the sight of Pharaoh.<sup>9</sup>It shall become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and become boils breaking out in sores on man and beast throughout all the land of Egypt."<sup>10</sup>So they took soot from the kiln and stood before Pharaoh. And Moses threw it in the air, and it became boils breaking out in sores on man and beast.<sup>11</sup>And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils came upon the magicians and upon all the Egyptians.<sup>12</sup>But the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he did not listen to them, as the LORD had spoken to Moses.<sup>13</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>14</sup>For this time I will send all my plagues on you yourself, and on your servants and your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth.<sup>15</sup>For by now I could have put out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth.<sup>16</sup>But for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth.<sup>17</sup>You are still exalting yourself against my people and will not let them go.<sup>18</sup>Behold, about this time tomorrow I will cause very heavy hail to fall, such as never has been in Egypt from the day it was founded until now.<sup>19</sup>Now therefore send, get your livestock and all that you have in the field into safe shelter, for every man and beast that is in the field and is not brought home will die when the hail falls on them."'"<sup>20</sup>Then whoever feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh hurried his slaves and his livestock into the houses,<sup>21</sup>but whoever did not pay attention to the word of the LORD left his slaves and his livestock in the field.<sup>22</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, on man and beast and every plant of the field, in the land of Egypt."<sup>23</sup>Then Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and fire ran down to the earth. And the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt.<sup>24</sup>There was hail and fire flashing continually in the midst of the hail, very heavy hail, such as had never been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.<sup>25</sup>The hail struck down everything that was in the field in all the land of Egypt, both man and beast. And the hail struck down every plant of the field and broke every tree of the field.<sup>26</sup>Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel were, was there no hail.<sup>27</sup>Then Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong.<sup>28</sup>Plead with the LORD, for there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. I will let you go, and you shall stay no longer."<sup>29</sup>Moses said to him, "As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will stretch out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's.<sup>30</sup>But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the LORD God."<sup>31</sup>(The flax and the barley were struck down, for the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud.<sup>32</sup>But the wheat and the emmer were not struck down, for they are late in coming up.)<sup>33</sup>So Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh and stretched out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder and the hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured upon the earth.<sup>34</sup>But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned yet again and hardened his heart, he and his servants.<sup>35</sup>So the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people of Israel go, just as the LORD had spoken through Moses.
9.overview:
The plagues press toward life and death: livestock die, boils break out, and the worst hail Egypt has ever seen falls. Again God distinguishes: Goshen is untouched, and Egyptians who fear the word of the LORD shelter their cattle and are spared.

At the centre stands a verse Paul will quote: God has raised Pharaoh up so that his name may be proclaimed in all the earth. Even the most hardened rebel serves the display of God's glory, and Pharaoh's fullest confession yet dissolves the moment the hail stops.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — Livestock, Boils, and a Deeper Distinction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-12: Egypt's livestock die and Israel's do not; boils from the kiln's soot; and for the first time the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.theology:
Livestock, Boils, and a Deeper Distinction

Pharaoh sees the evidence and refuses it, and is confirmed in the hardness he chose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a man who made himself hard for five rounds is confirmed in what he made himself. Now: evidence cannot cure a heart for which evidence has stopped deciding anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. For if you refuse to let them go and still hold them, behold, the hand of the LORD will fall with a very severe plague upon your livestock that are in the field, the horses, the donkeys, the camels, the herds, and the flocks. But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so that nothing of all that belongs to the people of Israel shall die."'" And the LORD set a time, saying, "Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land." And the next day the LORD did this thing. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one of the livestock of the people of Israel died. And Pharaoh sent, and behold, not one of the livestock of Israel was dead. But the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A severe plague. This was a deadly animal disease, perhaps anthrax, striking horses, donkeys, camels, herds and flocks in the field.

Many of Egypt’s gods were pictured as animals: Apis the sacred bull, Hathor the cow goddess. The plague exposes them as powerless.

Not one of Israel’s animals died. Pharaoh sends to check, sees the evidence, and still refuses.

All the livestock died. Yet there are cattle for the hail (v. 19) and horses for the chariots (14:9). “All” here means all kinds and all in the fields (v. 3), a common biblical way of speaking, not every single animal.

Evidence alone does not produce faith: a hardened heart can see the facts and still refuse (Luke 16:31).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from the kiln, and let Moses throw them in the air in the sight of Pharaoh. It shall become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and become boils breaking out in sores on man and beast throughout all the land of Egypt." So they took soot from the kiln and stood before Pharaoh. And Moses threw it in the air, and it became boils breaking out in sores on man and beast. And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, for the boils came upon the magicians and upon all the Egyptians. But the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he did not listen to them, as the LORD had spoken to Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soot from the kiln came from the furnace where Israel’s bricks were fired, so the furnace of slavery becomes the source of judgment.

The boils were festering sores breaking out in blisters. For the first time the plagues strike Egyptian bodies directly. The same disease is threatened on covenant breakers (Deuteronomy 28:27).

The magicians, unable to cure themselves, cannot stand before Moses and leave the contest.

The LORD hardened. This is the first time in the plagues that God is said to harden. Pharaoh had hardened himself repeatedly; now God confirms him in it (Romans 1:24).

God does not harden an innocent man. He gives Pharaoh over to the hardness he has chosen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13-21 — The Warning and the God-Fearers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-21: God explains himself before the hail, and warns Egypt to take shelter.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Warning and the God-Fearers

Judgment comes with a way of escape for anyone who believes God's word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the name was proclaimed, and forty years later Rahab in Jericho had heard what the LORD did for Israel (Josh. 2:10). Now: the line God draws runs between those who fear his word and those who do not (12:38).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise up early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, "Let my people go, that they may serve me. For this time I will send all my plagues on you yourself, and on your servants and your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth. For by now I could have put out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been cut off from the earth. But for this purpose I have raised you up, to show you my power, so that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth. You are still exalting yourself against my people and will not let them go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The remaining plagues will strike Pharaoh’s heart, his will and his very self. God could have ended Egypt with one plague; that Pharaoh is still alive is mercy.

For this purpose I have raised you up. Literally “caused you to stand”, that is, kept you alive and in power. Paul quotes it in Romans 9:17: God shows mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills.

Where Christians differ: did God make Pharaoh to destroy him? Some read only “kept you alive through the plagues”; others see God’s sovereign purpose in raising Pharaoh to power. This commentary’s view: both are true. God ordained Pharaoh’s place in history for his glory, and Pharaoh freely exalted himself against God’s people (v. 17). God’s purpose does not excuse Pharaoh’s sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, about this time tomorrow I will cause very heavy hail to fall, such as never has been in Egypt from the day it was founded until now. Now therefore send, get your livestock and all that you have in the field into safe shelter, for every man and beast that is in the field and is not brought home will die when the hail falls on them."'" Then whoever feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh hurried his slaves and his livestock into the houses, but whoever did not pay attention to the word of the LORD left his slaves and his livestock in the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is mercy within judgment: any Egyptian could escape by believing God’s word and sheltering his livestock. Some of Pharaoh’s own officials feared the word of the LORD and acted: even among the Egyptians, the fear of God begins to bear fruit, and they may be among the “mixed multitude” who left with Israel (12:38). Others ignored it and lost everything.

So the plagues were not aimed at Egypt’s people as a race; anyone who feared God’s word found refuge. God’s warnings are mercies still.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-35 — Hail and a Confession That Melts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-35: Hail and fire everywhere but Goshen; Pharaoh's confession; and sin again when the storm stops.
verseByVerse.theology:
Hail and a Confession That Melts

Pharaoh wants the thunder to stop, not his sin.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the wheat left standing was an inventory of what Egypt still had to lose. Now: worldly grief wants the noise to stop; godly grief leads to repentance (2 Cor. 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, so that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt, on man and beast and every plant of the field, in the land of Egypt." Then Moses stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and fire ran down to the earth. And the LORD rained hail upon the land of Egypt. There was hail and fire flashing continually in the midst of the hail, very heavy hail, such as had never been in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation. The hail struck down everything that was in the field in all the land of Egypt, both man and beast. And the hail struck down every plant of the field and broke every tree of the field. Only in the land of Goshen, where the people of Israel were, was there no hail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hail falls with lightning running along the ground, a storm unlike any in the history of Egypt, where rain is rare. Nut the sky goddess, Seth the storm god and Osiris the god of crops are all helpless, and whatever stood in the open is destroyed. Only Goshen is spared, as God protects his people in the midst of judgment.

Praise God who rules the weather (Psalm 148:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned; the LORD is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. Plead with the LORD, for there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. I will let you go, and you shall stay no longer." Moses said to him, "As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will stretch out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, so that you may know that the earth is the LORD's. But as for you and your servants, I know that you do not yet fear the LORD God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This time I have sinned. Pharaoh confesses, using God’s name and calling him just in his judgments. His question “Who is the LORD?” (5:2) has been answered in his own mouth.

The answered prayer will show that the earth is the LORD’s (Psalm 24:1); he is not a local god of the Hebrews.

You do not yet fear the LORD. Fear of God is reverent submission that changes behaviour. Pharaoh feared the consequences, not God. Confessing sin is never useless, but true repentance turns from sin, not only from its pain (2 Corinthians 7:10).

verseByVerse.quote: (The flax and the barley were struck down, for the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bud. But the wheat and the emmer were not struck down, for they are late in coming up.) So Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh and stretched out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder and the hail ceased, and the rain no longer poured upon the earth. But when Pharaoh saw that the rain and the hail and the thunder had ceased, he sinned yet again and hardened his heart, he and his servants. So the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people of Israel go, just as the LORD had spoken through Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flax for linen and barley were ripe; wheat and emmer sprouted later. The detail fits Egypt’s farming year, perhaps January or February.

The surviving wheat gives Egypt one more thing to lose, to the locusts (10:5, 15), but it also leaves room to repent.

Sinned yet again. Scripture calls his hardening sin, and his servants harden their hearts with him, just as the LORD had spoken.

When trouble passes, do you go back to the sin it exposed? If so, the door Pharaoh refused is still open to you.
verseByVerse.note: “Emmer” is a type of wheat (ESV note). The details date the hail to late winter.

9.theology:
The sovereignty of God in hardening. The LORD himself now hardens Pharaoh (v. 12), and declares that Pharaoh exists for the display of God's power (v. 16).

The glory of God as the goal of all things. "That my name may be proclaimed in all the earth" is the supreme purpose behind the plagues and behind history itself.

The futility of false repentance. Pharaoh's perfect confession melts when the pressure lifts. Words without a changed heart save no one.
9.examples:
Then: God brought Egypt to its knees with disease and the worst hailstorm in its history.
