Now: God still governs even the hardest hearts toward the proclamation of his glory. And we are warned: it is possible to confess sin with flawless words in a crisis and remain unchanged. True repentance bears fruit when the storm has passed.

10.title: Darkness Over the Land
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the heart of his servants, that I may show these signs of mine among them,<sup>2</sup>and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians and what signs I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD."<sup>3</sup>So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me.<sup>4</sup>For if you refuse to let my people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country,<sup>5</sup>and they shall cover the face of the land, so that no one can see the land. And they shall eat what is left to you after the hail, and they shall eat every tree of yours that grows in the field,<sup>6</sup>and they shall fill your houses and the houses of all your servants and of all the Egyptians, as neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen, from the day they came on earth to this day.'" Then he turned and went out from Pharaoh.<sup>7</sup>Then Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined?"<sup>8</sup>So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. And he said to them, "Go, serve the LORD your God. But which ones are to go?"<sup>9</sup>Moses said, "We will go with our young and our old. We will go with our sons and daughters and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD."<sup>10</sup>But he said to them, "The LORD be with you, if ever I let you and your little ones go! Look, you have some evil purpose in mind.<sup>11</sup>No! Go, the men among you, and serve the LORD, for that is what you are asking." And they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.<sup>12</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they may come upon the land of Egypt and eat every plant in the land, all that the hail has left."<sup>13</sup>So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day and all that night. When it was morning, the east wind had brought the locusts.<sup>14</sup>The locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled on the whole country of Egypt, such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before, nor ever will be again.<sup>15</sup>They covered the face of the whole land, so that the land was darkened, and they ate all the plants in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Not a green thing remained, neither tree nor plant of the field, through all the land of Egypt.<sup>16</sup>Then Pharaoh hastily called Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you.<sup>17</sup>Now therefore, forgive my sin, please, only this once, and plead with the LORD your God only to remove this death from me."<sup>18</sup>So he went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD.<sup>19</sup>And the LORD turned the wind into a very strong west wind, which lifted the locusts and drove them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust was left in all the country of Egypt.<sup>20</sup>But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go.<sup>21</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt."<sup>22</sup>So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was pitch darkness in all the land of Egypt three days.<sup>23</sup>They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days, but all the people of Israel had light where they lived.<sup>24</sup>Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD; your little ones also may go with you; only let your flocks and your herds remain behind."<sup>25</sup>But Moses said, "You must also let us have sacrifices and burnt offerings, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.<sup>26</sup>Our livestock also must go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind, for we must take of them to serve the LORD our God, and we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there."<sup>27</sup>But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go.<sup>28</sup>Then Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me; take care never to see my face again, for on the day you see my face you shall die."<sup>29</sup>Moses said, "As you say! I will not see your face again."
10.overview: Locusts and darkness push Egypt toward un-creation, as if the order God made were being undone. The locusts devour what the hail left; then a darkness "to be felt" covers the land for three days, while Israel has light. Pharaoh's bargaining grows desperate, but God will accept no partial exodus. He claims his people whole.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-20: A reason for the next generation, Pharaoh's officials breaking, the offer of the men only, and locusts.
verseByVerse.theology:
Locusts Devour the Land

Pharaoh's own officials break, but he will let only the men go.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the plagues were done for an audience not yet born. Now: worship detached from the next generation dies within a lifetime; it does not need to be abolished.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go in to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the heart of his servants, that I may show these signs of mine among them, and that you may tell in the hearing of your son and of your grandson how I have dealt harshly with the Egyptians and what signs I have done among them, that you may know that I am the LORD." So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and said to him, "Thus says the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me? Let my people go, that they may serve me. For if you refuse to let my people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your country, and they shall cover the face of the land, so that no one can see the land. And they shall eat what is left to you after the hail, and they shall eat every tree of yours that grows in the field, and they shall fill your houses and the houses of all your servants and of all the Egyptians, as neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen, from the day they came on earth to this day.'" Then he turned and went out from Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have hardened his heart. As at 4:21: God’s purpose and Pharaoh’s own will are both at work, and Pharaoh’s guilt is real.

Tell your son and grandson. The plagues are for future generations, so that Israel will know the LORD. The story is meant to be retold (Psalm 78:4–7), and faith is still passed on by stories told to children and grandchildren.

Humble yourself. The issue is pride: Pharaoh refuses to bow before God.

Desert locusts can form swarms of billions, stripping every green thing. They will eat what the hail left (9:32).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long shall this man be a snare to us? Let the men go, that they may serve the LORD their God. Do you not yet understand that Egypt is ruined?" So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. And he said to them, "Go, serve the LORD your God. But which ones are to go?" Moses said, "We will go with our young and our old. We will go with our sons and daughters and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD." But he said to them, "The LORD be with you, if ever I let you and your little ones go! Look, you have some evil purpose in mind. No! Go, the men among you, and serve the LORD, for that is what you are asking." And they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses has become a snare, a trap that ruins. Egypt is ruined: his officials see what Pharaoh will not.

Who are to go? Moses answers: young and old, sons and daughters, flocks and herds. Worship involves the whole people.

The LORD be with you is sarcasm: “As if I would let your little ones go!” By evil is on your mind Pharaoh means, “You plan to escape.”

His third compromise is to let only the men go, since families left in Egypt would draw the men back. But faith is not only for adults. Children belong among God’s worshipping people (Deuteronomy 31:12; Mark 10:14); do not leave yours in Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they may come upon the land of Egypt and eat every plant in the land, all that the hail has left." So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD brought an east wind upon the land all that day and all that night. When it was morning, the east wind had brought the locusts. The locusts came up over all the land of Egypt and settled on the whole country of Egypt, such a dense swarm of locusts as had never been before, nor ever will be again. They covered the face of the whole land, so that the land was darkened, and they ate all the plants in the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Not a green thing remained, neither tree nor plant of the field, through all the land of Egypt. Then Pharaoh hastily called Moses and Aaron and said, "I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you. Now therefore, forgive my sin, please, only this once, and plead with the LORD your God only to remove this death from me." So he went out from Pharaoh and pleaded with the LORD. And the LORD turned the wind into a very strong west wind, which lifted the locusts and drove them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust was left in all the country of Egypt. But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God rules the winds: an east wind from the desert brings the swarm.

I have sinned … forgive. This is Pharaoh’s most religious confession, yet he asks God to remove “this death”, not his sin. Words of repentance are not always false, but repentance shows itself in turning, not only in asking for relief.

The Red Sea is in Hebrew yam suph, “Sea of Reeds”. A west wind drives the locusts into it, foreshadowing the end of Egypt’s army.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21-29 — A Darkness to Be Felt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 21-29: Three days of darkness, light in Israel's homes, the last compromise refused, and a final parting.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Darkness to Be Felt

Egypt's chief god is dethroned, and not a hoof is left behind.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the sun Egypt worshipped did not rise. Now: the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it (John 1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, a darkness to be felt." So Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was pitch darkness in all the land of Egypt three days. They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days, but all the people of Israel had light where they lived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The darkness is a blow against Ra and against Pharaoh, who was called the son of Ra.

To be felt. The darkness was so dense it pressed in. No one could move or see another, and life stopped. The God who said “Let there be light” now says, in effect, let there be darkness, and the world of Egypt unravels.

Yet Israel has light where they lived: God’s people have light in a dark world (John 8:12).

Christ in view. At the cross darkness covered the land for three hours (Matthew 27:45; Mark 15:33). There it fell not on God’s enemies but on his own Son, in our place, so that we might have light.
verseByVerse.note: The sun god Ra was among Egypt’s chief gods.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh called Moses and said, "Go, serve the LORD; your little ones also may go with you; only let your flocks and your herds remain behind." But Moses said, "You must also let us have sacrifices and burnt offerings, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God. Our livestock also must go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind, for we must take of them to serve the LORD our God, and we do not know with what we must serve the LORD until we arrive there." But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go. Then Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me; take care never to see my face again, for on the day you see my face you shall die." Moses said, "As you say! I will not see your face again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh’s fourth and last compromise is that the flocks remain: something must stay in Egypt.

Not a hoof. Every animal must go, because they do not yet know what God will require for worship. Full obedience leaves nothing behind.

The day you see my face you shall die. Moses accepts Pharaoh’s threat. He will not see Pharaoh’s face again in this way (11:8).

Christians need not reject every compromise in practical matters. But in what God requires, partial obedience is disobedience. Is there one area of life you want to keep in Egypt? The God who redeemed all of you can be trusted with all of it.

10.theology:
The undoing of creation. Locusts and a darkness that could be felt reverse the order God established and show the LORD's mastery over creation itself.

The darkness that prefigures Calvary. There the true Firstborn bore judgment so his people might have light.

Generational testimony. God designs the exodus to be retold, that every generation may know he is the LORD.
10.examples:
Then: God stripped Egypt bare and dethroned the sun-god, yet Pharaoh still bargained and hardened.

Now: Those in Christ are children of light. And we, like Israel, are called to tell our children how the LORD has saved, that they too may know him.

11.title: The Announcement of the Last Plague
11.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Yet one plague more I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. Afterward he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you away completely.<sup>2</sup>Speak now in the hearing of the people, that they ask, every man of his neighbor and every woman of her neighbor, for silver and gold jewelry."<sup>3</sup>And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh's servants and in the sight of the people.<sup>4</sup>So Moses said, "Thus says the LORD: 'About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt,<sup>5</sup>and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, and all the firstborn of the cattle.<sup>6</sup>There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been, nor ever will be again.<sup>7</sup>But not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel, either man or beast, that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.'<sup>8</sup>And all these your servants shall come down to me and bow down to me, saying, 'Get out, you and all the people who follow you.' And after that I will go out." And he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.<sup>9</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt."<sup>10</sup>Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.
11.overview:
This brief chapter is the hush before the storm: the announcement of the tenth plague, the death of every firstborn in Egypt. Pharaoh refused to release God's firstborn (4:22), and now Egypt's firstborn will fall.

What will make the difference between Israel and Egypt that night is not Israel's merit, for Israel deserves death as much as Egypt, but the blood of a lamb. The heart of grace is not that some are better, but that some are covered. The firstborn of Egypt die; the firstborn of Israel live, because a substitute will die in their place. The shadow of the cross falls across this whole chapter.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-3 — Favor in the Eyes of the Egyptians
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-3: One plague more, and the promised favour with the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.theology:
Favor in the Eyes of the Egyptians

The fugitive is now honoured in the land that hunted him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the promise of 3:21-22 comes due. Now: God sometimes answers our objections not by refuting them but by outliving them.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Yet one plague more I will bring upon Pharaoh and upon Egypt. Afterward he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you away completely. Speak now in the hearing of the people, that they ask, every man of his neighbor and every woman of her neighbor, for silver and gold jewelry." And the LORD gave the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians. Moreover, the man Moses was very great in the land of Egypt, in the sight of Pharaoh's servants and in the sight of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharaoh will not merely permit them to go; he will drive you away completely.

The silver and gold jewellery was asked for, not stolen (3:21–22): back wages for generations of slavery, given because God turned Egyptian hearts towards Israel.

Moses was very great. The fugitive is now respected by Pharaoh’s own officials and people. This was not his own achievement; God gave the favour and honoured his servant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4-8 — The Death of the Firstborn Announced
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 4-8: At midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh's heir to the slave girl's at the handmill; against Israel not a dog shall growl. Moses leaves in hot anger.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Death of the Firstborn Announced

Rank gives no protection; only God's distinction does.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a way of escape was about to be published to every house. Now: the only distinction that saves is the blood of the Lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses said, "Thus says the LORD: 'About midnight I will go out in the midst of Egypt, and every firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne, even to the firstborn of the slave girl who is behind the handmill, and all the firstborn of the cattle. There shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there has never been, nor ever will be again. But not a dog shall growl against any of the people of Israel, either man or beast, that you may know that the LORD makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel.' And all these your servants shall come down to me and bow down to me, saying, 'Get out, you and all the people who follow you.' And after that I will go out." And he went out from Pharaoh in hot anger.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will go out. This is God himself acting, not a natural disaster.

Every firstborn. The firstborn son was the heir, the family’s future and pride, and from the throne to the millstone no family is exempt.

Why this judgment? Egypt had drowned Israel’s sons (1:22), and God had warned: Israel is my firstborn son; if you refuse, I will kill your firstborn (4:22–23). Nine plagues gave time to repent.

The cry Israel raised under slavery (3:7) will now fill Egypt, while against Israel not a dog shall growl: the distinction at its sharpest. Moses leaves in hot anger at the stubbornness that will bring such grief.

This is one of the hardest judgments in Scripture: children and young men die for a king's refusal, and every grieving Egyptian home is a real grief. God does not delight in death (Ezekiel 33:11), and these children are not punished for their own sin. A whole nation shares its ruler’s judgment, as Israel’s firstborn would too without the Passover lamb (12:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 9-10: A summary of the whole contest with Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hardening Completed

The refusals were the means by which the wonders multiplied.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Pharaoh's will and God's purpose ran together to the end. Now: the story stops on the edge of the worst night and turns to a lamb.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh will not listen to you, that my wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt." Moses and Aaron did all these wonders before Pharaoh, and the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the people of Israel go out of his land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That my wonders may be multiplied. Pharaoh’s refusal is foreseen and used for God’s purpose, to display his power and name.

The whole contest is summed up here: Pharaoh hardened himself, and God hardened him. God is not unjust in this (Romans 9:14). Pharaoh had every warning and chose rebellion; God’s hardening was justice, not cruelty.

11.theology:
The wages of sin is death. The final plague confronts us with judgment in its starkest form.

Distinguishing grace. God makes a distinction between Egypt and Israel, not by merit but, as ch. 12 reveals, by the blood of a substitute.

God's faithfulness to ancient promises. The plundering of Egypt fulfills the word given to Abraham four centuries earlier (Gen. 15:14).
11.examples:
Then: God announced a judgment that exposed all Egypt, palace and hovel alike, and could be escaped only by the distinction God himself would make.

Now: None can escape judgment on the basis of merit. Christ, the true Firstborn, died that we might live.

12.title: Christ Our Passover
12.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt,<sup>2</sup>"This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you.<sup>3</sup>Tell all the congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month every man shall take a lamb according to their fathers' houses, a lamb for a household.<sup>4</sup>And if the household is too small for a lamb, then he and his nearest neighbor shall take according to the number of persons; according to what each can eat you shall make your count for the lamb.<sup>5</sup>Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats,<sup>6</sup>and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill their lambs at twilight.<sup>7</sup>"Then they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it.<sup>8</sup>They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted on the fire; with unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it.<sup>9</sup>Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted, its head with its legs and its inner parts.<sup>10</sup>And you shall let none of it remain until the morning; anything that remains until the morning you shall burn.<sup>11</sup>In this manner you shall eat it: with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. And you shall eat it in haste. It is the LORD's Passover.<sup>12</sup>For I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments: I am the LORD.<sup>13</sup>The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.<sup>14</sup>"This day shall be for you a memorial day, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD; throughout your generations, as a statute forever, you shall keep it as a feast.<sup>15</sup>Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven out of your houses, for if anyone eats what is leavened, from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall be cut off from Israel.<sup>16</sup>On the first day you shall hold a holy assembly, and on the seventh day a holy assembly. No work shall be done on those days. But what everyone needs to eat, that alone may be prepared by you.<sup>17</sup>And you shall observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt. Therefore you shall observe this day, throughout your generations, as a statute forever.<sup>18</sup>In the first month, from the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the month at evening.<sup>19</sup>For seven days no leaven is to be found in your houses. If anyone eats what is leavened, that person will be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether he is a sojourner or a native of the land.<sup>20</sup>You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwelling places you shall eat unleavened bread."<sup>21</sup>Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Go and select lambs for yourselves according to your clans, and kill the Passover lamb.<sup>22</sup>Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the basin. None of you shall go out of the door of his house until the morning.<sup>23</sup>For the LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians, and when he sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, the LORD will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you.<sup>24</sup>You shall observe this rite as a statute for you and for your sons forever.<sup>25</sup>And when you come to the land that the LORD will give you, as he has promised, you shall keep this service.<sup>26</sup>And when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?'<sup>27</sup>you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt, when he struck the Egyptians but spared our houses.'" And the people bowed their heads and worshiped.<sup>28</sup>Then the people of Israel went and did so; as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.<sup>29</sup>At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of the livestock.<sup>30</sup>And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians. And there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead.<sup>31</sup>Then he summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, "Up, go out from among my people, both you and the people of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as you have said.<sup>32</sup>Take your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone, and bless me also!"<sup>33</sup>The Egyptians were urgent with the people to send them out of the land in haste. For they said, "We shall all be dead."<sup>34</sup>So the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneading bowls being bound up in their cloaks on their shoulders.<sup>35</sup>The people of Israel had also done as Moses told them, for they had asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing.<sup>36</sup>And the LORD had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they let them have what they asked. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.<sup>37</sup>And the people of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children.<sup>38</sup>A mixed multitude also went up with them, and very much livestock, both flocks and herds.<sup>39</sup>And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough that they had brought out of Egypt, for it was not leavened, because they were thrust out of Egypt and could not wait, nor had they prepared any provisions for themselves.<sup>40</sup>The time that the people of Israel lived in Egypt was 430 years.<sup>41</sup>At the end of 430 years, on that very day, all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt.<sup>42</sup>It was a night of watching by the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt; so this same night is a night of watching kept to the LORD by all the people of Israel throughout their generations.<sup>43</sup>And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the statute of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it,<sup>44</sup>but every slave that is bought for money may eat of it after you have circumcised him.<sup>45</sup>No foreigner or hired worker may eat of it.<sup>46</sup>It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not take any of the flesh outside the house, and you shall not break any of its bones.<sup>47</sup>All the congregation of Israel shall keep it.<sup>48</sup>If a stranger shall sojourn with you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, let all his males be circumcised. Then he may come near and keep it; he shall be as a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person shall eat of it.<sup>49</sup>There shall be one law for the native and for the stranger who sojourns among you."<sup>50</sup>All the people of Israel did just as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron.<sup>51</sup>And on that very day the LORD brought the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their hosts.
12.overview:
This is the beating heart of the book. Here the gospel is preached in shadow so clearly that Paul can simply call Christ our Passover lamb. On this night God delivers his people not by their strength or worthiness, but by the blood of a lamb.

The Israelites inside were not safer than the Egyptians because they were better; they were safe because they were covered. Salvation is by substitution, the lamb for the firstborn, and the question that night was not "Are you an Israelite?" but "Is there blood on your door?" This is the chapter that explains the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-13 — The Lamb and the Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-13: A new calendar, a lamb for each household, the blood on the doorframe, a meal eaten dressed to travel, and the promise when I see the blood, I will pass over you.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lamb and the Blood

Redemption begins at home, with a substitute God himself appoints.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: every house was as safe as the blood on its doorframe, and no safer. Now: the decisive question is whether we are covered by Christ's blood.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, "This month shall be for you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The beginning of months. Israel will count its year from its redemption. A civil year still began in autumn, but the religious year began with the exodus.

Christians, too, date their lives from their redemption in Christ. That is where your story really begins (2 Corinthians 5:17).
verseByVerse.note: The month was Abib (later Nisan), in March–April.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell all the congregation of Israel that on the tenth day of this month every man shall take a lamb according to their fathers' houses, a lamb for a household. And if the household is too small for a lamb, then he and his nearest neighbor shall take according to the number of persons; according to what each can eat you shall make your count for the lamb. Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male a year old. You may take it from the sheep or from the goats, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, when the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill their lambs at twilight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Congregation is used here for the first time: the whole assembly of Israel, a people gathered before God.

A lamb for a household. The Hebrew seh means a young sheep or goat. Redemption begins at home, not in a temple, and small households share with neighbours.

The lamb is to be without blemish, with no defect, a male a year old in its prime. It is kept four days with the family, time to see that it had no flaw, and killed in the late afternoon.

Christ in view. Jesus entered Jerusalem before Passover and was questioned and examined for days, and Pilate found no fault in him (John 18:38). He is “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), a lamb “without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19).
verseByVerse.note: “At twilight” is literally “between the two evenings” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they shall take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the lintel of the houses in which they eat it. They shall eat the flesh that night, roasted on the fire; with unleavened bread and bitter herbs they shall eat it. Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted, its head with its legs and its inner parts. And you shall let none of it remain until the morning; anything that remains until the morning you shall burn. In this manner you shall eat it: with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. And you shall eat it in haste. It is the LORD's Passover.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The blood is life given in death (Leviticus 17:11), and it goes on the outside of the house, where God would see it: on the sides and top of the doorway, not the threshold, so that no one would tread on it (Hebrews 10:29).

The lamb is roasted whole over fire. The unleavened bread is flat bread made without yeast, because there was no time for dough to rise (v. 39), and the bitter herbs recall the bitterness of slavery (1:14).

They eat dressed to travel, belt fastened and sandals on, by faith in a deliverance not yet seen.

The LORD’s Passover. Hebrew pesach, from the verb “pass over”, which may also mean to shield or protect (Isaiah 31:5).

The blood was not a magic charm, and safety was not a reward for being Israelite. Any Israelite house without blood would have lost its firstborn too. Safety lay in God’s provision, received by obedient faith (Hebrews 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: For I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and on all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments: I am the LORD. The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you, and no plague will befall you to destroy you, when I strike the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On all the gods of Egypt. The night exposes every idol. Pharaoh, honoured as a god, cannot protect even his own son.

When I see the blood. Safety depends not on the family’s goodness but on the blood of the substitute: judgment falls on the lamb instead of the firstborn.

Christ in view. “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). His blood shields us from God’s judgment (Romans 5:9). Thank God that he sees the blood of Christ over you.

How Jewish readers take it. For Jewish families Passover is above all the festival of redemption, kept at the Seder, where each generation is to see itself as brought out of Egypt (Mishnah Pesachim 10:5). Since the temple fell no lamb is sacrificed; a roasted bone on the Seder plate recalls it. Many Jewish interpreters see the blood as a sign of obedience and belonging rather than an offering for sin. Both traditions look back to the God who rescues his people and forward to a greater redemption. This commentary hears that hope answered in Christ, our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-28: The night made a memorial before it happens, instructions to the elders, and the children's question.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Memorial Forever

Each generation is to receive the rescue as its own.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the strange meal was built to make children ask. Now: the redeemed hunt the old leaven out of the house (1 Cor. 5:6-8), and the Lord's Supper recalls the Lamb until he comes.

verseByVerse.quote: "This day shall be for you a memorial day, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD; throughout your generations, as a statute forever, you shall keep it as a feast. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. On the first day you shall remove leaven out of your houses, for if anyone eats what is leavened, from the first day until the seventh day, that person shall be cut off from Israel. On the first day you shall hold a holy assembly, and on the seventh day a holy assembly. No work shall be done on those days. But what everyone needs to eat, that alone may be prepared by you. And you shall observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread, for on this very day I brought your hosts out of the land of Egypt. Therefore you shall observe this day, throughout your generations, as a statute forever. In the first month, from the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the month at evening. For seven days no leaven is to be found in your houses. If anyone eats what is leavened, that person will be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether he is a sojourner or a native of the land. You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwelling places you shall eat unleavened bread."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A memorial day is a day of remembrance that makes the past present to each generation.

Leaven was yeast, or a piece of old fermented dough used to raise new dough. A little spreads through the whole batch (1 Corinthians 5:6–8).

To be cut off meant exclusion from Israel, or death at God’s hand: disregarding his ordinance was serious. A holy assembly was a sacred gathering for worship, on which no ordinary work was done.

Where Christians differ: should Christians keep Passover? Some keep a Christian Seder. This commentary’s view: Passover is fulfilled in Christ, and Jesus made his last Passover the Lord’s Supper (Luke 22:15–20). Learning from a Seder can be helpful, but it is not required (Colossians 2:16–17).

Clear out the “old leaven” in your life, not to earn redemption but because you have been redeemed.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) became a picture of sin spreading through a whole lump of dough.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, "Go and select lambs for yourselves according to your clans, and kill the Passover lamb. Take a bunch of hyssop and dip it in the blood that is in the basin, and touch the lintel and the two doorposts with the blood that is in the basin. None of you shall go out of the door of his house until the morning. For the LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians, and when he sees the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts, the LORD will pass over the door and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike you. You shall observe this rite as a statute for you and for your sons forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hyssop was used like a brush (Leviticus 14:4; Numbers 19:18). David prays, “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean” (Psalm 51:7). At the cross a sponge on hyssop was lifted to Jesus (John 19:29).

The basin may be the “threshold”, where the blood was caught at the doorway. No one is to go out, for safety was inside the blood-marked house.

The destroyer. God says he strikes (v. 12) and that he will not let the destroyer enter (v. 23). This commentary’s view: the destroyer is God’s agent, perhaps an angel (2 Samuel 24:16; Hebrews 11:28), acting under his command. The judgment is God’s.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was a small bushy plant used for sprinkling.

verseByVerse.quote: And when you come to the land that the LORD will give you, as he has promised, you shall keep this service. And when your children say to you, 'What do you mean by this service?' you shall say, 'It is the sacrifice of the LORD's Passover, for he passed over the houses of the people of Israel in Egypt, when he struck the Egyptians but spared our houses.'" And the people bowed their heads and worshiped. Then the people of Israel went and did so; as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When your children say. Worship is meant to raise questions, and the Jewish Passover Seder still includes the children’s questions. The answer is the story of what God did: a sacrifice that spared them.

The people did as the LORD had commanded, acting in faith before they saw the result. When children ask about baptism or the Lord’s Supper, tell them the story of the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 29-51: The firstborn struck at midnight, Israel driven out with Egypt's silver and a mixed multitude, the 430 years fulfilled to the day, and who may eat the Passover.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Exodus at Midnight

Every condition Pharaoh set is surrendered, and the door is opened to any foreigner who joins the covenant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: membership was by covenant sign, not bloodline. Now: the redeemed come from every nation (Rev. 7:9).

verseByVerse.quote: At midnight the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat on his throne to the firstborn of the captive who was in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of the livestock. And Pharaoh rose up in the night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians. And there was a great cry in Egypt, for there was not a house where someone was not dead. Then he summoned Moses and Aaron by night and said, "Up, go out from among my people, both you and the people of Israel; and go, serve the LORD, as you have said. Take your flocks and your herds, as you have said, and be gone, and bless me also!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Egypt drowned Israel’s sons; now its own sons die, and a great cry goes up from every house.

Three kinds of firstborn meet in this night. Egypt’s firstborn died. Israel’s firstborn was spared by a lamb. God’s own firstborn Son was not spared, so that we might be (Romans 8:32).

Rise up, go. Every condition Pharaoh made is gone: children, flocks, everything. In bless me also the king who claimed to be a god asks a blessing from the slaves’ God.

God does not delight in suffering, and the grief of that night was real. Nine warnings preceded it, and judgment came only when mercy was refused (Romans 2:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: The Egyptians were urgent with the people to send them out of the land in haste. For they said, "We shall all be dead." So the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneading bowls being bound up in their cloaks on their shoulders. The people of Israel had also done as Moses told them, for they had asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing. And the LORD had given the people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, so that they let them have what they asked. Thus they plundered the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The dough carried out before it was leavened is the origin of the unleavened bread of the feast (v. 39).

Asked … plundered. This was not theft. As foretold (3:21–22; Genesis 15:14), Israel asked, God gave them favour, and the Egyptians gave willingly: spoil won without battle, and wages for unpaid labour. God keeps his promises to the letter.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides women and children. A mixed multitude also went up with them, and very much livestock, both flocks and herds. And they baked unleavened cakes of the dough that they had brought out of Egypt, for it was not leavened, because they were thrust out of Egypt and could not wait, nor had they prepared any provisions for themselves. The time that the people of Israel lived in Egypt was 430 years. At the end of 430 years, on that very day, all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt. It was a night of watching by the LORD, to bring them out of the land of Egypt; so this same night is a night of watching kept to the LORD by all the people of Israel throughout their generations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They travel from Rameses, the store city (1:11), to Succoth, a camp east in the delta whose name means “booths”.

Where Christians differ: the numbers. Some read the Hebrew elef (“thousand”) as “clan” or “military unit”, giving far smaller numbers. Others hold the large figure, supported by the census totals (Numbers 1:46; Exodus 38:25–26). This commentary’s view: the plain reading is a very large company; the alternative is held by faithful scholars and does not affect the truth of the event.

A mixed multitude. Non-Israelites joined them, perhaps Egyptians who feared God’s word (9:20). God’s people was never a pure bloodline.

Genesis 15:13 rounds the 430 years to 400, and the exodus comes on that very day: God’s timetable is exact. As the LORD kept watch over them that night, they keep watch in remembrance.
verseByVerse.note: Six hundred thousand men implies a total population of perhaps two million, though some take the numbers differently.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "This is the statute of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it, but every slave that is bought for money may eat of it after you have circumcised him. No foreigner or hired worker may eat of it. It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not take any of the flesh outside the house, and you shall not break any of its bones. All the congregation of Israel shall keep it. If a stranger shall sojourn with you and would keep the Passover to the LORD, let all his males be circumcised. Then he may come near and keep it; he shall be as a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person shall eat of it. There shall be one law for the native and for the stranger who sojourns among you." All the people of Israel did just as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron. And on that very day the LORD brought the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No foreigner. The line is not race but covenant: a foreigner here is an outsider who had not joined God’s people. A slave or a resident foreigner who took the covenant sign given to Abraham, circumcision (Genesis 17), could eat as one born in the land. One law covers native and foreigner: grace is open to all who come in God’s way.

Not break any of its bones. Fulfilled at the cross: the soldiers did not break Jesus’ legs, “that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘Not one of his bones will be broken’” (John 19:36).

The gospel does not exclude outsiders. In Christ, Gentiles are brought near (Ephesians 2:12–13); faith, not ancestry, is the condition. Thank God for the Lamb whose death was planned and foretold in every detail.

12.theology:
Substitution. The lamb dies in the place of the firstborn: salvation is by a substitute's blood, not by merit.

Christ our Passover. The spotless lamb, the applied blood, the unbroken bones: all are fulfilled in Jesus.

Redemption remembered. The Passover becomes a perpetual memorial, fulfilled in the Lord's Supper, by which the church proclaims Christ's death until he comes.
12.examples:
Then: On the night of judgment God's people went free, not by their worth but by the blood.

Now: Whoever trusts Christ is covered by his blood, and the judgment passes over them for ever. Every Lord's Supper recalls this redemption until he comes.

13.title: Consecration and the Guiding Presence
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine."<sup>3</sup>Then Moses said to the people, "Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for by a strong hand the LORD brought you out from this place. No leavened bread shall be eaten.<sup>4</sup>Today, in the month of Abib, you are going out.<sup>5</sup>And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this service in this month.<sup>6</sup>Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Unleavened bread shall be eaten for seven days; no leavened bread shall be seen with you, and no leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory.<sup>8</sup>You shall tell your son on that day, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.'<sup>9</sup>And it shall be to you as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes, that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth. For with a strong hand the LORD has brought you out of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>You shall therefore keep this statute at its appointed time from year to year.<sup>11</sup>"When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your fathers, and shall give it to you,<sup>12</sup>you shall set apart to the LORD all that first opens the womb. All the firstborn of your animals that are males shall be the LORD's.<sup>13</sup>Every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.<sup>14</sup>And when in time to come your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' you shall say to him, 'By a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery.<sup>15</sup>For when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of man and the firstborn of animals. Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all the males that first open the womb, but all the firstborn of my sons I redeem.'<sup>16</sup>It shall be as a mark on your hand or frontlets between your eyes, for by a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt."<sup>17</sup>When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, "Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt."<sup>18</sup>But God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the people of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt equipped for battle.<sup>19</sup>Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the sons of Israel solemnly swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones with you from here."<sup>20</sup>And they moved on from Succoth and encamped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night.<sup>22</sup>The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before the people.
13.overview:
Redeemed people belong wholly to God. So the first command after the exodus is the consecration of the firstborn: because God spared Israel's firstborn on Passover night, every firstborn now belongs to him.

The chapter also sets the feast and the teaching of children, and then gives one of Scripture's most tender images: the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. He goes before them, leading every step; the God who came down to deliver now travels with his people. He does not redeem his people and leave them to find their own way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-16: The firstborn claimed, the feast to be kept and explained, and the price of redemption.
verseByVerse.theology:
Consecrate the Firstborn

Those God has redeemed now belong to him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the claim on the firstborn was a receipt, not a tax. Now: "you are not your own, for you were bought with a price" (1 Cor. 6:19-20), and the unclean live because the clean died for them (1 Pet. 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To consecrate is to set apart as holy, belonging to God. The claim covers the firstborn male of people and animals.

It is mine. The firstborn were spared by the lamb’s blood; their lives now belong to the one who redeemed them (Numbers 3:13).

This never meant that firstborn children were to be sacrificed. Israel’s firstborn sons were redeemed by a payment (v. 13; Numbers 18:15–16). Child sacrifice was an abomination (Leviticus 18:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to the people, "Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt, out of the house of slavery, for by a strong hand the LORD brought you out from this place. No leavened bread shall be eaten. Today, in the month of Abib, you are going out. And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, which he swore to your fathers to give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this service in this month. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD. Unleavened bread shall be eaten for seven days; no leavened bread shall be seen with you, and no leaven shall be seen with you in all your territory. You shall tell your son on that day, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.' And it shall be to you as a sign on your hand and as a memorial between your eyes, that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth. For with a strong hand the LORD has brought you out of Egypt. You shall therefore keep this statute at its appointed time from year to year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember is the key word: remembering what God did keeps faith alive. The month Abib means “ear of grain”, the spring month when barley ripened.

A sign on your hand … between your eyes. The feast is a reminder that shapes what you do (the hand) and how you think (the mind).

Where Christians differ: literal or figurative? Later Judaism wore tefillin, small boxes holding these words, on arm and forehead. This commentary’s view: the purpose clause, “that the law of the LORD may be in your mouth”, shows the main aim: God’s word governing life. Jesus condemned wearing them for show (Matthew 23:5), not the practice itself.

Obedience did not earn the rescue; they obey because God has already brought them out. Build habits of remembering: Scripture, the Lord’s Day, the Lord’s Supper. You will forget otherwise.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your fathers, and shall give it to you, you shall set apart to the LORD all that first opens the womb. All the firstborn of your animals that are males shall be the LORD's. Every firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. Every firstborn of man among your sons you shall redeem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clean firstborn animals were sacrificed. The donkey was unclean, unfit for the altar, so it must be redeemed with a lamb or have its neck broken. Redeem here is Hebrew padah, to release by paying a price: a lamb dies in the donkey’s place.

Every firstborn of man. Israel’s sons stand where the donkey stands: unable to be offered, needing a substitute. Later they were redeemed with five shekels (Numbers 18:16), and the Levites were taken in their place (Numbers 3:12).

Christ in view. Jesus, the firstborn, was himself presented and redeemed as a baby (Luke 2:22–24), and then gave his life as the ransom for us (Mark 10:45).

verseByVerse.quote: And when in time to come your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' you shall say to him, 'By a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, from the house of slavery. For when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both the firstborn of man and the firstborn of animals. Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD all the males that first open the womb, but all the firstborn of my sons I redeem.' It shall be as a mark on your hand or frontlets between your eyes, for by a strong hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When your son asks. The faith is taught by answering children’s questions, and the answer tells the whole story: not only rescue but judgment too, Pharaoh’s refusal and the death of Egypt’s firstborn. The cost explains the redemption.

Parents, do not leave out the hard parts when you tell children the gospel: sin, judgment and the cost of the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17-22 — The Pillar of Cloud and Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 17-22: The long road, Joseph's bones, and the pillar that did not depart.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pillar of Cloud and Fire

God chooses the road his people can bear, and goes on it with them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a promise made to a dying man was kept through the long years. Now: God's detours are not evidence that he has mislaid the map, and his guidance is his presence.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, "Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt." But God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the people of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt equipped for battle. Moses took the bones of Joseph with him, for Joseph had made the sons of Israel solemnly swear, saying, "God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones with you from here." And they moved on from Succoth and encamped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness. And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, that they might travel by day and by night. The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The coastal road was guarded by Egyptian forts. It was perhaps two weeks’ march to Canaan, but they would meet war at once, and God knew their weakness.

Equipped for battle may mean “in orderly ranks”: organised, but not yet ready to fight.

Joseph had made Israel swear to carry them home (Genesis 50:25). Hebrews calls it faith (Hebrews 11:22).

The pillar of cloud and fire was the visible sign of God’s presence, leading by day and giving light by night. It did not depart for forty years, through every grumbling and rebellion.

The longer road was not punishment: God chose the way they could bear (1 Corinthians 10:13). When he leads you by a longer road than you wanted, he may be sparing you a battle you were not ready for. Thank God who goes before you and never leaves (Hebrews 13:5).
verseByVerse.note: “The way of the land of the Philistines” was the coastal military road; God led them away from war. Moses took Joseph’s bones as promised.

13.theology:
Redemption and consecration. Those whom God redeems, he claims. The firstborn are his; we who are redeemed by Christ are not our own.

The wisdom of God's leading. God chooses the road his people can bear, and his detours are mercies.

The guiding presence of God. The pillar of cloud and fire reveals a God who never departs from his people, a presence fulfilled in Christ and the Spirit who lives in us.
13.examples:
Then: Having redeemed his people, God claimed their firstborn as his own and led them out himself.

Now: Redeemed by Christ, we belong wholly to God. And we are never left to find our own way: he leads us by his Word and Spirit, choosing wise paths, promising never to leave us nor forsake us.

14.title: The LORD Will Fight for You
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"Tell the people of Israel to turn back and encamp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon; you shall encamp facing it, by the sea.<sup>3</sup>For Pharaoh will say of the people of Israel, 'They are wandering in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.'<sup>4</sup>And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." And they did so.<sup>5</sup>When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, the mind of Pharaoh and his servants was changed toward the people, and they said, "What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?"<sup>6</sup>So he made ready his chariot and took his army with him,<sup>7</sup>and took six hundred chosen chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt with officers over all of them.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the people of Israel while the people of Israel were going out defiantly.<sup>9</sup>The Egyptians pursued them, all Pharaoh's horses and chariots and his horsemen and his army, and overtook them encamped at the sea, by Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon.<sup>10</sup>When Pharaoh drew near, the people of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them, and they feared greatly. And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD.<sup>11</sup>They said to Moses, "Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us in bringing us out of Egypt?<sup>12</sup>Is not this what we said to you in Egypt: 'Leave us alone that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness."<sup>13</sup>And Moses said to the people, "Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today. For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall never see again.<sup>14</sup>The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent."<sup>15</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward.<sup>16</sup>Lift up your staff, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, that the people of Israel may go through the sea on dry ground.<sup>17</sup>And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they shall go in after them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, his chariots, and his horsemen.<sup>18</sup>And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I have gotten glory over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen."<sup>19</sup>Then the angel of God who was going before the host of Israel moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them,<sup>20</sup>coming between the host of Egypt and the host of Israel. And there was the cloud and the darkness. And it lit up the night without one coming near the other all night.<sup>21</sup>Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided.<sup>22</sup>And the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.<sup>23</sup>The Egyptians pursued and went in after them into the midst of the sea, all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots, and his horsemen.<sup>24</sup>And in the morning watch the LORD in the pillar of fire and of cloud looked down on the Egyptian forces and threw the Egyptian forces into a panic,<sup>25</sup>clogging their chariot wheels so that they drove heavily. And the Egyptians said, "Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians."<sup>26</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, that the water may come back upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen."<sup>27</sup>So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its normal course when the morning appeared. And as the Egyptians fled into it, the LORD threw the Egyptians into the midst of the sea.<sup>28</sup>The waters returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen; of all the host of Pharaoh that had followed them into the sea, not one of them remained.<sup>29</sup>But the people of Israel walked on dry ground through the sea, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.<sup>30</sup>Thus the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.<sup>31</sup>Israel saw the great power that the LORD used against the Egyptians, so the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.
14.overview:
Trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea, with no human way out, Israel panics. And there, in utter helplessness, God works his greatest salvation: "The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent." Salvation is received, not achieved. We do not contribute to it; we behold it.

God divides the sea, and Israel passes through on dry ground from death to life, while the same waters destroy their enemies. The army that terrified them at nightfall lies dead on the shore by morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-14 — Trapped, Terrified, and Told to Stand Still
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-14: A deliberate camp against the sea, Pharaoh's pursuit, Israel's panic, and Moses' answer: stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology:
Trapped, Terrified, and Told to Stand Still

The trap is God's, set for his glory over Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the people rewrote slavery as safety. Now: a known misery can feel safer than an unknown deliverance, and some rescues ask only that we stop thrashing.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Tell the people of Israel to turn back and encamp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon; you shall encamp facing it, by the sea. For Pharaoh will say of the people of Israel, 'They are wandering in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.' And I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and he will pursue them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, and the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." And they did so. When the king of Egypt was told that the people had fled, the mind of Pharaoh and his servants was changed toward the people, and they said, "What is this we have done, that we have let Israel go from serving us?" So he made ready his chariot and took his army with him, and took six hundred chosen chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt with officers over all of them. And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt, and he pursued the people of Israel while the people of Israel were going out defiantly. The Egyptians pursued them, all Pharaoh's horses and chariots and his horsemen and his army, and overtook them encamped at the sea, by Pi-hahiroth, in front of Baal-zephon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Turn back and encamp. God leads them deliberately into a dead end, with the sea behind. Pi-hahiroth, Migdol and Baal-zephon were places near the sea; their sites are uncertain.

Israel looks lost and cornered, wandering and shut in: bait for Pharaoh. As before, Pharaoh’s own will and God’s purpose meet, and God will get glory, showing his weight and honour over Pharaoh and his army.

Egypt sends six hundred chosen chariots, its elite force: the grief of the tenth plague has given way to anger at the loss of their labour.

God does not lead his people into danger carelessly. He leads them where his power will be seen.

verseByVerse.quote: When Pharaoh drew near, the people of Israel lifted up their eyes, and behold, the Egyptians were marching after them, and they feared greatly. And the people of Israel cried out to the LORD. They said to Moses, "Is it because there are no graves in Egypt that you have taken us away to die in the wilderness? What have you done to us in bringing us out of Egypt? Is not this what we said to you in Egypt: 'Leave us alone that we may serve the Egyptians'? For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness." And Moses said to the people, "Fear not, stand firm, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will work for you today. For the Egyptians whom you see today, you shall never see again. The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No graves in Egypt? This is bitter sarcasm, for Egypt was famous for tombs. They already rewrite slavery as better than freedom.

Fear not, stand firm, see. They are to stand their ground and watch what God will do. The salvation here is rescue from death, worked wholly by God, for the LORD will fight for you: the battle is his (2 Chronicles 20:15–17). To be silent is to stop panicking and complaining.

This is not a rule of passivity for every situation; next God says “go forward” (v. 15). It concerns the battle only God can win. In a crisis you cannot fix, stop the panic and look to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 15-25: Go forward; the pillar moves behind; the sea divides all night; Egypt's wheels clog.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sea Divided

Israel walks through on dry ground, and Egypt confesses too late that the LORD fights for them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel had to step towards the water before it opened. Now: Christ is a fragrance of life to some and of death to others (2 Cor. 2:16).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Why do you cry to me? Tell the people of Israel to go forward. Lift up your staff, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it, that the people of Israel may go through the sea on dry ground. And I will harden the hearts of the Egyptians so that they shall go in after them, and I will get glory over Pharaoh and all his host, his chariots, and his horsemen. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I have gotten glory over Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen." Then the angel of God who was going before the host of Israel moved and went behind them, and the pillar of cloud moved from before them and stood behind them, coming between the host of Egypt and the host of Israel. And there was the cloud and the darkness. And it lit up the night without one coming near the other all night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why do you cry to me? A time for prayer gives way to a time for obedience. Prayer is not wrong, but it does not replace obedience when God has spoken.

Go forward. They must walk towards the water before it parts: faith acts on God’s word.

The angel is God’s own presence in the pillar (23:20–21), darkness to the enemy and light to his people (2 Corinthians 2:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the LORD drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided. And the people of Israel went into the midst of the sea on dry ground, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left. The Egyptians pursued and went in after them into the midst of the sea, all Pharaoh's horses, his chariots, and his horsemen. And in the morning watch the LORD in the pillar of fire and of cloud looked down on the Egyptian forces and threw the Egyptian forces into a panic, clogging their chariot wheels so that they drove heavily. And the Egyptians said, "Let us flee from before Israel, for the LORD fights for them against the Egyptians."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A strong east wind all night. God uses means and takes time: a real event in the physical world, controlled by him.

The waters stood like a wall on both sides. Dry ground is the same word as Genesis 1:9: this is a new creation, as land emerges from the waters.

In the morning watch, the last part of the night before dawn, God looked down and threw the army into panic, clogging their chariot wheels.

Where Christians differ: the Red Sea or a Sea of Reeds? Hebrew yam suph can mean “sea of reeds”, and some place the crossing at a shallow lake in the delta. This commentary’s view: the location is uncertain, but the text describes deep water standing as walls and an army drowned. Whatever the place, it was a miracle, not a wade through marsh.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew phrase behind “Red Sea” may mean “Sea of Reeds.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 26-31: The waters return, and Israel fears and believes.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Enemy Swallowed Up

The same waters save and judge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore. Now: the enemy that owned us — sin, death, accusation — lies still on the shore behind those who are in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea, that the water may come back upon the Egyptians, upon their chariots, and upon their horsemen." So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to its normal course when the morning appeared. And as the Egyptians fled into it, the LORD threw the Egyptians into the midst of the sea. The waters returned and covered the chariots and the horsemen; of all the host of Pharaoh that had followed them into the sea, not one of them remained. But the people of Israel walked on dry ground through the sea, the waters being a wall to them on their right hand and on their left. Thus the LORD saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore. Israel saw the great power that the LORD used against the Egyptians, so the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not one remained. The army that hunted them is gone, in the waters where Egypt drowned Israel’s sons (1:22).

Saved is Hebrew yasha, the root of the name “Jesus”.

Feared the LORD and believed. Reverent awe and trust were the purpose of the trap, and they believed Moses, God’s servant, too.

Paul calls the crossing a baptism into Moses (1 Corinthians 10:1–2): passing through judgment safely, united to the deliverer, with the old enemy drowned behind. Yet many fell later; being part of the crossing did not guarantee faithfulness.

Christ in view. Jesus passed through the waters of death for us (Luke 12:50), and in him we pass from death to life.

Their faith was not yet secure: three days later they grumble (15:24). Experiences must become steady trust. Praise God who saves from enemies you could never defeat.

14.theology:
Salvation belongs to the LORD. Israel only watches; God does the saving.

The Red Sea as baptism. The crossing is the pattern of Christian baptism: through the waters from death to life, "baptized into Moses" (1 Cor. 10:2).

The same waters save and judge. Salvation and judgment flow from one hand.
14.examples:
Then: Trapped between army and sea, Israel was told to stand still and see God save.

Now: When we are cornered with no way out, the gospel call is the same: stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD. At the cross our true enemies were defeated, and in Christ we have passed through the waters of judgment into new life.

15.title: The Song of the Redeemed
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD, saying, "I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.<sup>2</sup>The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father's God, and I will exalt him.<sup>3</sup>The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.<sup>4</sup>"Pharaoh's chariots and his host he cast into the sea, and his chosen officers were sunk in the Red Sea.<sup>5</sup>The floods covered them; they went down into the depths like a stone.<sup>6</sup>Your right hand, O LORD, glorious in power, your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy.<sup>7</sup>In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries; you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble.<sup>8</sup>At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up; the floods stood up in a heap; the deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.<sup>9</sup>The enemy said, 'I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, my desire shall have its fill of them. I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them.'<sup>10</sup>You blew with your wind; the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters.<sup>11</sup>"Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders?<sup>12</sup>You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them.<sup>13</sup>"You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed; you have guided them by your strength to your holy abode.<sup>14</sup>The peoples have heard; they tremble; pangs have seized the inhabitants of Philistia.<sup>15</sup>Now are the chiefs of Edom dismayed; trembling seizes the leaders of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan have melted away.<sup>16</sup>Terror and dread fall upon them; because of the greatness of your arm, they are still as a stone, till your people, O LORD, pass by, till the people pass by whom you have purchased.<sup>17</sup>You will bring them in and plant them on your own mountain, the place, O LORD, which you have made for your abode, the sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have established.<sup>18</sup>The LORD will reign forever and ever."<sup>19</sup>For when the horses of Pharaoh with his chariots and his horsemen went into the sea, the LORD brought back the waters of the sea upon them, but the people of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea.<sup>20</sup>Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.<sup>21</sup>And Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea."<sup>22</sup>Then Moses made Israel set out from the Red Sea, and they went into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water.<sup>23</sup>When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter; therefore it was named Marah.<sup>24</sup>And the people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What shall we drink?"<sup>25</sup>And he cried to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the LORD made for them a statute and a rule, and there he tested them,<sup>26</sup>saying, "If you will diligently listen to the voice of the LORD your God, and do that which is right in his eyes, and give ear to his commandments and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer."<sup>27</sup>Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped there by the water.
15.overview: Redeemed people sing. The first thing Israel does on the far shore is break into the Song of the Sea, the oldest hymn of salvation in Scripture: no dirge but an explosion of doxology, for the saved cannot keep silent. The song celebrates who God is: the warrior who fights for his people, majestic in holiness, the King who reigns forever. It looks back at the sea and forward to the sanctuary his hands will establish. Then, three days later, bitter water tests whether praise has become trust.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-12 — The LORD Is a Warrior
