verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-12: The victory at the sea, and the enemy's boasts answered by one breath.
verseByVerse.theology:
The LORD Is a Warrior

The song celebrates what God has done, not what Israel did.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the first thing God's people are recorded singing is their rescue. Now: mercy to slaves and judgment on slavers are one act seen from two ends.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD, saying, "I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea. The LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father's God, and I will exalt him. The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name. "Pharaoh's chariots and his host he cast into the sea, and his chosen officers were sunk in the Red Sea. The floods covered them; they went down into the depths like a stone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worship responds to redemption. Triumphed gloriously is literally “he is highly exalted”: the song is about God, not Israel.

My strength and my song. God gives the strength and is the theme of the song, and he is my rescue. The words are echoed in Psalm 118:14 and Isaiah 12:2. “My God … my father’s God” joins personal faith and inherited faith.

A man of war. God is a warrior who fights for his people. This is no violent God who loves bloodshed. He fights for slaves against their oppressor, and his warfare is justice. Christ fights the final battle by his word (Revelation 19:15).
verseByVerse.note: The first song the Bible calls a song: Israel’s hymn of victory.

verseByVerse.quote: Your right hand, O LORD, glorious in power, your right hand, O LORD, shatters the enemy. In the greatness of your majesty you overthrow your adversaries; you send out your fury; it consumes them like stubble. At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up; the floods stood up in a heap; the deeps congealed in the heart of the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s right hand, the hand of strength and skill, is his power in action, and his fury is his burning anger against those who rose against his people. The blast of your nostrils is the east wind of 14:21, and the waters that congealed are poetry for walls of water standing still.

Praise God whose power is greater than every force you fear.

verseByVerse.quote: The enemy said, 'I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the spoil, my desire shall have its fill of them. I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them.' You blew with your wind; the sea covered them; they sank like lead in the mighty waters. "Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders? You stretched out your right hand; the earth swallowed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will pursue, I will overtake. The enemy makes six boasts of “I will”; pride speaks loudly. One breath from God answers them all.

Who is like you … among the gods? The plagues judged Egypt’s gods (12:12). God is majestic in holiness, utterly other and pure.

This does not make other gods real rivals. It is the language of incomparability: no so-called god compares (Psalm 96:5; 1 Corinthians 8:4–6).

The earth swallowed them: “earth” here may mean the sea, or the grave.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-18: The nations, the sanctuary, and the everlasting reign.
verseByVerse.theology:
Leading to the Sanctuary

The exodus is a beginning: it leads to worship where God dwells.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: "Who is like you, O LORD?" answers Pharaoh's "Who is the LORD?" Now: the redeemed still sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb (Rev. 15:3-4).

verseByVerse.quote: "You have led in your steadfast love the people whom you have redeemed; you have guided them by your strength to your holy abode. The peoples have heard; they tremble; pangs have seized the inhabitants of Philistia. Now are the chiefs of Edom dismayed; trembling seizes the leaders of Moab; all the inhabitants of Canaan have melted away. Terror and dread fall upon them; because of the greatness of your arm, they are still as a stone, till your people, O LORD, pass by, till the people pass by whom you have purchased. You will bring them in and plant them on your own mountain, the place, O LORD, which you have made for your abode, the sanctuary, O Lord, which your hands have established. The LORD will reign forever and ever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Steadfast love is Hebrew hesed, loyal covenant love that does not let go; this is its first appearance in Exodus.

Your holy abode … your sanctuary is the place where God will dwell among them: Sinai, the land, and finally Jerusalem’s temple (Psalm 78:54).

Philistia, Edom, Moab and Canaan hear and tremble (Joshua 2:9–11). Purchased may also be translated “created”: God has acquired a people for himself.

The song climbs to its climax: the LORD is King for ever. The song begun on the shore of the Red Sea will be completed before the throne, where the victorious sing, “Great and amazing are your deeds, O Lord God the Almighty!” (Revelation 15:3). Sing to the King who redeemed you and is leading you home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 19-21: Miriam leads the women in the refrain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Miriam's Song

Joy in salvation overflows into the whole community.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the girl who watched the basket in the reeds sees the sea take an army. Now: not everyone writes the song, but everyone may sing it.

verseByVerse.quote: For when the horses of Pharaoh with his chariots and his horsemen went into the sea, the LORD brought back the waters of the sea upon them, but the people of Israel walked on dry ground in the midst of the sea. Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing. And Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Miriam the prophetess is probably the sister who watched the basket (2:4). A prophetess speaks God’s word; here she leads praise.

Tambourine and dancing are joyful worship with the body, and Israel’s women often celebrated victories this way (1 Samuel 18:6). Not every service must include dancing, but whole-hearted, physical joy in God has its place (Psalm 149:3).
verseByVerse.note: Miriam is the first woman in the Bible called a prophetess.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-27: Bitter water at Marah, made sweet, a new name for God, and the springs of Elim.
verseByVerse.theology:
Marah and Elim

The God who saved at the sea heals in the desert.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the same mouths sang on the shore and grumbled three days later. Now: God does not always take his people around the bitter place, but through it to the springs.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses made Israel set out from the Red Sea, and they went into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water. When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter; therefore it was named Marah. And the people grumbled against Moses, saying, "What shall we drink?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shur lay on the road to Sinai. After three days the same mouths that sang now complain, and the water at Marah is undrinkable, perhaps brackish.

They grumbled against their leader, but in truth against God (16:8). Their need was not imaginary, for thirst in the desert is deadly; the sin is distrust, not need. When praise is quickly followed by trouble, bring your need to God, not your grumbling to others.
verseByVerse.note: “Marah” means bitterness (ESV note). Shur was the wilderness east of Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: And he cried to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a log, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the LORD made for them a statute and a rule, and there he tested them, saying, "If you will diligently listen to the voice of the LORD your God, and do that which is right in his eyes, and give ear to his commandments and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer." Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they encamped there by the water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A log, or “a tree”, is an ordinary means. Some early Christian writers saw a picture of the cross, which makes bitter things sweet.

God tested a people he had already redeemed, to show whether they would trust and obey. The diseases of Egypt are the plagues: God, who struck Egypt, can keep Israel from such judgments.

I am the LORD, your healer. The God who restores and makes whole leads them on to Elim, with twelve springs and seventy palms: rest and plenty after bitterness.

Where Christians differ: does God promise health to the obedient? Some teach that faith and obedience guarantee healing. This commentary’s view: the promise belongs to Israel’s covenant life in the land, set beside its curses (Deuteronomy 28). God does heal, and will heal fully at the resurrection, but faithful believers still get ill (2 Timothy 4:20).

Thank God, your healer, for every healing and for the final healing to come.

15.theology:
Praise as the response to redemption. Salvation accomplished overflows into worship, and theology rightly ends in praise.

No one is like God. The song magnifies the unique, holy, warrior-King.

The everlasting reign of God. "The LORD will reign forever and ever." The exodus opens onto the eternal kingdom, fulfilled in Christ.
15.examples:
Then: Standing on the far shore with their enemies dead behind them, the redeemed people sang.

Now: We who have been brought through the waters in Christ join the song of Moses and the Lamb. Our worship now is the rehearsal of the eternal praise we will sing before the throne.

16.title: Bread from Heaven
16.text: <sup>1</sup>They set out from Elim, and all the congregation of the people of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>And the whole congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness,<sup>3</sup>and the people of Israel said to them, "Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger."<sup>4</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not.<sup>5</sup>On the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather daily."<sup>6</sup>So Moses and Aaron said to all the people of Israel, "At evening you shall know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt,<sup>7</sup>and in the morning you shall see the glory of the LORD, because he has heard your grumbling against the LORD. For what are we, that you grumble against us?"<sup>8</sup>And Moses said, "When the LORD gives you in the evening meat to eat and in the morning bread to the full, because the LORD has heard your grumbling that you grumble against him— what are we? Your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses said to Aaron, "Say to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, 'Come near before the LORD, for he has heard your grumbling.'"<sup>10</sup>And as soon as Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud.<sup>11</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>12</sup>"I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Say to them, 'At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Then you shall know that I am the LORD your God.'"<sup>13</sup>In the evening quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay around the camp.<sup>14</sup>And when the dew had gone up, there was on the face of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground.<sup>15</sup>When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.<sup>16</sup>This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Gather of it, each one of you, as much as he can eat. You shall each take an omer, according to the number of the persons that each of you has in his tent.'"<sup>17</sup>And the people of Israel did so. They gathered, some more, some less.<sup>18</sup>But when they measured it with an omer, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. Each of them gathered as much as he could eat.<sup>19</sup>And Moses said to them, "Let no one leave any of it over till the morning."<sup>20</sup>But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it till the morning, and it bred worms and stank. And Moses was angry with them.<sup>21</sup>Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat; but when the sun grew hot, it melted.<sup>22</sup>On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two omers each. And when all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses,<sup>23</sup>he said to them, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD; bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and all that is left over lay aside to be kept till the morning.'"<sup>24</sup>So they laid it aside till the morning, as Moses commanded them, and it did not stink, and there were no worms in it.<sup>25</sup>Moses said, "Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD; today you will not find it in the field.<sup>26</sup>Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is a Sabbath, there will be none."<sup>27</sup>On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they found none.<sup>28</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?<sup>29</sup>See! The LORD has given you the Sabbath; therefore on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Remain each of you in his place; let no one go out of his place on the seventh day."<sup>30</sup>So the people rested on the seventh day.<sup>31</sup>Now the house of Israel called its name manna. It was like coriander seed, white, and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey.<sup>32</sup>Moses said, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Let an omer of it be kept throughout your generations, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.'"<sup>33</sup>And Moses said to Aaron, "Take a jar, and put an omer of manna in it, and place it before the LORD to be kept throughout your generations."<sup>34</sup>As the LORD commanded Moses, so Aaron placed it before the testimony to be kept.<sup>35</sup>The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land. They ate the manna till they came to the border of the land of Canaan.<sup>36</sup>(An omer is the tenth part of an ephah.)
16.overview:
Barely a month out of Egypt, the redeemed grumble against God, wishing they had died in Egypt where at least there was bread. Even the redeemed heart is prone to forget grace and crave its old slavery. Yet God answers with mercy: he rains "bread from heaven."

The manna is a daily lesson in dependence. It must be gathered each morning and cannot be hoarded, except before the Sabbath, when a double portion keeps. God teaches his people to trust him one day at a time and to rest. The manna was the shadow; Christ, the bread of life, is the substance.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-12: One month out, grumbling for Egypt's meat pots, and God's answer: bread from heaven, a day at a time.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grumbling and Grace

God answers slander with provision, and complaint against his servants reaches him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: hunger rewrote slavery as good catering. Now: God still meets our grumbling with patience before he corrects it.

verseByVerse.quote: They set out from Elim, and all the congregation of the people of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after they had departed from the land of Egypt. And the whole congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, and the people of Israel said to them, "Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meat pots and bread to the full. Memory edits the past. Egypt was whips and drowned sons, but under pressure they remember only food.

They even accuse God’s servants of plotting to kill the whole assembly. Hunger is not sin; the sin is ingratitude and distrust after so many signs of God’s care. When you are tempted to romanticise life before Christ, remember what it really was.
verseByVerse.note: The wilderness of Sin lay in the Sinai peninsula; the name is unrelated to the English word.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not. On the sixth day, when they prepare what they bring in, it will be twice as much as they gather daily." So Moses and Aaron said to all the people of Israel, "At evening you shall know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the LORD, because he has heard your grumbling against the LORD. For what are we, that you grumble against us?" And Moses said, "When the LORD gives you in the evening meat to eat and in the morning bread to the full, because the LORD has heard your grumbling that you grumble against him— what are we? Your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rain bread from heaven. God’s answer to slander is grace.

A day’s portion every day. Enough for today only: the daily provision teaches daily dependence, as Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread (Matthew 6:11). God gives it that I may test them, to reveal and train their hearts: will they trust and obey?

Your grumbling is against the LORD. Complaints against God’s servants reach God himself.

Planning ahead is not wrong. Joseph stored grain for famine at God’s word (Genesis 41). The manna trained trust where God himself had promised daily supply.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses said to Aaron, "Say to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, 'Come near before the LORD, for he has heard your grumbling.'" And as soon as Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the people of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the LORD appeared in the cloud. And the LORD said to Moses, "I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Say to them, 'At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread. Then you shall know that I am the LORD your God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The grumblers are summoned into God’s presence, and the glory of the LORD appeared, his visible majesty in the cloud. His answer to complaint is to show himself, and to promise a double provision: meat at twilight and bread in the morning.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-21: Quail and manna; enough for each; and what was hoarded rots.
verseByVerse.theology:
Bread from Heaven

Provision that cannot be stockpiled teaches trust.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul used verse 18 to argue for generosity (2 Cor. 8:15). Now: what is grasped past the day it was given for goes bad in the hand.

verseByVerse.quote: In the evening quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay around the camp. And when the dew had gone up, there was on the face of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground. When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat. This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Gather of it, each one of you, as much as he can eat. You shall each take an omer, according to the number of the persons that each of you has in his tent.'" And the people of Israel did so. They gathered, some more, some less. But when they measured it with an omer, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. Each of them gathered as much as he could eat.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Quail are migrating birds that often land exhausted in Sinai.

What is it? Hebrew man hu, the origin of “manna”.

An omer was a day’s ration. Whoever gathered much or little had exactly enough. Paul uses this to urge Christians to share (2 Corinthians 8:13–15).

Where Christians differ: what was manna? Some compare a sweet resin produced by tamarisk shrubs in Sinai. This commentary’s view: that resin is small, seasonal and local. Manna fell in quantity enough for a nation, daily for forty years, stopped on the Sabbath and ended when they entered Canaan (Joshua 5:12). It was God’s miraculous provision.
verseByVerse.note: An omer was about 2 quarts (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to them, "Let no one leave any of it over till the morning." But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it till the morning, and it bred worms and stank. And Moses was angry with them. Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat; but when the sun grew hot, it melted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The command to leave none till morning asked them to trust God for tomorrow, and they disobeyed on the very first day. The hoarded manna bred worms and stank: greed and anxiety spoil good gifts.

This is not a ban on saving or wise stewardship. It was a specific test of trust in God’s daily provision. But the lesson holds: hoarding in fear, instead of trusting, spoils.

Is anxiety about tomorrow leading you to grasp more than you need (Matthew 6:34)?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-36 — The Sabbath Provision and a Memorial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-36: A double portion and Israel's first Sabbath, weeks before Sinai; an omer kept as a memorial; forty years of manna.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sabbath Provision and a Memorial

Rest arrives as a gift before it is a rule.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). Now: Jesus is the bread from heaven that a man may eat and not die (John 6:31-51).

verseByVerse.quote: On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two omers each. And when all the leaders of the congregation came and told Moses, he said to them, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Tomorrow is a day of solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD; bake what you will bake and boil what you will boil, and all that is left over lay aside to be kept till the morning.'" So they laid it aside till the morning, as Moses commanded them, and it did not stink, and there were no worms in it. Moses said, "Eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD; today you will not find it in the field. Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day, which is a Sabbath, there will be none." On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they found none. And the LORD said to Moses, "How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws? See! The LORD has given you the Sabbath; therefore on the sixth day he gives you bread for two days. Remain each of you in his place; let no one go out of his place on the seventh day." So the people rested on the seventh day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A day of solemn rest is a complete rest, a day set apart for God.

Israel keeps the Sabbath weeks before the Ten Commandments: rest rooted in creation (Genesis 2:2–3) and given as a gift.

It did not stink. The same food that rotted overnight on other days kept for the Sabbath: obedience, not technique, decides.

How long will you refuse? God’s exasperated question at repeated disobedience.

The Sabbath is given: a gift to enjoy, not a burden to carry.

Where Christians differ: is the Sabbath binding today? Some say this pre-Sinai Sabbath shows it binds all people. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath was given to Israel as a sign of the covenant (31:13) and is fulfilled in Christ, who gives true rest (Hebrews 4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17). The Lord’s Day is a glad privilege for worship and rest, not a legal burden.
verseByVerse.note: The first explicit mention of the Sabbath as a command to Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the house of Israel called its name manna. It was like coriander seed, white, and the taste of it was like wafers made with honey. Moses said, "This is what the LORD has commanded: 'Let an omer of it be kept throughout your generations, so that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.'" And Moses said to Aaron, "Take a jar, and put an omer of manna in it, and place it before the LORD to be kept throughout your generations." As the LORD commanded Moses, so Aaron placed it before the testimony to be kept.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Manna looked like coriander seed, small, round and white, and tasted sweet like wafers made with honey.

A jar of manna was kept as a memorial, so that later generations could see the bread God gave.

Before the testimony means in front of the ark, which held “the testimony”, the tablets of the law (25:16). The jar was placed there later, with Aaron’s staff (Hebrews 9:4).

Keep reminders of God’s past provision. They strengthen faith for the future.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land. They ate the manna till they came to the border of the land of Canaan. (An omer is the tenth part of an ephah.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Forty years. Every morning, through every rebellion, God fed them (Deuteronomy 8:3–4). An omer is a tenth of an ephah.

The lesson is that “man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3).

Christ in view. Jesus said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). Those who ate manna died; whoever eats the living bread from heaven will live for ever (John 6:49–51).

Thank God for daily bread, and for the Bread of Life.
verseByVerse.note: An ephah was about 3/5 bushel (ESV note).

16.theology:
The grumbling heart and patient grace. The redeemed forget grace and idealize bondage, yet God answers murmuring with merciful provision.

Daily dependence. The manna teaches trust for each day, contentment and Sabbath rest.

Christ the bread of life. The manna is fulfilled in Jesus, the living bread from heaven who alone satisfies the soul's hunger for ever.
16.examples:
Then: When the redeemed grumbled and longed for Egypt's bread, God fed them daily for forty years.

Now: We still crave the security of our old slaveries and forget past mercies. God still calls us to daily dependence, and offers us himself, the true bread from heaven. Feeding on Christ by faith, we shall never hunger.

17.title: The Rock and the Uplifted Hands
17.text: <sup>1</sup>All the congregation of the people of Israel moved on from the wilderness of Sin by stages, according to the commandment of the LORD, and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink.<sup>2</sup>Therefore the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Give us water to drink." And Moses said to them, "Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD?"<sup>3</sup>But the people thirsted there for water, and the people grumbled against Moses and said, "Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?"<sup>4</sup>So Moses cried to the LORD, "What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me."<sup>5</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go.<sup>6</sup>Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel.<sup>7</sup>And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarreling of the people of Israel, and because they tested the LORD by saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"<sup>8</sup>Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim.<sup>9</sup>So Moses said to Joshua, "Choose for us men, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand."<sup>10</sup>So Joshua did as Moses told him, and fought with Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.<sup>11</sup>Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.<sup>12</sup>But Moses' hands grew weary, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. So his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.<sup>13</sup>And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.<sup>14</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the ears of Joshua, that I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven."<sup>15</sup>And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner,<sup>16</sup>saying, "A hand upon the throne of the LORD! The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."
17.overview:
Two scenes, both pointing to Christ. First, the people thirst and quarrel, testing God: "Is the LORD among us or not?" God has Moses strike the rock at Horeb, and water gushes out for a thirsting people. The Rock must be struck for the water of life to flow.

Second, Amalek attacks, and while Moses' hands are lifted Israel prevails; when they tire, Aaron and Hur hold them up until sunset. The battle below is won by the uplifted hands above.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Water from the Struck Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-7: No water at Rephidim, a quarrel close to stoning, and water from the struck rock at Horeb.
verseByVerse.theology:
Water from the Struck Rock

A quarrelling people is answered with water, not with judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the place was named for the people's testing, not for God's gift. Now: more evidence rarely settles "Is the LORD among us or not?"

verseByVerse.quote: All the congregation of the people of Israel moved on from the wilderness of Sin by stages, according to the commandment of the LORD, and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink. Therefore the people quarreled with Moses and said, "Give us water to drink." And Moses said to them, "Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD?" But the people thirsted there for water, and the people grumbled against Moses and said, "Why did you bring us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our livestock with thirst?" So Moses cried to the LORD, "What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel moves from camp to camp as God leads, to Rephidim, near Sinai; its site is uncertain.

Quarreled is Hebrew riv, to bring a legal complaint, to accuse: this is worse than grumbling (15:24).

To test the LORD is to demand that God prove himself on our terms, doubting his presence and goodness (v. 7). Jesus refused to do this (Matthew 4:7).

Asking God for help is not testing him. They did not ask; they accused. When you are desperate, pray as Moses did: “What shall I do?”

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel. And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarreling of the people of Israel, and because they tested the LORD by saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some of the elders come as witnesses, as in a court case, and the staff is the one that struck the Nile, the rod of judgment.

I will stand before you on the rock. God places himself on the rock, then Moses strikes it. The judgment falls where God stands, and life flows to the guilty quarrellers.

Christ in view. Paul says Israel “drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). Christ was struck for us, and from him flows the Spirit, living water (John 7:37–39).

Later, told to speak to a rock, Moses struck it in anger, and was barred from Canaan (Numbers 20:8–12). The rock needed striking only once (Hebrews 9:28).

Psalm 95:8–9 remembers Massah and Meribah and warns, “do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah”.

Is the LORD among us? This is the real question behind their complaint: doubt of God’s presence.
verseByVerse.note: Massah means “testing” and Meribah “quarreling” (ESV notes).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — The Uplifted Hands and the Battle with Amalek
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 8-13: Amalek attacks; Joshua fights below while Moses' hands are held up on the hill.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Uplifted Hands and the Battle with Amalek

Victory is God's, and the hands lifted to him need others to hold them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Joshua fought, Moses prayed, and Aaron and Hur held him up. Now: the work goes on because someone holds up the arms of the one who cannot, and Christ always lives to intercede (Heb. 7:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim. So Moses said to Joshua, "Choose for us men, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand." So Joshua did as Moses told him, and fought with Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed. But Moses' hands grew weary, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. So his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Amalek was a desert people (Genesis 36:12). Deuteronomy says they attacked the weak stragglers at the rear (Deuteronomy 25:17–18).

Joshua is the man who will lead Israel into the land. His name means “the LORD saves”.

The staff of God in my hand is a sign of dependence on God’s power, perhaps raised in prayer.

When Moses’ hands grew weary, the leader needed others. Hur was an elder, in Jewish tradition Miriam’s husband, and with Aaron he held Moses’ hands steady.

Raised hands do not work like magic. Victory comes from God, and the picture is of dependent prayer, which needs support. Hold up the hands of your pastor and leaders in prayer and practical help.
verseByVerse.note: Amalek descended from Esau. This is the first mention of Joshua.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-16 — The LORD Is My Banner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-16: A memorial written in a book, and an altar named The LORD Is My Banner.
verseByVerse.theology:
The LORD Is My Banner

God himself is Israel's rallying point.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the victory is written down and an altar built, so that it will not be forgotten. Now: God's people rally to a standard the enemy cannot touch.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in a book and recite it in the ears of Joshua, that I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven." And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner, saying, "A hand upon the throne of the LORD! The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Write this … in a book. The first command in the Bible to write something down.

Blot out the memory of Amalek. God will judge Amalek completely (1 Samuel 15:2–3).

The LORD Is My Banner. A banner was the standard raised in battle to rally troops.

A hand upon the throne. Perhaps an oath raised to God’s throne, or Amalek’s hand raised against it. Either way, war against Amalek is God’s cause.

Where Christians differ: why perpetual war with Amalek? Some see harsh ethnic hostility. This commentary’s view: Amalek attacked a nation of fleeing slaves from behind, killing the weak, and set itself against God. The judgment is on a persistent enemy of God’s purpose, not on ethnicity, and it gives Christians no licence for violence: our battle is not against flesh and blood (Ephesians 6:12).

Rally to Christ, lifted up for us (John 12:32).

17.theology:
Christ the struck Rock. Christ was struck by God's judgment that living water might flow to thirsting sinners.

The ministry of intercession. Moses' uplifted hands prefigure Christ's ever-living intercession and the church's call to persevering prayer.

The LORD our Banner. The battle and the victory are God's, and the triumph is credited to him alone.
17.examples:
Then: God gave water to a doubting people and victory to a weary one.

Now: Christ our Rock was struck that the living water of the Spirit might flow to us; he ever lives, with hands once outstretched on the cross, to intercede for us. And the church wins its battles under the LORD's banner, holding up one another in prayer.

18.title: Wise Counsel and Shared Burdens
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.<sup>2</sup>Now Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had taken Zipporah, Moses' wife, after he had sent her home,<sup>3</sup>along with her two sons. The name of the one was Gershom (for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land"),<sup>4</sup>and the name of the other, Eliezer (for he said, "The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh").<sup>5</sup>Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness where he was encamped at the mountain of God.<sup>6</sup>And when he sent word to Moses, "I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons with her,"<sup>7</sup>Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. And they asked each other of their welfare and went into the tent.<sup>8</sup>Then Moses told his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake, all the hardship that had come upon them in the way, and how the LORD had delivered them.<sup>9</sup>And Jethro rejoiced for all the good that the LORD had done to Israel, in that he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians.<sup>10</sup>Jethro said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharaoh and has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians.<sup>11</sup>Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people."<sup>12</sup>And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God; and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God.<sup>13</sup>The next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from morning till evening.<sup>14</sup>When Moses' father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, "What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning till evening?"<sup>15</sup>And Moses said to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to inquire of God;<sup>16</sup>when they have a dispute, they come to me and I decide between one person and another, and I make them know the statutes of God and his laws."<sup>17</sup>Moses' father-in-law said to him, "What you are doing is not good.<sup>18</sup>You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone.<sup>19</sup>Now obey my voice; I will give you advice, and God be with you! You shall represent the people before God and bring their cases to God,<sup>20</sup>and you shall warn them about the statutes and the laws, and make them know the way in which they must walk and what they must do.<sup>21</sup>Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people as chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.<sup>22</sup>And let them judge the people at all times. Every great matter they shall bring to you, but any small matter they shall decide themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you.<sup>23</sup>If you do this, God will direct you, you will be able to endure, and all this people also will go to their place in peace."<sup>24</sup>So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said.<sup>25</sup>Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people, chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.<sup>26</sup>And they judged the people at all times. Any hard case they brought to Moses, but any small matter they decided themselves.<sup>27</sup>Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away to his own country.
18.overview:
After the great deliverance comes a quieter chapter on leadership and community. Jethro, Moses' Midianite father-in-law, hears what God has done and confesses the LORD: an early fruit of the exodus among the nations.

Then Jethro watches Moses judge the people alone from morning to evening and counsels him to share the load. Ministry is a shared calling, and the qualifications are spiritual before they are managerial.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-12: Jethro brings Moses' family, hears the whole story, confesses the LORD, and eats with the elders before God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jethro's Worship

A foreign priest hears testimony and believes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the Egyptians were told they would know and did not; a foreign priest heard and believed. Now: a testimony with the hard parts left in is more convincing, not less.

verseByVerse.quote: Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt. Now Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, had taken Zipporah, Moses' wife, after he had sent her home, along with her two sons. The name of the one was Gershom (for he said, "I have been a sojourner in a foreign land"), and the name of the other, Eliezer (for he said, "The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh"). Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, came with his sons and his wife to Moses in the wilderness where he was encamped at the mountain of God. And when he sent word to Moses, "I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you with your wife and her two sons with her,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At some point Moses had sent Zipporah and the boys back, perhaps for safety during the plagues.

The names of Gershom and Eliezer tell Moses’ story: Gershom recalls “a sojourner there” (2:22).

The mountain of God is Horeb (Sinai), where Israel is camped.
verseByVerse.note: Eliezer means “My God is help” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Moses went out to meet his father-in-law and bowed down and kissed him. And they asked each other of their welfare and went into the tent. Then Moses told his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake, all the hardship that had come upon them in the way, and how the LORD had delivered them. And Jethro rejoiced for all the good that the LORD had done to Israel, in that he had delivered them out of the hand of the Egyptians. Jethro said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians and out of the hand of Pharaoh and has delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians. Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people." And Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God; and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Moses' father-in-law before God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses tells the whole story, the deliverance and the hardships along the way.

Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods. A pagan priest comes to know the LORD through testimony. Like Rahab, Ruth and the Magi, an outsider sees what many insiders miss.

To eat bread before God is to share a covenant meal of fellowship with Israel’s leaders.

This does not mean all religions honour the same God: Jethro turns from other gods to confess the LORD. Tell people what God has done for you; testimony can bring others to worship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 13-23: You are not able to do it alone, and the remedy: delegation to godly men in tiers.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jethro's Counsel

Moses keeps the work before God and teaching, and shares the judging.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the pattern returns in the seventy elders and the seven of Acts 6. Now: the work is real, the servant is finite, and the answer is structure, not heroism.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from morning till evening. When Moses' father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, "What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, and all the people stand around you from morning till evening?" And Moses said to his father-in-law, "Because the people come to me to inquire of God; when they have a dispute, they come to me and I decide between one person and another, and I make them know the statutes of God and his laws." Moses' father-in-law said to him, "What you are doing is not good. You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses sits to settle disputes and teach God’s will, as the people come to inquire of God, bringing their cases for God’s decision through him.

Not good. These are the same words as Genesis 2:18: being alone is not good.

Wear yourselves out is literally “wither”, like a fading leaf; both the leader and the people waiting suffer. Moses’ motives were not wrong, but sincere devotion can still be unwise. Leaders, parents and carers: doing everything yourself can harm the people you serve.

verseByVerse.quote: Now obey my voice; I will give you advice, and God be with you! You shall represent the people before God and bring their cases to God, and you shall warn them about the statutes and the laws, and make them know the way in which they must walk and what they must do. Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people as chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. And let them judge the people at all times. Every great matter they shall bring to you, but any small matter they shall decide themselves. So it will be easier for you, and they will bear the burden with you. If you do this, God will direct you, you will be able to endure, and all this people also will go to their place in peace."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses keeps his unique role, to represent the people before God and to teach his statutes.

Able men who fear God, trustworthy, who hate a bribe. The four qualifications are competence, godliness, honesty and integrity about money: character comes before structure.

Jethro submits his advice to God’s approval: if God so commands.

Where Christians differ: a model for church government? Some see here a pattern for elders and deacons. This commentary’s view: it shows the wisdom of shared leadership by qualified, godly people, which the New Testament also teaches (Acts 6:1–6; 1 Timothy 3), but it is not a blueprint for every church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 24-27: Moses listens, and Jethro goes home.
verseByVerse.theology:
Moses Listens

The man who spoke with God takes counsel from an outsider.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the meekest man on earth (Num. 12:3) took correction from a newcomer. Now: not everyone who helps God's people is called to stay, and a brief contribution is not a small one.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said. Moses chose able men out of all Israel and made them heads over the people, chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. And they judged the people at all times. Any hard case they brought to Moses, but any small matter they decided themselves. Then Moses let his father-in-law depart, and he went away to his own country.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The man who spoke with God from the bush humbly takes advice from an outsider. The difficult cases came to Moses; the others were settled by the judges.

Not every piece of advice must be accepted; Moses tested this against God’s will (v. 23). Be willing to receive wise counsel, even from unexpected people (Proverbs 15:22).

18.theology:
The nations drawn to worship. Jethro the Gentile confesses the LORD's supremacy — a first fruit of God's purpose to be known among all peoples.

Shared leadership and delegation. Ministry is a shared calling. Wise leaders multiply themselves through godly, qualified people rather than carrying every burden alone.

Character before competence. The qualifications for leadership are chiefly spiritual, anticipating New Testament eldership.
18.examples:
Then: A Gentile priest worshipped the God of the exodus, then gave Moses wise counsel, and the humble leader listened.

Now: Our salvation testifies to the watching world and draws others to worship. And the work of ministry is shared: God raises up qualified, godly leaders to carry the load together.

19.title: The Mountain That Burned with Fire
19.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third new moon after the people of Israel had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that day they came into the wilderness of Sinai.<sup>2</sup>They set out from Rephidim and came into the wilderness of Sinai, and they encamped in the wilderness. There Israel encamped before the mountain,<sup>3</sup>while Moses went up to God. The LORD called to him out of the mountain, saying, "Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and tell the people of Israel:<sup>4</sup>'You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.<sup>5</sup>Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine;<sup>6</sup>and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.' These are the words that you shall speak to the people of Israel."<sup>7</sup>So Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him.<sup>8</sup>All the people answered together and said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses reported the words of the people to the LORD.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am coming to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with you, and may also believe you forever." When Moses told the words of the people to the LORD,<sup>10</sup>the LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments<sup>11</sup>and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.<sup>12</sup>And you shall set limits for the people all around, saying, 'Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it. Whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death.<sup>13</sup>No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot; whether beast or man, he shall not live.' When the trumpet sounds a long blast, they shall come up to the mountain."<sup>14</sup>So Moses went down from the mountain to the people and consecrated the people; and they washed their garments.<sup>15</sup>And he said to the people, "Be ready for the third day; do not go near a woman."<sup>16</sup>On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled.<sup>17</sup>Then Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they took their stand at the foot of the mountain.<sup>18</sup>Now Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire. The smoke of it went up like the smoke of a kiln, and the whole mountain trembled greatly.<sup>19</sup>And as the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him in thunder.<sup>20</sup>The LORD came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. And the LORD called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down and warn the people, lest they break through to the LORD to look and many of them perish.<sup>22</sup>Also let the priests who come near to the LORD consecrate themselves, lest the LORD break out against them."<sup>23</sup>And Moses said to the LORD, "The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai, for you yourself warned us, saying, 'Set limits around the mountain and consecrate it.'"<sup>24</sup>And the LORD said to him, "Go down, and come up bringing Aaron with you. But do not let the priests and the people break through to come up to the LORD, lest he break out against them."<sup>25</sup>So Moses went down to the people and told them.
19.overview:
In the third month, about two months after leaving Egypt, Israel arrives at Sinai, and God's opening words are pure grace: "I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself." Redemption comes first, then covenant; deliverance first, then law. We obey because we are saved, not in order to be saved.

His purpose is breathtaking: that they be his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. The redeemed are God's prized treasure, set apart to make his presence known to the world. But this God is holy: the mountain quakes in fire and smoke, the people tremble, and bounds are set so that none may touch it and die. The trembling at Sinai prepares us to marvel that in Christ the same holiness becomes our welcome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-6: At the mountain of the bush, God reminds Israel what he has done before he offers the covenant.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Kingdom of Priests

The covenant is offered to a people already carried to God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: eighteen chapters of grace come before one commandment. Now: the church too is called out first and then commissioned.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third new moon after the people of Israel had gone out of the land of Egypt, on that day they came into the wilderness of Sinai. They set out from Rephidim and came into the wilderness of Sinai, and they encamped in the wilderness. There Israel encamped before the mountain, while Moses went up to God. The LORD called to him out of the mountain, saying, "Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob, and tell the people of Israel: 'You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel camps before Sinai, where the bush burned, and the promise of 3:12 is fulfilled.

Eagles’ wings picture strong, protective care, carrying the young (Deuteronomy 32:11). God has brought you to myself: the goal of the exodus is not only a place but God himself.

Grace before law. God reminds them of what he has done before he gives commands. The law is given to a redeemed people, not as a way to be redeemed (20:2).
verseByVerse.note: Israel reached Sinai about two months after leaving Egypt and stayed nearly a year.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.' These are the words that you shall speak to the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To obey my voice and keep my covenant is to live as God’s people. Obedience does not earn their election, for God has already redeemed them (v. 4); it is the way to live in the covenant.

Treasured possession is Hebrew segullah, a king’s personal treasure, kept apart from the general wealth. All the earth is mine: God chooses Israel not because he owns nothing else but for a purpose among the nations.

A kingdom of priests. A priest brings God to people and people to God, and Israel was to represent God to the nations as a holy nation, set apart for him and distinct in life and worship.

Christ in view. Peter gives these titles to the church: “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-15 — Consecration for the Holy God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 7-15: The people's promise, three days of consecration, and a boundary round the mountain.
verseByVerse.theology:
Consecration for the Holy God

Sinners must be made ready to meet him.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the same promise is made twice more and broken at the calf. Now: sincerity in the moment of promising is not the same as power to keep it.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the LORD had commanded him. All the people answered together and said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses reported the words of the people to the LORD. And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am coming to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with you, and may also believe you forever." When Moses told the words of the people to the LORD,
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the LORD has spoken we will do. The promise is sincere, but overconfident. They will say it again (24:3, 7) and make the golden calf within weeks (32:1–6).

In a thick cloud God reveals himself while veiling his glory, and he confirms Moses as his spokesman so that the people may believe him for ever.

Their promise was not hypocritical. It shows the weakness of human resolve and our need for a new heart (Jeremiah 31:31–33). Make your promises to God humbly, relying on his grace and his Spirit, not your strength.

verseByVerse.quote: the LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people. And you shall set limits for the people all around, saying, 'Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it. Whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death. No hand shall touch him, but he shall be stoned or shot; whether beast or man, he shall not live.' When the trumpet sounds a long blast, they shall come up to the mountain." So Moses went down from the mountain to the people and consecrated the people; and they washed their garments. And he said to the people, "Be ready for the third day; do not go near a woman."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To consecrate themselves is to set themselves apart, preparing to meet the holy God. Washing their garments is outward cleanness picturing inward readiness.

A boundary is set around the mountain, and whoever touches it must die: God’s holiness is dangerous to sinners. A long blast on the ram’s horn will signal when they may approach.

Do not go near a woman. Husbands and wives abstain from marital relations for the three days of consecration (1 Samuel 21:4–5). This is not because sex is sinful, but because they set aside even good things to prepare to meet God (1 Corinthians 7:5).

Prepare your heart before you come to worship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 16-25: Thunder, fire, a quaking mountain and a growing trumpet, and a second warning not to break through.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theophany

God comes down in majesty, and the barrier keeps the people alive.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: no one could touch the mountain and live. Now: believers have come not to Sinai but to Mount Zion and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Heb. 12:18-24).

verseByVerse.quote: On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled. Then Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they took their stand at the foot of the mountain. Now Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire. The smoke of it went up like the smoke of a kiln, and the whole mountain trembled greatly. And as the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him in thunder. The LORD came down on Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. And the LORD called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The whole mountain trembled. Creation shakes at God’s presence (Psalm 68:8), and a trumpet with no human player grows louder and louder.

God answered him in thunder, or “with a voice”: God speaks. He is not unapproachable for ever, for he comes down to make a covenant with them.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down and warn the people, lest they break through to the LORD to look and many of them perish. Also let the priests who come near to the LORD consecrate themselves, lest the LORD break out against them." And Moses said to the LORD, "The people cannot come up to Mount Sinai, for you yourself warned us, saying, 'Set limits around the mountain and consecrate it.'" And the LORD said to him, "Go down, and come up bringing Aaron with you. But do not let the priests and the people break through to come up to the LORD, lest he break out against them." So Moses went down to the people and told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Break through to the LORD to look. This is curiosity that treats holiness lightly. The priests here were perhaps the firstborn or heads of families, who served as priests before the Levites were appointed.

Break out against them. God’s holiness consumes those who approach carelessly (2 Samuel 6:6–7).

The barrier that kept people out at Sinai is opened by Christ’s blood (Hebrews 12:18–24). Approach God with confidence through Christ, and with reverence and awe, “for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:29).

19.theology:
Grace before law. God redeems first, then gives the covenant. Obedience flows from salvation and never earns it.

A treasured, priestly people. God claims the redeemed as his treasured possession and a kingdom of priests, fulfilled in the church.

The holiness of God. Sinai reveals a holy God whom sinners cannot approach casually, and drives us to the Mediator.
19.examples:
Then: God established his covenant at a mountain that burned with fire, calling redeemed slaves to be his own people.

Now: We are saved by grace and then called to holy obedience. The terror of Sinai reminds us how holy God is — and how amazing it is that in Christ we now draw near to that same God with boldness and joy.

20.title: The Ten Words: Law as Gift
20.text: <sup>1</sup>And God spoke all these words, saying,<sup>2</sup>"I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.<sup>3</sup>"You shall have no other gods before me.<sup>4</sup>"You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.<sup>5</sup>You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me,<sup>6</sup>but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.<sup>7</sup>"You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.<sup>8</sup>"Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.<sup>9</sup>Six days you shall labor, and do all your work,<sup>10</sup>but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates.<sup>11</sup>For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.<sup>12</sup>"Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.<sup>13</sup>"You shall not murder.<sup>14</sup>"You shall not commit adultery.<sup>15</sup>"You shall not steal.<sup>16</sup>"You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.<sup>17</sup>"You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's."<sup>18</sup>Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off<sup>19</sup>and said to Moses, "You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die."<sup>20</sup>Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin."<sup>21</sup>The people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.<sup>22</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Thus you shall say to the people of Israel: 'You have seen for yourselves that I have talked with you from heaven.<sup>23</sup>You shall not make gods of silver to be with me, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold.<sup>24</sup>An altar of earth you shall make for me and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you.<sup>25</sup>If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it.<sup>26</sup>And you shall not go up by steps to my altar, that your nakedness be not exposed on it.'
20.overview:
The Ten Commandments do not begin with a command but with the gospel. God speaks first as Redeemer, then as Lawgiver: the commandments are not a ladder by which slaves climb to freedom but the shape of life for a people already redeemed.

The first four govern love for God; the last six, with the fifth as the hinge, love for neighbour, and Jesus summed them up in those two loves. The law also exposes our inability to keep it and drives us to Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-11 — The First Table: Love for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-11: A sentence of history before any command, then the four commandments about God: no other gods, no images, the name, the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.theology:
The First Table: Love for God

God alone, worshipped in his own way, his name honoured, his rest received.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law was given to a people already rescued. Now: Christ's people keep it as children, not as candidates.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke all these words, saying, "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything depends on God's rescue being verse 2 rather than verse 20. The commandments do not begin "obey me and I will be your God." They begin with a God who has already acted, addressing people who are already his: the LORD your God. Israel is not told how to earn deliverance but how a delivered people lives.

Get that order wrong and the Decalogue (the “ten words”) becomes a way of earning. Keep it, and the commandments are the shape of gratitude: If you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15) puts the love first and the keeping second, in the same order Sinai does.

Do the Ten Commandments bind Christians? The law God gave Israel had three strands. Its ceremonial laws, sacrifices, feasts and food rules, were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Col 2:16–17; Heb 10:1). Its civil laws governed Israel as a nation ruled directly under God, and ended when that nation did. Its moral law, summed up here, rests on God’s own character and still binds: Jesus and the apostles repeat these commandments (Matt 19:18–19; Rom 13:9; Eph 6:2). The Christian keeps them not to be saved but as one saved, with the law written on the heart (Jer 31:33) by the Spirit who now moves God's people to walk in his ways (Ezek 36:27). The fourth, as this commentary reads it, is the one the New Testament treats as fulfilled in Christ (see on vv. 9–11, where the views are set out).
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew calls them “the ten words” (ESV note at 34:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall have no other gods before me. "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth. You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, but showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before me is literally before my face: not merely "ahead of me in rank" but "in my presence," which is everywhere. There is no place where a rival may be quietly kept.

The second commandment is distinct, and it matters. The first forbids worshipping the wrong God; the second forbids worshipping the right God in the wrong way. Israel's calf will not be a foreign deity: Aaron announces a feast to the LORD (32:5). They break the second while sincerely intending to keep the first.

The reason given is jealousy, and the word needs explaining. Jealousy is contemptible when a man has no claim on the woman; it is right when he does. God's jealousy is not insecurity but a husband's response to a wife's unfaithfulness, Scripture's own repeated image.

The clause that troubles readers most, iniquity visited to the third and fourth generation, needs two things said. The words of those who hate me do real work: this is not innocent descendants punished for an ancestor's sin, and Ezekiel states the principle flatly: the soul who sins shall die, and a son shall not bear the guilt of his father (Ezek. 18:20). What is described is idolatry spreading through a family that keeps choosing it. And the real point is the asymmetry: three or four generations against thousands. Judgment is measured in handfuls of generations; steadfast love in thousands.

Does this forbid pictures of Jesus? It plainly forbids images made to be worshipped or to represent God, since Israel saw no form at Sinai (Deut 4:15–16). Christians differ over depictions of Christ. Many hold that since he took a real human body he may be pictured, especially for teaching. The Reformed confessions answer that no image can show the person who is God and man, and that an image used in worship breaks this commandment. The Reformed caution is the safer course: no image of Christ in worship or as an aid to prayer. Art in general, which God himself commanded for the tabernacle, is not forbidden.
verseByVerse.note: “Before me” can be rendered “besides me”; “thousands” may mean “the thousandth generation” (ESV notes). Roman Catholics and Lutherans count the commandments differently, joining “no other gods” and “no images” and dividing the tenth in two; the words themselves are the same. Deuteronomy 5 repeats them with small differences, such as a different reason for the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain. "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In vain. Empty, worthless, to no purpose. Casual swearing is included, but the commandment is much wider than bad language. To bear God's name emptily is to carry it without weight: to invoke it in an oath you do not intend to keep, to claim his authority for your own preference, to be called by his name and live in a way that makes it meaningless to those watching.

The heaviest form is the one nobody notices: a person who bears the name of Christ and whose life empties it of content before the people who know them. That is why the LORD will not hold such a one guiltless. Yet the way back is open: whoever confesses finds Christ faithful to forgive and cleanse (1 John 1:9), and the name he emptied is the name that saves him.

Remember the Sabbath. Not "institute": Israel had kept it since the manna (16:23), weeks before this mountain. The commandment codifies a gift already given.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. On it you shall not do any work, you, or your son, or your daughter, your male servant, or your female servant, or your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates. For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Read the list in verse 10. It is not a list of people who may rest but of people the head of the household is forbidden to make work: sons, daughters, servants, foreign workers, animals. No one could keep this commandment privately while running his farm on somebody else's labour. The Sabbath is the first labour law in Scripture, protecting those with no power to protect themselves, given to a nation that was itself a slave labour force weeks ago. Deuteronomy makes the link explicit: you shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt (Deut. 5:15).

The reason given here is larger: God's own six days and his rest. The rhythm is not an arrangement for productivity; it is built into the world, and keeping it is an act of imitation.

The verse also says something about the creation week itself. Israel's six days of work answer to God's six days, and its seventh to his seventh; the comparison is plainest if his days were ordinary days like theirs, and this commentary reads them so, with the evening and morning of each day in Genesis 1 and Jesus' from the beginning of creation (Mark 10:6). Faithful Christians who read the days as long ages, as a literary framework, or as God's workdays described by analogy to ours answer that the commandment needs only a likeness of pattern, not the same length. Either way, the week Israel kept was patterned on the week God worked.

Underneath it is a claim about trust, which is why the manna taught it first. To stop for a day is to act out the belief that the world is held up by someone else, and that six days of your labour plus God is more than seven days of your labour alone. Refusing to rest is usually a quiet statement about who is keeping things going.

The New Testament handles this commandment carefully. Jesus called himself lord of the Sabbath (Mark 2:28) and healed on it, insisting it was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Paul tells the Colossians not to let anyone pass judgment on them regarding a Sabbath, since these things are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ (Col. 2:16-17). And Hebrews says there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, entered by faith (Heb. 4:9-10). Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the Sabbath is a creation ordinance moved by Christ's resurrection to the first day, so that the Lord's Day is the Christian Sabbath (Acts 20:7; Rev 1:10), and their reasons deserve respect; their strongest is this very verse, which grounds the day in creation, not in Israel's history. This commentary answers that a pattern from creation can still be fulfilled: Hebrews 4 joins God's seventh-day rest (4:4) to the rest Christ gives, so the pattern reaches its goal in him. Seventh-day Adventists hold that Saturday still binds. The weight of the New Testament, as this commentary reads it, is that the day was a shadow now fulfilled in Christ, so that no one may bind another's conscience about days (Rom. 14:5–6).

So what does a Christian do on a Sunday? Gather gladly with God's people to worship, rest where you can, and delight in the Lord and his gifts. The Lord's Day is a gift, kept out of joy and wisdom, not a law with rules about work that bind the conscience. And the rest finally comes not from a day but from a person who said come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — The Second Table: Love for Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 12-17: The commandments about neighbour, from the hinge of the fifth to the tenth, which no court could try.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second Table: Love for Neighbor

Parents, life, marriage, property, truth and the heart are guarded.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the commandments protected the weak in Israel's courts and homes. Now: Jesus reads them at the level of the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fifth commandment is the hinge between the commandments about God and those about neighbour. It stands at the join because the family is where a child first meets authority, and contempt learned at home rarely stays there.

Honor is weightier than obey. Obedience has an expiry date; honour does not. A grown man no longer obliged to obey his father is still obliged to honour him, which in practice meant caring for parents who could no longer work, in a world without pensions. Jesus attacked the Pharisees at this point, for a device that let a man dedicate his assets to the temple and so avoid supporting his parents (Mark 7:9-13).

Paul calls it the first commandment with a promise (Eph. 6:2-3), and the promise is corporate as much as personal: a people whose generations hold together lasts in the land God gives.
