A word is owed to those for whom this commandment is hard, because some readers had fathers who were cruel and mothers who were absent. Honour is not the same as pretending, and it does not require calling evil good or handing an abuser continued access. It is a real command with real content — respect for the office, care where care is possible, refusal to hold contempt — and it is not a command to lie about what happened. Anyone still being harmed should seek safety at once.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not murder. "You shall not commit adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Murder. Hebrew ratsach, killing a person outside the law's sanction. It covers manslaughter too, which is why the cities of refuge exist (Numbers 35:11), but never lawful judicial killing or war. The reason lies in Genesis: man is made in God's image, so an assault on a person is an assault on the one he images (Gen. 9:6).

Jesus takes the commandment deeper: everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment (Matt. 5:21-22). He is not adding a stricter rule but exposing what it was always about: the heart the act comes out of.

Adultery. The seventh runs the same way. Marriage is the Bible's picture of God's covenant with his people, which is why unfaithfulness is treated so gravely, and Jesus again takes it inward: everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt. 5:27-28).

Read at the level Jesus reads them, the commandments leave nobody standing, which Paul says is one of their functions: through the law comes knowledge of sin (Rom. 3:20). But the one who read the law so deeply also kept it perfectly in our place, and through his obedience the many are made righteous (Rom. 5:19).

What does the commandment cover? Because it forbids unlawful killing, the same law can give the state the sword (21:12). Killing in self-defence is not murder (22:2), nor is a just war. But it covers the unborn, whom God forms in the womb (Ps 139:13–16; cf. 21:22–25), and so forbids abortion, as it forbids euthanasia and suicide. Anyone who carries grief or guilt from one of these should hear the next word too: no sin is beyond the cleansing of Christ’s blood, and the LORD is near the brokenhearted (Ps 34:18).
verseByVerse.note: Accidental killing (Numbers 35:11) was grave but not capital: the killer fled to a city of refuge.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not steal. "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor. "You shall not covet your neighbor's house; you shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male servant, or his female servant, or his ox, or his donkey, or anything that is your neighbor's."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not steal. Property is real: a person may own something, and taking it is wrong, which sounds obvious until you recall Egypt taking Israel's labour unpaid. The commandment also protects the poor, who have least margin when what little they have is taken.

False witness. Narrower than "do not lie" and sharper, it is set in a courtroom and forbids testimony that destroys a person. Where there was no police force, a false witness was a weapon capable of killing, and a proven false witness received the sentence he sought for his victim (Deut. 19:19). Words about people are treated as actions done to them.

The tenth is unlike all the others. Every earlier commandment could be broken visibly; no court could try this one, and a man could keep the other nine in public while breaking it continuously in private. Its presence shows that the commandments were always about the heart.

Paul, blameless under the law by his own account, said this commandment finished him: I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, "You shall not covet" (Rom. 7:7). The commandment no court could prosecute convicted the most scrupulous of Pharisees.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-21 — The Trembling People and the Mediator
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 18-21: The people stand far off and beg for a mediator, and Moses goes into the darkness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trembling People and the Mediator

Sinners need someone to stand between them and God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: one man went into the dark for the people. Now: the curtain is torn, and the far-off are brought near.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off and said to Moses, "You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die." Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin." The people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They had promised in 19:8 to do everything God said; now they back away and ask Moses to speak instead. Ten commandments heard in God's holy presence have convinced them they cannot survive direct contact. That instinct is correct, and the priesthood, tabernacle and sacrifice that follow are God's answer to the request.

Moses' reply looks contradictory and is not: do not fear, so that you may fear. Two different things share one word: the terror that runs from God is to go; the reverence that keeps from sin is to remain.

Verse 21 is the whole chapter in a single image: the people far off, one man drawing near to the darkness. That is the shape of the old covenant, and its limitation: Israel's access was only ever as good as their mediator, and this one would die on the wrong side of the Jordan.

Which is why the tearing of the temple curtain mattered: the same holiness, and a mediator who did not merely walk into the dark for the people but bore it. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ (Eph. 2:13). Sinai's people sent one man in. At Calvary one man went in and brought the distant people with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-26: An altar of earth or unhewn stone, without steps.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Altar of Earth

Nothing of the worshipper's workmanship may appear where atonement is made.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law came with its own way of forgiveness. Now: at its end stands a cross to which no one can add a chisel mark.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Thus you shall say to the people of Israel: 'You have seen for yourselves that I have talked with you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver to be with me, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold. An altar of earth you shall make for me and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where I cause my name to be remembered I will come to you and bless you. If you make me an altar of stone, you shall not build it of hewn stones, for if you wield your tool on it you profane it. And you shall not go up by steps to my altar, that your nakedness be not exposed on it.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
The closing instructions about altars look like an anticlimax after the thunder. They are not.

Israel's first authorised altar must be made of dirt or unshaped stones. Every surrounding nation carved its holy places elaborately; Israel may not improve on the raw material at all.

Craftsmanship is not wrong: God will fill the tabernacle with Spirit-given skill (31:1-5). The point is what an altar is for. It is where a substitute dies in the worshipper's place, and nothing the worshipper contributes may appear on it. A tooled stone would let a man look at the place of atonement and see his own workmanship.

The last verse forbids steps, so that nakedness is not exposed on the way up: even the approach displays nothing of the worshipper.

So the chapter closes where it began, in grace: ten commandments no one in the camp will keep, and in the same breath an altar with no human contribution in it, the way to be forgiven for not keeping them. At the end of that road stands a cross on which the offering was made entirely by God.

20.theology:
Law framed by grace. The law is a gift to the redeemed, not a price for rescue.

The two tables of love. Love for God and love for neighbour, summarised by Jesus as the whole of the law.

The law as guardian. The perfect standard exposes our sin and leads us to Christ (Gal. 3:24), who kept it for us and bore its curse.
20.examples:
Then: From a mountain of fire God spoke ten words to his redeemed people, and the terrified people begged for a mediator.

Now: The law shows us how to love God and neighbour and how far we fall short. We obey not to be saved but because we are saved, in grateful love to our Redeemer and by the Spirit he has given us.

21.title: The Dignity of Persons Under God's Law
21.text: <sup>1</sup>"Now these are the rules that you shall set before them.<sup>2</sup>When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing.<sup>3</sup>If he comes in single, he shall go out single; if he comes in married, then his wife shall go out with him.<sup>4</sup>If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master's, and he shall go out alone.<sup>5</sup>But if the slave plainly says, 'I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,'<sup>6</sup>then his master shall bring him to God, and he shall bring him to the door or the doorpost. And his master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall be his slave forever.<sup>7</sup>"When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go out as the male slaves do.<sup>8</sup>If she does not please her master, who has designated her for himself, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her.<sup>9</sup>If he designates her for his son, he shall deal with her as with a daughter.<sup>10</sup>If he takes another wife to himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, or her marital rights.<sup>11</sup>And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money.<sup>12</sup>"Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death.<sup>13</sup>But if he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.<sup>14</sup>But if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die.<sup>15</sup>"Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death.<sup>16</sup>"Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death.<sup>17</sup>"Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.<sup>18</sup>"When men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist and the man does not die but takes to his bed,<sup>19</sup>then if the man rises again and walks outdoors with his staff, he who struck him shall be clear; only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall have him thoroughly healed.<sup>20</sup>"When a man strikes his slave, male or female, with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, he shall be avenged.<sup>21</sup>But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be avenged, for the slave is his money.<sup>22</sup>"When men strive together and hit a pregnant woman, so that her children come out, but there is no harm, the one who hit her shall surely be fined, as the woman's husband shall impose on him, and he shall pay as the judges determine.<sup>23</sup>But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life,<sup>24</sup>eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,<sup>25</sup>burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.<sup>26</sup>"When a man strikes the eye of his slave, male or female, and destroys it, he shall let the slave go free because of his eye.<sup>27</sup>If he knocks out the tooth of his slave, male or female, he shall let the slave go free because of his tooth.<sup>28</sup>"When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten, but the owner of the ox shall not be liable.<sup>29</sup>But if the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death.<sup>30</sup>If a ransom is imposed on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed on him.<sup>31</sup>If it gores a man's son or daughter, he shall be dealt with according to this same rule.<sup>32</sup>If the ox gores a slave, male or female, the owner shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.<sup>33</sup>"When a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,<sup>34</sup>the owner of the pit shall make restoration. He shall give money to its owner, and the dead beast shall be his.<sup>35</sup>"When one man's ox butts another's, so that it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and share its price, and the dead beast also they shall share.<sup>36</sup>Or if it is known that the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he shall repay ox for ox, and the dead beast shall be his.
21.overview:
After the Ten Commandments comes the Book of the Covenant (chs. 21-23), case law applying the moral law to life in a fallen, ancient world. Read rightly, these laws reveal a God concerned with justice, mercy and the dignity of every person, especially the weak, and they are notably humane beside the codes of Israel's neighbours.

The chapter opens with servants, and at once we see God's heart: even bondservice is limited, regulated and directed toward freedom. Then it turns to violence, injury and negligence. "Eye for eye" is not a licence for vengeance but a restraint on it, and human life is precious to God because it is made in his image.
21.theology:
The dignity of the image of God. Every person, servant, child or victim, is precious because made in God's image. The law surrounds the vulnerable with protection.

Justice and its limits. The law of "eye for eye" restrains vengeance and guarantees proportion. God's justice is exacting but never cruel.

Personal responsibility before God. We answer to God for our neighbor's welfare and safety.
21.examples:
Then: God's covenant law applied his holy character to daily life, protecting servants, restraining violence, and upholding the dignity of every person in a brutal ancient world.

Now: God still cares for the vulnerable and still holds us responsible for our neighbor's welfare. None of us has kept this law to the edge of the field, but Christ obeyed it perfectly in our place, his obedience is counted as ours (Rom. 5:19), and his Spirit now makes us able to love our neighbour. The Redeemer who gave his life to ransom ours is the final proof of how precious human life is to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-11: Debt-servitude limited to six years, the servant who chooses to stay, and protections for a daughter sold into service.
verseByVerse.theology:
Laws About Slaves

An existing institution is regulated, and pointed toward release.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law gave the vulnerable party the exit. Now: those set free by Christ owe others the freedom they were given.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these are the rules that you shall set before them. When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing. If he comes in single, he shall go out single; if he comes in married, then his wife shall go out with him. If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children shall be her master's, and he shall go out alone. But if the slave plainly says, 'I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,' then his master shall bring him to God, and he shall bring him to the door or the doorpost. And his master shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall be his slave forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after the thunder of Sinai comes case law. The Ten Commandments state principles; these chapters show what those principles look like when two men's oxen collide. A law that never touches Tuesday is not a law anyone lives under.

The first case is slavery, startling in a book about God freeing slaves. Scripture is not endorsing the institution but regulating one that existed everywhere, and the regulation is radical by ancient standards: Hebrew debt-servitude runs six years and ends, for nothing. A man sold himself to clear a debt, and the debt could not own him for life.

The pierced ear. The servant who loves the household and stays is marked at the doorpost as belonging by choice, not because he is owned. Many Christians have heard in it an echo of the Son who freely took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7; Mark 10:45).

Why does the wife stay with the master (v. 4)? She was herself a servant under her own term, given by the master, and her children were born into his house. The law does not let the man take what is not his; it gives him the choice to stay with his family for life (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.note: This section (21–23) is called the Book of the Covenant (24:7). Israel’s slave laws limited service to six years and protected the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go out as the male slaves do. If she does not please her master, who has designated her for himself, then he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her. If he designates her for his son, he shall deal with her as with a daughter. If he takes another wife to himself, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, or her marital rights. And if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing, without payment of money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The rules for a daughter sold into service protect rather than permit: she may not be sold to foreigners, must be treated as a daughter if given to a son, and if a man takes another wife he may not reduce her food, clothing or marital rights. If he fails, she goes free with no payment. The vulnerable party is given an exit with no financial penalty.

It is fair to feel the distance between this and the abolition we would want, and honest to say that Scripture moves toward it rather than arriving at once. Jesus gave the reason when he spoke of divorce: some things Moses permitted and regulated because of your hardness of heart, though from the beginning it was not so (Matt. 19:8). And see where it ends: Paul asks a slave-owner to receive a runaway no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother (Philem. 16), and once that sentence exists in the church, the institution has no ground left to stand on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — Capital Crimes Against Life and Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 12-17: Capital cases: murder distinguished by intent, the parent, and kidnapping.
verseByVerse.theology:
Capital Crimes Against Life and Family

Intent distinguishes crime from accident, and stealing a person is capital.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: a place of refuge stood ready for the accidental killer. Now: the guilty find their refuge in Christ (Heb. 6:18).

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death. But if he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee. But if a man willfully attacks another to kill him by cunning, you shall take him from my altar, that he may die. "Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death. "Whoever steals a man and sells him, and anyone found in possession of him, shall be put to death. "Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The capital cases draw careful distinctions. Murder is death, but where there was no lying in wait, there is a place of refuge. Intent changes everything, and Israelite law will not treat an accident as a crime.

Striking or cursing a parent is capital, which shows how load-bearing the fifth commandment was. So is kidnapping. Set that beside verse 2: voluntary debt-servitude with a fixed term is regulated; stealing a person is a capital crime. The slave trade that later crossed the Atlantic was, by this chapter's standard, a capital crime at every stage.

Do these death penalties still apply? They were civil laws for Israel as a nation ruled directly under God, and they ended with that nation. The moral principle remains: Jesus rebukes those who dishonour father and mother (Mark 7:9–13), and kidnapping and slave-trading stand condemned (1 Tim 1:10). The severity shows how seriously God takes the family and human freedom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-27 — Injury, Restitution, and the Limit of Vengeance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 18-27: Injury and compensation, eye for eye, and two laws protecting servants from their masters.
verseByVerse.theology:
Injury, Restitution, and the Limit of Vengeance

The penalty may not exceed the harm.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the rule was a ceiling, not a floor. Now: Jesus forbids his disciples to insist even on the just amount (Matt. 5:38-39).

verseByVerse.quote: "When men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist and the man does not die but takes to his bed, then if the man rises again and walks outdoors with his staff, he who struck him shall be clear; only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall have him thoroughly healed. "When a man strikes his slave, male or female, with a rod and the slave dies under his hand, he shall be avenged. But if the slave survives a day or two, he is not to be avenged, for the slave is his money. "When men strive together and hit a pregnant woman, so that her children come out, but there is no harm, the one who hit her shall surely be fined, as the woman's husband shall impose on him, and he shall pay as the judges determine. But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe. "When a man strikes the eye of his slave, male or female, and destroys it, he shall let the slave go free because of his eye. If he knocks out the tooth of his slave, male or female, he shall let the slave go free because of his tooth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eye for eye. It sounds savage and is the opposite. In a world of blood feuds where an insult could escalate into a massacre, this is a ceiling, not a floor: the penalty may not exceed the injury. Its whole force is to stop revenge from growing.

Jesus quotes it and does something unexpected: But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil (Matt. 5:38-39). He is not calling the law unjust. He moves the question from what a court may impose to what a disciple may personally demand.

What do verses 20–21 mean by for the slave is his money? They do not license beating. The master who kills his slave is to be punished, which other ancient law codes seldom required. If the slave survives a day or two, the death is not judged deliberate murder, and the master’s loss of a worker is the penalty. And a master who knocks out a slave’s eye or tooth must set him free (vv. 26–27).

What of the pregnant woman in verses 22–25? The ESV reads so that her children come out, a premature birth. If there is no harm, the man pays a fine; if there is harm, to mother or child, the penalty is life for life. Some read the passage as a miscarriage, with a fine for the child’s death and the full penalty only for harm to the mother, which would make the unborn worth less. But the Hebrew words normally describe a live birth, and the law sets the harm to either in the same scale. The better reading treats the unborn child as a person whose life the law protects.

The servant laws are remarkable for their time: a single tooth costs the master the servant himself, because damage to a servant's body forfeits the right to hold him.
verseByVerse.note: “Eye for eye” limited revenge: the penalty was to fit the crime, set by judges, not taken privately.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28-36 — The Goring Ox and the Responsible Owner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 28-36: The goring ox, the open pit, and liability for known risk.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Goring Ox and the Responsible Owner

What the owner knew decides what he owes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: known risk ignored became the owner's responsibility. Now: the God of the thunder claims the field and the well as well as the altar.

verseByVerse.quote: "When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten, but the owner of the ox shall not be liable. But if the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it in, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner also shall be put to death. If a ransom is imposed on him, then he shall give for the redemption of his life whatever is imposed on him. If it gores a man's son or daughter, he shall be dealt with according to this same rule. If the ox gores a slave, male or female, the owner shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.
verseByVerse.commentary: An ox that gores someone to death is destroyed and the owner is not liable: the animal did something unforeseeable. But if it was known to gore and the owner was warned and did not keep it in, he is liable for a death. It turns on the question a modern negligence court would ask: what did he know, and what did he do about it?
verseByVerse.note: Thirty shekels, the price of a slave, was about 12 ounces of silver (ESV note: a shekel was about 2/5 ounce). It was the sum Judas took for Jesus (Matthew 26:15), the price Zechariah had called the lordly price at which the shepherd was valued (Zechariah 11:12–13; Matthew 27:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "When a man opens a pit, or when a man digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restoration. He shall give money to its owner, and the dead beast shall be his. "When one man's ox butts another's, so that it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and share its price, and the dead beast also they shall share. Or if it is known that the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has not kept it in, he shall repay ox for ox, and the dead beast shall be his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pit left uncovered and the ox that kills another man's ox are settled the same way: whoever could reasonably have prevented the loss bears it.

These cases are strikingly ordinary. God has just appeared on a mountain in fire, and within a chapter he is legislating about livestock and open pits. That is not a descent from the sublime; it is the point of the covenant: the God of the thunder intends to govern the field, the well and the argument between neighbours, and a holiness that does not reach the ox is not the holiness he is offering.

22.title: Care for the Vulnerable
22.text: <sup>1</sup>"If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep.<sup>2</sup>If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him,<sup>3</sup>but if the sun has risen on him, there shall be bloodguilt for him. He shall surely pay. If he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft.<sup>4</sup>If the stolen beast is found alive in his possession, whether it is an ox or a donkey or a sheep, he shall pay double.<sup>5</sup>"If a man causes a field or vineyard to be grazed over, or lets his beast loose and it feeds in another man's field, he shall make restitution from the best in his own field and in his own vineyard.<sup>6</sup>"If fire breaks out and catches in thorns so that the stacked grain or the standing grain or the field is consumed, he who started the fire shall make full restitution.<sup>7</sup>"If a man gives to his neighbor money or goods to keep safe, and it is stolen from the man's house, then, if the thief is found, he shall pay double.<sup>8</sup>If the thief is not found, the owner of the house shall come near to God to show whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property.<sup>9</sup>For every breach of trust, whether it is for an ox, for a donkey, for a sheep, for a cloak, or for any kind of lost thing, of which one says, 'This is it,' the case of both parties shall come before God. The one whom God condemns shall pay double to his neighbor.<sup>10</sup>"If a man gives to his neighbor a donkey or an ox or a sheep or any beast to keep safe, and it dies or is injured or is driven away, without anyone seeing it,<sup>11</sup>an oath by the LORD shall be between them both to see whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property. The owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not make restitution.<sup>12</sup>But if it is stolen from him, he shall make restitution to its owner.<sup>13</sup>If it is torn by beasts, let him bring it as evidence. He shall not make restitution for what has been torn.<sup>14</sup>"If a man borrows anything of his neighbor, and it is injured or dies, the owner not being with it, he shall make full restitution.<sup>15</sup>If the owner was with it, he shall not make restitution; if it was hired, it came for its hiring fee.<sup>16</sup>"If a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall give the bride-price for her and make her his wife.<sup>17</sup>If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall pay money equal to the bride-price for virgins.<sup>18</sup>"You shall not permit a sorceress to live.<sup>19</sup>"Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death.<sup>20</sup>"Whoever sacrifices to any god, other than the LORD alone, shall be devoted to destruction.<sup>21</sup>"You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.<sup>22</sup>You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child.<sup>23</sup>If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry,<sup>24</sup>and my wrath will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children fatherless.<sup>25</sup>"If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him.<sup>26</sup>If ever you take your neighbor's cloak in pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down,<sup>27</sup>for that is his only covering, and it is his cloak for his body; in what else shall he sleep? And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate.<sup>28</sup>"You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people.<sup>29</sup>"You shall not delay to offer from the fullness of your harvest and from the outflow of your presses. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me.<sup>30</sup>You shall do the same with your oxen and with your sheep: seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to me.<sup>31</sup>"You shall be consecrated to me. Therefore you shall not eat any flesh that is torn by beasts in the field; you shall throw it to the dogs.
22.overview:
The covenant law continues with property, restitution and social responsibility, but its deepest pulse is the protection of the vulnerable. God's justice aims at restoration, not only retribution.

Then come the sojourner, the widow and the fatherless, the most defenceless in ancient society, and the motive is the exodus itself. Grace received becomes grace extended (Matthew 10:8). The God of the burning bush who heard Israel's cry still bends his ear to the cry of the poor. Concern for the marginalised is not an add-on to biblical faith; it flows from the very heart of the God who redeems.
22.theology:
Restorative justice. Restitution aims to make the victim whole.

God the defender of the vulnerable. The sojourner, widow, and orphan are under God's own protection.

Grace received, grace extended. Remembered redemption fuels mercy toward the weak.
22.examples:
Then: God's law placed the most defenceless under his personal protection.

Now: The God who redeemed us calls us to care for the vulnerable as he cared for us, and gives his Spirit to make us merciful. He still hears the cry of the poor and warns those who oppress them. None of us has kept this law as it asks; Christ kept it perfectly in our place, and his obedience, counted as ours, is the way back for all who confess (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-15: Theft and restitution, the burglar at night and by day, and property held on trust.
verseByVerse.theology:
Laws About Restitution

The law asks first what the victim has lost.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the thief restored more than he took. Now: wrongs done to others are still to be put right where they can be, as a fruit of grace, not a price for it.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man steals an ox or a sheep, and kills it or sells it, he shall repay five oxen for an ox, and four sheep for a sheep. If a thief is found breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no bloodguilt for him, but if the sun has risen on him, there shall be bloodguilt for him. He shall surely pay. If he has nothing, then he shall be sold for his theft. If the stolen beast is found alive in his possession, whether it is an ox or a donkey or a sheep, he shall pay double. "If a man causes a field or vineyard to be grazed over, or lets his beast loose and it feeds in another man's field, he shall make restitution from the best in his own field and in his own vineyard. "If fire breaks out and catches in thorns so that the stacked grain or the standing grain or the field is consumed, he who started the fire shall make full restitution. "If a man gives to his neighbor money or goods to keep safe, and it is stolen from the man's house, then, if the thief is found, he shall pay double. If the thief is not found, the owner of the house shall come near to God to show whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The law on theft turns on restitution rather than punishment. The thief does not merely suffer; he restores, and restores more than he took, so that the victim ends up better off than before the crime. Our reflex is to ask what the offender deserves. Israel's law asks first what the injured party has lost, and makes the offender carry it.

The principle turns up in the New Testament in the mouth of a man nobody expected. Zacchaeus said, if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold (Luke 19:8): this chapter's rate for a stolen sheep, applied voluntarily to a tax career's worth of extortion. Grace had reached him moments earlier, and the first thing it produced was restitution.

The burglar. If a burglar is killed breaking in at night, there is no bloodguilt; the same killing after sunrise brings it. The distinction is visibility. In the dark you cannot know whether the intruder is armed or how many there are; in daylight you can, and lethal force stops being self-defence.

verseByVerse.quote: For every breach of trust, whether it is for an ox, for a donkey, for a sheep, for a cloak, or for any kind of lost thing, of which one says, 'This is it,' the case of both parties shall come before God. The one whom God condemns shall pay double to his neighbor. "If a man gives to his neighbor a donkey or an ox or a sheep or any beast to keep safe, and it dies or is injured or is driven away, without anyone seeing it, an oath by the LORD shall be between them both to see whether or not he has put his hand to his neighbor's property. The owner shall accept the oath, and he shall not make restitution. But if it is stolen from him, he shall make restitution to its owner. If it is torn by beasts, let him bring it as evidence. He shall not make restitution for what has been torn. "If a man borrows anything of his neighbor, and it is injured or dies, the owner not being with it, he shall make full restitution. If the owner was with it, he shall not make restitution; if it was hired, it came for its hiring fee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cases of property held on trust turn on where the risk sits. If a man was paid to keep the animal, he bears more; if the owner was present, he bears it himself; if there is no evidence, the matter goes to an oath before God, and the owner accepts it. In a world without contracts, insurance or CCTV, the system rests on people telling the truth in God's presence.

The quiet assumption underneath the whole chapter is that these laws only work among people who fear God. Once the oath means nothing, the system collapses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 16-20: The seducer pays the bride-price; sorcery, bestiality and sacrifice to other gods carry death.
verseByVerse.theology:
Purity Guarded

The man carries the whole cost, and the nation's boundaries are drawn sharply.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the woman was protected from being discarded. Now: God still cares who carries the cost of sexual sin.

verseByVerse.quote: "If a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall give the bride-price for her and make her his wife. If her father utterly refuses to give her to him, he shall pay money equal to the bride-price for virgins. "You shall not permit a sorceress to live. "Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death. "Whoever sacrifices to any god, other than the LORD alone, shall be devoted to destruction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man who seduces an unbetrothed virgin must pay the bride-price and marry her, or, if her father refuses, pay it anyway. A woman in that culture had lost her marriage prospects and with them her economic future, and the law makes the man carry the full cost with no option to walk away.

Sorcery, bestiality and sacrifice to any god but the LORD each carry death. They are the boundary markers of a nation that is to be different, severe because the nations of Canaan were known for all of them (Leviticus 18:23–24; Deuteronomy 18:9–12).

Does verse 18 justify witch trials? The death penalty belonged to Israel’s civil law, and sorcery there was treason against the covenant God. The church has no such sword (John 18:36), and the witch-hunts of later centuries had no warrant from this text. What remains is the prohibition itself: occult practice, seeking the spirits or the dead, is forbidden to God’s people (Deut 18:10–12; Gal 5:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 21-27: The sojourner, the widow and the fatherless; no interest from the poor; the cloak returned by sunset.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mercy for the Vulnerable

Memory of Egypt becomes mercy to the weak.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: those who had been strangers were to protect strangers. Now: James catches the tone of this section: pure religion visits orphans and widows in their affliction (James 1:27).

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child. If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry, and my wrath will burn, and I will kill you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children fatherless. "If you lend money to any of my people with you who is poor, you shall not be like a moneylender to him, and you shall not exact interest from him. If ever you take your neighbor's cloak in pledge, you shall return it to him before the sun goes down, for that is his only covering, and it is his cloak for his body; in what else shall he sleep? And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the heart of the chapter, and where Israel's law is least like its neighbours'.

The sojourner. The reason is memory: you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. Israel is not told that foreigners have rights in the abstract; it is told to remember what it felt like, which is far harder to argue your way out of. Christians hear the same argument at a deeper level: we too were strangers to God's promises, and in Christ we are no longer strangers and aliens but members of his household (Eph. 2:12, 19).

The widow and the fatherless. The warning has startling heat: the punishment is shaped exactly like the crime, the oppressors' own wives made widows and their children fatherless. God does not merely disapprove of exploiting the defenceless; he undertakes to answer it personally.

The law on lending is not a ban on commerce but a ban on making money out of a neighbour's disaster.

The cloak. Here is what kind of God stands behind this legislation. In the middle of a code about oxen and pits, he stops to consider whether a particular poor man will be cold tonight, and legislates on the strength of it. The guarantee attached is not a penalty clause but a character reference: I will hear, for I am compassionate. The God of the thunder on the mountain is listening for one cold man's complaint about a coat.

Is lending at interest sin? The law forbids profiting from a poor neighbour in his need (cf. Lev 25:35–37), and the principle stands. It did not forbid all interest: Israel could charge interest to a foreigner in trade (Deut 23:20), and Jesus speaks of money placed with bankers to earn it (Matt 25:27). Ordinary commercial lending and saving are not sin; exploiting the desperate is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28-31 — Reverence Toward God and Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 28-31: Reverence for God and rulers, firstfruits and firstborn, and the reason for it all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reverence Toward God and Men

Everything belongs to God first.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul honoured verse 28 at his own trial (Acts 23:5). Now: the redeemed belong to God before they do anything for him.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler of your people. "You shall not delay to offer from the fullness of your harvest and from the outflow of your presses. The firstborn of your sons you shall give to me. You shall do the same with your oxen and with your sheep: seven days it shall be with its mother; on the eighth day you shall give it to me. "You shall be consecrated to me. Therefore you shall not eat any flesh that is torn by beasts in the field; you shall throw it to the dogs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter closes with commands that seem unrelated and share one root: everything belongs to God first. The firstfruits and firstborn are given without delay, and the newborn animal stays seven days with its mother, a small mercy tucked inside a sacrificial regulation.

The last line supplies the reason: You shall be consecrated to me. Not "you shall be moral," but set apart, belonging to someone. Every regulation in these chapters flows from that sentence, which is why Peter could write to Gentile churches, as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct (1 Pet. 1:15).

Did God demand child sacrifice (v. 29)? No. Firstborn sons were given to God and redeemed with a payment (13:13; Num 18:15–16), and the law condemns child sacrifice as an abomination (Lev 18:21; Deut 12:31). The firstborn of Israel lived because the firstborn of Egypt died, and every redeemed son pointed to the Son whom God did not spare.

23.title: Sacred Time and the Guiding Angel
23.text: <sup>1</sup>"You shall not spread a false report. You shall not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness.<sup>2</sup>You shall not fall in with the many to do evil, nor shall you bear witness in a lawsuit, siding with the many, so as to pervert justice,<sup>3</sup>nor shall you be partial to a poor man in his lawsuit.<sup>4</sup>"If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him.<sup>5</sup>If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying down under its burden, you shall refrain from leaving him with it; you shall rescue it with him.<sup>6</sup>"You shall not pervert the justice due to your poor in his lawsuit.<sup>7</sup>Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and righteous, for I will not acquit the wicked.<sup>8</sup>And you shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of those who are in the right.<sup>9</sup>"You shall not oppress a sojourner. You know the heart of a sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.<sup>10</sup>"For six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield,<sup>11</sup>but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave the beasts of the field may eat. You shall do likewise with your vineyard, and with your olive orchard.<sup>12</sup>"Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest; that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant woman, and the alien, may be refreshed.<sup>13</sup>"Pay attention to all that I have said to you, and make no mention of the names of other gods, nor let it be heard on your lips.<sup>14</sup>"Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me.<sup>15</sup>You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. As I commanded you, you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, for in it you came out of Egypt. None shall appear before me empty-handed.<sup>16</sup>You shall keep the Feast of Harvest, of the firstfruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field. You shall keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather in from the field the fruit of your labor.<sup>17</sup>Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD.<sup>18</sup>"You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the fat of my feast remain until the morning.<sup>19</sup>"The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.<sup>20</sup>"Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared.<sup>21</sup>Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him.<sup>22</sup>"But if you carefully obey his voice and do all that I say, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries.<sup>23</sup>"When my angel goes before you and brings you to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, and I blot them out,<sup>24</sup>you shall not bow down to their gods nor serve them, nor do as they do, but you shall utterly overthrow them and break their pillars in pieces.<sup>25</sup>You shall serve the LORD your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you.<sup>26</sup>None shall miscarry or be barren in your land; I will fulfill the number of your days.<sup>27</sup>I will send my terror before you and will throw into confusion all the people against whom you shall come, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you.<sup>28</sup>And I will send hornets before you, which shall drive out the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites from before you.<sup>29</sup>I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you.<sup>30</sup>Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and possess the land.<sup>31</sup>And I will set your border from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates, for I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you.<sup>32</sup>You shall make no covenant with them and their gods.<sup>33</sup>They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against me; for if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you."
23.overview:
The covenant code concludes with laws on justice, sacred time, and a promise of God's guiding presence. Justice in God's kingdom is blind to bribes and faction, and reaches even the enemy's straying ox.

Then God appoints sacred time: the sabbath year, the weekly Sabbath and three annual feasts. God structures time itself around worship, rest and remembrance. Life is not an endless grind but a pilgrimage punctuated by celebration of his goodness. The chapter crescendos with a breathtaking promise: an angel who bears God's name, in whom many have seen the Son before his incarnation. The same Lord who bears the divine name leads his people still, and God never sends his people anywhere he does not go with them.
23.theology:
Impartial justice and enemy-love. God's law forbids partiality and commands kindness even to enemies.

Sacred time. Sabbaths and feasts sanctify time around rest, worship, and remembrance, anticipating the eternal rest of God's people.

The guiding presence of God. The Angel in whom God's name dwells leads and guards his people to the prepared place, fulfilled in Christ, Immanuel.
23.examples:
Then: God sent his Angel to lead Israel to the prepared land.

Now: God still calls his people to truth, justice and love of enemies. We fail at all three; Christ did not, and his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Phil. 3:9), while his Spirit makes us able to love even those who hate us (Gal. 5:22). And he never sends us anywhere alone: in Christ, God with us, the guiding presence leads us home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-9: Laws for the courtroom, partiality forbidden both ways, and an enemy's fallen donkey.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justice for All

Truth in the witness box, and help for the enemy in the road.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the law protected the court from crowd, bribe and sympathy alike. Now: the God who loved us while we were his enemies (Rom. 5:10) asks us to lift our enemy's load.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall not spread a false report. You shall not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness. You shall not fall in with the many to do evil, nor shall you bear witness in a lawsuit, siding with the many, so as to pervert justice, nor shall you be partial to a poor man in his lawsuit. "If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey going astray, you shall bring it back to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you lying down under its burden, you shall refrain from leaving him with it; you shall rescue it with him. "You shall not pervert the justice due to your poor in his lawsuit. Keep far from a false charge, and do not kill the innocent and righteous, for I will not acquit the wicked. And you shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of those who are in the right. "You shall not oppress a sojourner. You know the heart of a sojourner, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The laws on justice go after the ways courts actually fail, and they are uncomfortably current.

The many. Beside the false report and the malicious witness stands the commonest failure of all: crowd pressure. It is neither bribery nor malice, but the ordinary instinct to go where the room is going. The number of people holding a view is not evidence for it, and a witness who trims his testimony to the majority has perverted justice as surely as one who lied for money.

Partial to the poor. A startling balance: favouring the poor in his lawsuit is forbidden a few verses from perverting the justice due to the poor. The law is fiercely protective of the poor everywhere except in the witness box, where sympathy is as corrupting as contempt. Justice is not the same thing as taking the weaker side.

Your enemy's donkey. This small law has a long reach. It is not enough to refrain from harming your enemy: go and heave his animal upright alongside him, in the road, where you will both be sweating and neither will know what to say. It is very hard to keep hating a man you have just done that with, which is presumably the idea. Centuries later it became a principle: Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you (Matt. 5:44).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10-13 — The Sabbath Year and the Sabbath Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 10-13: The sabbath year for the poor, and the weekly Sabbath for the worker.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sabbath Year and the Sabbath Day

Rest is given to those who own nothing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the poor and the worker were the ones the rest was for. Now: rest is a mercy the strong owe the weak.

verseByVerse.quote: "For six years you shall sow your land and gather in its yield, but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave the beasts of the field may eat. You shall do likewise with your vineyard, and with your olive orchard. "Six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest; that your ox and your donkey may have rest, and the son of your servant woman, and the alien, may be refreshed. "Pay attention to all that I have said to you, and make no mention of the names of other gods, nor let it be heard on your lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sabbath principle extends from the week to the calendar: every seventh year the land lies fallow. It is good agriculture, but that is not the reason given: the beneficiary named is the poor, who may glean freely from the untended fields, and the wild animals get the remainder. God builds a year into Israel's economy that transfers the whole harvest to those with no land.

The weekly Sabbath is restated with the same emphasis: once again the list is of those who do not own the land they work. The rhythm that began as a gift of manna has become the means by which Israel is kept from grinding down its own workforce.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 14-19: Three pilgrim feasts a year.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Three Annual Feasts

The calendar is built around harvest, gratitude and God's presence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the nation left its fields in trust three times a year. Now: Christ died at Passover and the Spirit came at Pentecost; the final ingathering is still to come.

verseByVerse.quote: "Three times in the year you shall keep a feast to me. You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. As I commanded you, you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days at the appointed time in the month of Abib, for in it you came out of Egypt. None shall appear before me empty-handed. You shall keep the Feast of Harvest, of the firstfruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field. You shall keep the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year, when you gather in from the field the fruit of your labor. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD. "You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the fat of my feast remain until the morning. "The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring into the house of the LORD your God. "You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each festival is tied to a harvest: Unleavened Bread in the spring, Harvest at the first fruits, Ingathering at the end of the year. The whole nation stops work three times a year and travels, a substantial act of trust for a farming people: the fields are left, and God undertakes to look after them.

These three are also the frame on which the gospel later hangs. Christ was crucified at Passover and Unleavened Bread, raised as the firstfruits (Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Cor. 15:20), and the Spirit was poured out at the Feast of Weeks, Pentecost. Two of the three were fulfilled on their own festival days, in the same city, within fifty days. The third, Ingathering, has not happened yet.

Why not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk (v. 19)? Nobody knows for certain. Older scholars thought it a Canaanite ritual, though the ancient text once cited for this is now read differently; many think it simply forbade turning what was meant to nourish a young animal into the means of cooking it. The later Jewish rule of separating all meat and dairy grew from this verse. Christians are not bound by it, since the food laws are fulfilled in Christ (Mark 7:19).
verseByVerse.note: The three pilgrim feasts: Unleavened Bread (with Passover), Harvest (later called Weeks or Pentecost), and Ingathering (Booths).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20-33 — The Angel and the Promise of Conquest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 20-33: The angel who bears God's name, conquest little by little, and a warning against compromise.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Angel and the Promise of Conquest

God goes ahead of his people, at a pace they can hold.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the land was taken at the pace it could be held. Now: compromise with what God has judged is still a snare.

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, I send an angel before you to guard you on the way and to bring you to the place that I have prepared. Pay careful attention to him and obey his voice; do not rebel against him, for he will not pardon your transgression, for my name is in him. "But if you carefully obey his voice and do all that I say, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to your adversaries. "When my angel goes before you and brings you to the Amorites and the Hittites and the Perizzites and the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, and I blot them out, you shall not bow down to their gods nor serve them, nor do as they do, but you shall utterly overthrow them and break their pillars in pieces. You shall serve the LORD your God, and he will bless your bread and your water, and I will take sickness away from among you. None shall miscarry or be barren in your land; I will fulfill the number of your days. I will send my terror before you and will throw into confusion all the people against whom you shall come, and I will make all your enemies turn their backs to you. And I will send hornets before you, which shall drive out the Hivites, the Canaanites, and the Hittites from before you. I will not drive them out from before you in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you. Little by little I will drive them out from before you, until you have increased and possess the land. And I will set your border from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates, for I will give the inhabitants of the land into your hand, and you shall drive them out before you. You shall make no covenant with them and their gods. They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against me; for if you serve their gods, it will surely be a snare to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter ends with a promise stranger than it looks. Israel is to obey this messenger as they would obey God. He is the same figure who appeared in the bush and spoke as God in the first person (3:2–6).

Little by little. This promise answers a question people ask about their own lives. God explains his own slowness: he could clear Canaan in a season, but a nation of that size in an empty country would be overrun by wilderness before it could fill the space. So progress is deliberately gradual, matched to what Israel can occupy and hold.

The same pattern governs the Christian life. Sanctification is almost never a single clearance; it is territory taken slowly, and the slowness is not God's reluctance but his knowledge of the ground. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Phil. 1:6): the completion is certain and the timetable is his.

No covenant with them. The final warning is about compromise: their gods will be a snare. Israel will ignore it, and the book of Judges tells what followed.

Who is this angel? My name is in him, and he can withhold pardon (v. 21), as only God can. He is not a created angel but the LORD present with his people, most likely the Son before his incarnation. Paul says that the Rock that followed Israel was Christ (1 Cor 10:4).

Was it just for God to command the Canaanites destroyed (vv. 23–24)? The question should be felt at full strength, for whole communities fell. It was his judgment on peoples whose sin had reached its full measure (Gen 15:16), which included child sacrifice (Deut 12:31), and Israel was warned that it would be judged in the same way if it did the same (Lev 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out by Israel under God, and it gives no warrant for any later war in God’s name. Christ’s kingdom is not of this world, and his servants do not fight for it with the sword (John 18:36).

24.title: The Blood of the Covenant
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Then he said to Moses, "Come up to the LORD, you and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and worship from afar.<sup>2</sup>Moses alone shall come near to the LORD, but the others shall not come near, and the people shall not come up with him."<sup>3</sup>Moses came and told the people all the words of the LORD and all the rules. And all the people answered with one voice and said, "All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do."<sup>4</sup>And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. He rose early in the morning and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel.<sup>5</sup>And he sent young men of the people of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen to the LORD.<sup>6</sup>And Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he threw against the altar.<sup>7</sup>Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. And they said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient."<sup>8</sup>And Moses took the blood and threw it on the people and said, "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words."<sup>9</sup>Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up,<sup>10</sup>and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness.<sup>11</sup>And he did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people of Israel; they beheld God, and ate and drank.<sup>12</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Come up to me on the mountain and wait there, that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and the commandment, which I have written for their instruction."<sup>13</sup>So Moses rose with his assistant Joshua, and Moses went up into the mountain of God.<sup>14</sup>And he said to the elders, "Wait here for us until we return to you. And behold, Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever has a dispute, let him go to them."<sup>15</sup>Then Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain.<sup>16</sup>The glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. And on the seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.<sup>17</sup>Now the appearance of the glory of the LORD was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the sight of the people of Israel.<sup>18</sup>Moses entered the cloud and went up on the mountain. And Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
24.overview:
The covenant is ratified, and the means is blood, thrown against the altar and over the people. A covenant between a holy God and a sinful people can be sealed only in blood (Heb. 9:22), and Jesus deliberately echoes this moment at the Last Supper. Every drop at the altar of Sinai was a signpost to Calvary.

Then the elders go up the mountain, see the God of Israel, and eat and drink in his presence: sinners feasting before the holy One and not consumed. Finally Moses goes up into the cloud, and the people are left to wait.
24.theology:
The covenant sealed in blood. A holy God and sinful people can be bound only through sacrificial blood, fulfilled in Christ's blood of the new covenant (Matt. 26:28).

Communion with God as the goal. The elders see God and eat and drink in his presence.

The mediator who ascends. Moses enters God's glory for the people, prefiguring Christ who entered heaven itself on our behalf (Heb. 9:24).
24.examples:
Then: The covenant was ratified in blood thrown on altar and people, and the elders ate and drank in God's presence.

Now: By the blood of Christ, poured out for the forgiveness of sins, we are brought into communion with God, and feast at the Lord's table until we eat with him face to face.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-8 — The Blood of the Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-8: An altar with twelve pillars, the Book of the Covenant read, the people's third promise, and the blood.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Blood of the Covenant

One death stands over both parties.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the people promised a third time, and meant it. Now: the new covenant rests on a better promise than ours.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to Moses, "Come up to the LORD, you and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel, and worship from afar. Moses alone shall come near to the LORD, but the others shall not come near, and the people shall not come up with him." Moses came and told the people all the words of the LORD and all the rules. And all the people answered with one voice and said, "All the words that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses wrote down all the words of the LORD. He rose early in the morning and built an altar at the foot of the mountain, and twelve pillars, according to the twelve tribes of Israel. And he sent young men of the people of Israel, who offered burnt offerings and sacrificed peace offerings of oxen to the LORD. And Moses took half of the blood and put it in basins, and half of the blood he threw against the altar. Then he took the Book of the Covenant and read it in the hearing of the people. And they said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do, and we will be obedient." And Moses took the blood and threw it on the people and said, "Behold the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you in accordance with all these words."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve pillars stand round the altar, one for each tribe; young men offer burnt offerings and peace offerings; and the ceremony that gives this chapter its weight follows.

Blood on both sides. Half goes on the altar, which is God's side, and half on the people, which is theirs, with the Book of the Covenant read between and the people's third promise. One basin is divided between the two parties, so that the same death now stands over both. That is what a covenant is: not a contract between equals but a bond sealed in death, with both sides inside it.

Hebrews takes this scene as its proof that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins, quoting Moses' words almost exactly: This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you (Heb. 9:18-22).

The sentence has a more famous afterlife. On the night he was betrayed, at Passover, Jesus took a cup and said: This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many (Mark 14:24). His disciples would have known where the words came from: they belonged to Moses and a basin and a mountain. And he took them and made it my blood.

He was not inventing a metaphor. He was announcing that the ceremony at the foot of Sinai had found its original: the blood thrown against an altar and over a crowd was always a rehearsal for blood that would be poured out for many, and the covenant it sealed was about to be replaced by one that could actually be kept.

Which matters because of what the people had just promised. They meant it, standing under blood, and within forty days they would be dancing round a calf. The blood of Exodus 24 sealed a covenant Israel broke almost immediately. The blood of the new covenant seals one where the obedience required has already been supplied by the one whose blood it is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-11 — They Beheld God and Ate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 9-11: Seventy-four men see the God of Israel, and eat.
verseByVerse.theology:
They Beheld God and Ate

Sinners under the blood sit at God's table and live.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the elders saw only what was under his feet, and it was enough. Now: the Lord's table is a meal in the presence of the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up, and they saw the God of Israel. There was under his feet as it were a pavement of sapphire stone, like the very heaven for clearness. And he did not lay his hand on the chief men of the people of Israel; they beheld God, and ate and drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These three verses are so unexpected that readers often pass over them without registering what happened. Seventy-four men climbed a mountain and saw God. The text says it twice, plainly, and goes out of its way to record that nobody died, which tells you what everyone in the story expected to happen.

Under his feet. The description is careful about its limits: a pavement of sapphire (or lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone), like the sky for clearness. The narrator will describe the floor and will not describe the person standing on it.

Ate and drank. This is the point. On the mountain fenced with a death penalty five chapters ago, where touching the base of it was fatal, seventy-four men sat down in the presence of God and had lunch. It is a rare and astonishing moment in Scripture when human beings eat in God's company and live, and it happens immediately after blood has been thrown over them.

That order is the logic of the Bible: blood first, then a meal. It is why the church's central act is a table, and why the upper room runs the same way, the cup of the covenant and then bread and wine with the one whose blood it was. And it is where all of it is going: Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev. 19:9).

But no one can see God and live (33:20), and No one has ever seen God (John 1:18). What the elders saw was a revealed form, and the text itself describes only what was under his feet. They did not see God in his essence, as no one can; they saw what he chose to show, and lived to eat in his presence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-18 — Into the Cloud of Glory
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 12-18: Moses goes up for the tablets, into the cloud, for forty days.
verseByVerse.theology:
Into the Cloud of Glory

The mediator disappears into the fire, and the people must wait.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the people at the foot watched a fire with their leader inside it. Now: waiting for God is part of trusting him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Come up to me on the mountain and wait there, that I may give you the tablets of stone, with the law and the commandment, which I have written for their instruction." So Moses rose with his assistant Joshua, and Moses went up into the mountain of God. And he said to the elders, "Wait here for us until we return to you. And behold, Aaron and Hur are with you. Whoever has a dispute, let him go to them." Then Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain. The glory of the LORD dwelt on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. And on the seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud. Now the appearance of the glory of the LORD was like a devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the sight of the people of Israel. Moses entered the cloud and went up on the mountain. And Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is called higher, for the tablets God himself has written. He leaves Aaron and Hur in charge, which will turn out badly, and takes Joshua part of the way. The cloud covers the mountain for six days, and on the seventh God calls him into it.

A devouring fire. Hebrews uses the phrase of God at the end of its argument about the two mountains (our God is a consuming fire, Heb. 12:29). The people at the bottom watch a blaze on a summit and know their leader has walked into it.

Forty days. A long time to watch a fire on a mountain with no word from the man inside it. The narrator drops the detail without comment, and the reader can already hear the talk starting at the bottom of the hill: as for this Moses... we do not know what has become of him (32:1). The golden calf is not built by people who have forgotten God. It is built by people who got tired of waiting for him, nearly six weeks after promising to do everything he said, with the fire still burning in plain sight.

25.title: That I May Dwell in Their Midst
25.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"Speak to the people of Israel, that they take for me a contribution. From every man whose heart moves him you shall receive the contribution for me.<sup>3</sup>And this is the contribution that you shall receive from them: gold, silver, and bronze,<sup>4</sup>blue and purple and scarlet yarns and fine twined linen, goats' hair,<sup>5</sup>tanned rams' skins, goatskins, acacia wood,<sup>6</sup>oil for the lamps, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense,<sup>7</sup>onyx stones, and stones for setting, for the ephod and for the breastpiece.<sup>8</sup>And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst.<sup>9</sup>Exactly as I show you concerning the pattern of the tabernacle, and of all its furniture, so you shall make it.<sup>10</sup>"They shall make an ark of acacia wood. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, a cubit and a half its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height.<sup>11</sup>You shall overlay it with pure gold, inside and outside shall you overlay it, and you shall make on it a molding of gold around it.<sup>12</sup>You shall cast four rings of gold for it and put them on its four feet, two rings on the one side of it, and two rings on the other side of it.<sup>13</sup>You shall make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold.<sup>14</sup>And you shall put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark by them.<sup>15</sup>The poles shall remain in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it.<sup>16</sup>And you shall put into the ark the testimony that I shall give you.<sup>17</sup>"You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half shall be its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth.<sup>18</sup>And you shall make two cherubim of gold; of hammered work shall you make them, on the two ends of the mercy seat.<sup>19</sup>Make one cherub on the one end, and one cherub on the other end. Of one piece with the mercy seat shall you make the cherubim on its two ends.<sup>20</sup>The cherubim shall spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, their faces one to another; toward the mercy seat shall the faces of the cherubim be.<sup>21</sup>And you shall put the mercy seat on the top of the ark, and in the ark you shall put the testimony that I shall give you.<sup>22</sup>There I will meet with you, and from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim that are on the ark of the testimony, I will speak with you about all that I will give you in commandment for the people of Israel.<sup>23</sup>"You shall make a table of acacia wood. Two cubits shall be its length, a cubit its breadth, and a cubit and a half its height.<sup>24</sup>You shall overlay it with pure gold and make a molding of gold around it.<sup>25</sup>And you shall make a rim around it a handbreadth wide, and a molding of gold around the rim.<sup>26</sup>And you shall make for it four rings of gold, and fasten the rings to the four corners at its four legs.<sup>27</sup>Close to the frame the rings shall lie, as holders for the poles to carry the table.<sup>28</sup>You shall make the poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold, and the table shall be carried with these.<sup>29</sup>And you shall make its plates and dishes for incense, and its flagons and bowls with which to pour drink offerings; you shall make them of pure gold.<sup>30</sup>And you shall set the bread of the Presence on the table before me regularly.<sup>31</sup>"You shall make a lampstand of pure gold. The lampstand shall be made of hammered work: its base, its stem, its cups, its calyxes, and its flowers shall be of one piece with it.<sup>32</sup>And there shall be six branches going out of its sides, three branches of the lampstand out of one side of it and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side of it;<sup>33</sup>three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on one branch, and three cups made like almond blossoms, each with calyx and flower, on the other branch—so for the six branches going out of the lampstand.<sup>34</sup>And on the lampstand itself there shall be four cups made like almond blossoms, with their calyxes and flowers,<sup>35</sup>and a calyx of one piece with it under each pair of the six branches going out from the lampstand.<sup>36</sup>Their calyxes and their branches shall be of one piece with it, the whole of it a single piece of hammered work of pure gold.<sup>37</sup>You shall make seven lamps for it. And the lamps shall be set up so as to give light on the space in front of it.<sup>38</sup>Its tongs and their trays shall be of pure gold.<sup>39</sup>It shall be made, with all these utensils, out of a talent of pure gold.<sup>40</sup>And see that you make them after the pattern for them, which is being shown you on the mountain.
25.overview:
Here begins the theme that crowns Exodus: God's desire to dwell with his people. The God who came down to deliver now comes down to stay, and the whole tabernacle exists so that the holy God might live among those he has redeemed. This is the heartbeat of the gospel: God with us.

The instructions open with a freewill offering and then move from the centre outwards: first the ark with its golden lid, the mercy seat, where God promises to meet his people; then the table of the bread of the Presence and the golden lampstand. Everything follows the pattern shown on the mountain, and the tent points forward to the incarnation, when the Word "became flesh and dwelt among us" (John 1:14, literally "tabernacled"), and to the New Jerusalem, where "the dwelling place of God is with man" (Rev. 21:3). All of it whispers: God wants to be with you.
25.theology:
God's desire to dwell with his people. The goal of redemption is not only escape from Egypt but God's presence, a purpose fulfilled in Christ and completed in the New Jerusalem.

The mercy seat and atonement. God meets sinners only where blood covers the broken law. There justice and mercy meet, and Paul names Christ as that meeting place (Rom. 3:25).

Worship after the heavenly pattern. Because the tent copies a heavenly reality, nothing in it is left to human invention; God himself says how he is to be approached.
25.examples:
Then: willing hearts built a sanctuary after a heavenly pattern, with a blood-sprinkled lid as the place where God would meet his redeemed people.
