Yet each ordinance whispers the gospel. Nothing in the worship of God is arbitrary; every detail is a finger pointing to Christ, in whom all the shadows find their substance.
30.theology:
Worship ordained by God. We approach God on his terms, not our own. Reformed churches have drawn from the second commandment what is called the regulative principle: worship should include only what God has commanded. Many faithful Christians hold instead that worship may include what Scripture does not forbid; both sides agree that God, not our taste, sets its terms.

Prayer as incense. The altar of incense pictures the prayers of the saints rising before God, made acceptable through Christ's mediation (Ps. 141:2; Rev. 5:8).

Ransom and cleansing. The atonement money and the basin point to the ransom of Christ's blood (1 Pet. 1:18-19) and the washing of new birth (Titus 3:5).
30.examples:
Then: God prescribed every detail of worship, teaching Israel that all worship needs atonement and cleansing.

Now: our prayers are made acceptable by Christ our Intercessor, we are ransomed by his blood and washed by his Spirit, and we worship God on his terms, in spirit and truth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-10: The altar of incense before the veil, burning morning and evening, its horns receiving blood once a year.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sacrifice Outside, Prayer Inside

Prayer rises nearest the ark, and even its altar must be atoned for.
verseByVerse.examples: The smoke rose at the hours the lambs died. Christian prayer still rises on the strength of a sacrifice, not on its own merit.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall make an altar on which to burn incense; you shall make it of acacia wood. A cubit shall be its length, and a cubit its breadth. It shall be square, and two cubits shall be its height. Its horns shall be of one piece with it. You shall overlay it with pure gold, its top and around its sides and its horns. And you shall make a molding of gold around it. And you shall make two golden rings for it. Under its molding on two opposite sides of it you shall make them, and they shall be holders for poles with which to carry it. You shall make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. And you shall put it in front of the veil that is above the ark of the testimony, in front of the mercy seat that is above the testimony, where I will meet with you. And Aaron shall burn fragrant incense on it. Every morning when he dresses the lamps he shall burn it, and when Aaron sets up the lamps at twilight, he shall burn it, a regular incense offering before the LORD throughout your generations. You shall not offer unauthorized incense on it, or a burnt offering, or a grain offering, and you shall not pour a drink offering on it. Aaron shall make atonement on its horns once a year. With the blood of the sin offering of atonement he shall make atonement for it once in the year throughout your generations. It is most holy to the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The altar of incense sits as close to the ark as anything can without being behind the curtain. Twice a day, at the hours the lambs were killed in the courtyard, smoke rose just before the veil. Sacrifice outside, prayer inside, at the same moment.

Scripture is explicit about the smoke. Let my prayer be counted as incense before you (Ps. 141:2), and in Revelation the elders' golden bowls are full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8). Luke opens his Gospel at this altar: Zechariah burns incense while the whole multitude of the people were praying outside at the hour of incense, and an angel appears beside it (Luke 1:8-11).

Hebrews 9:4 links this golden altar with the Most Holy Place, probably because its work belonged to the inner room it stood before (compare 1 Kings 6:22). Once a year its horns receive blood from the sin offering. Even the place where prayer ascends must be atoned for: a plain admission that our prayers are not clean either, and that they are heard because of the blood, not because of their quality.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 11-16: The census tax, a ransom for each life, the same half shekel for rich and poor.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Flat Price

Every counted life is ransomed at the same small price, and the silver is given to the service of the tent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: rich and poor paid one price for their lives. Now: every believer is ransomed by the same infinitely costly payment, and none adds anything to it.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "When you take the census of the people of Israel, then each shall give a ransom for his life to the LORD when you number them, that there be no plague among them when you number them. Each one who is numbered in the census shall give this: half a shekel according to the shekel of the sanctuary (the shekel is twenty gerahs), half a shekel as an offering to the LORD. Everyone who is numbered in the census, from twenty years old and upward, shall give the LORD's offering. The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel, when you give the LORD's offering to make atonement for your lives. You shall take the atonement money from the people of Israel and shall give it for the service of the tent of meeting, that it may bring the people of Israel to remembrance before the LORD, so as to make atonement for your lives."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reason given for the census tax is unexpected: to be counted in Israel, a man had to pay a ransom for his own life.

Everybody pays the same small sum. The point is not revenue but a statement no Israelite could miss: a human life is not graded by wealth, and no one can pay more to be worth more.

Peter shows what it pointed to: you were ransomed from the futile ways inherited from your forefathers, not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet. 1:18-19). The half shekel was flat because the real price would be flat: one payment of infinite value, with nobody in the queue contributing anything to it.

And this silver became the bases of the tabernacle (26:19). The whole house of God stood on ransom money.

Why would counting the people bring a plague? Each life belonged to the LORD who had redeemed it, and the ransom acknowledged that. A census without it treated the people as the leader’s own strength, as David found (2 Sam 24). And the price is the same for rich and poor (v. 15): every life costs God the same.
verseByVerse.note: Half a shekel was about 1/5 ounce of silver (ESV note: a shekel was about 2/5 ounce).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 17-21: The bronze basin between altar and tent, where the priests must wash or die.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Bath, Many Washings

The priests wash hands and feet every time they come near to minister.
verseByVerse.examples: Nobody walked from the altar into God's house without stopping at the basin. A Christian, once washed, still comes back daily for his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "You shall also make a basin of bronze, with its stand of bronze, for washing. You shall put it between the tent of meeting and the altar, and you shall put water in it, with which Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet. When they go into the tent of meeting, or when they come near the altar to minister, to burn a food offering to the LORD, they shall wash with water, so that they may not die. They shall wash their hands and their feet, so that they may not die. It shall be a statute forever to them, even to him and to his offspring throughout their generations."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests were washed once at their ordination, and that was never repeated. But hands get dirty doing the work and feet get dirty walking the courtyard, so they wash at the basin every time they approach.

One bath, many washings. It is the distinction Jesus made when Peter demanded a complete bath instead of a foot-washing: The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean (John 13:10). A believer is not re-converted every time he sins. He is washed once, counted clean in Christ, and keeps coming back for his feet, in daily confession and the mercy God promised.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 22-33: The anointing oil for the tent and the priests, forbidden for any other use.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Anointed One

The oil consecrates; whoever copies it or puts it to common use is cut off.
verseByVerse.examples: The scent was to mean one thing only, and every drop of this oil looked ahead to the one whose title is simply the Anointed.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take the finest spices: of liquid myrrh 500 shekels, and of sweet-smelling cinnamon half as much, that is, 250, and 250 of aromatic cane, and 500 of cassia, according to the shekel of the sanctuary, and a hin of olive oil. And you shall make of these a sacred anointing oil blended as by the perfumer; it shall be a holy anointing oil. With it you shall anoint the tent of meeting and the ark of the testimony, and the table and all its utensils, and the lampstand and its utensils, and the altar of incense, and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils and the basin and its stand. You shall consecrate them, that they may be most holy. Whatever touches them will become holy. You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them, that they may serve me as priests. And you shall say to the people of Israel, 'This shall be my holy anointing oil throughout your generations. It shall not be poured on the body of an ordinary person, and you shall make no other like it in composition. It is holy, and it shall be holy to you. Whoever compounds any like it or whoever puts any of it on an outsider shall be cut off from his people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything in the tent is anointed with this oil, and Aaron and his sons. The prohibition is severe: no reproduction for ordinary use, no anointing an outsider.

The recipe was not secret. The smell was to mean one thing only. Anyone in Israel who caught that scent knew what it belonged to; worn socially, the association would have dissolved within a generation. Holiness in Scripture is largely a matter of things not being interchangeable.

Messiah is Hebrew for anointed one; Christ is the same word in Greek. Every object and priest in this tent is anointed in anticipation of a person whose title would simply be the anointed. When a woman broke a flask of costly ointment over Jesus' head and the room complained of waste, he said she had done it to prepare me for burial (Matt. 26:12).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 34-38: The holy incense, under the same restriction.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Restricted Thing, Given Away

The incense is holy to the LORD and may not be made for private use.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: no Israelite could wear it. Now: the church itself is called the aroma of Christ to God (2 Cor. 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Take sweet spices, stacte, and onycha, and galbanum, sweet spices with pure frankincense (of each shall there be an equal part), and make an incense blended as by the perfumer, seasoned with salt, pure and holy. You shall beat some of it very small, and put part of it before the testimony in the tent of meeting where I shall meet with you. It shall be most holy for you. And the incense that you shall make according to its composition, you shall not make for yourselves. It shall be for you holy to the LORD. Whoever makes any like it to use as perfume shall be cut off from his people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take the two recipes together and the chapter has a shape. Israel is given a fragrance for prayer and a fragrance for anointing, and forbidden to use either for itself. Not because God is stingy with pleasant things, but because a sign used for everything stops signifying anything.

Paul uses the language of fragrance in a new way: God through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere, and we are the aroma of Christ to God (2 Cor. 2:14-15). This is an echo rather than a fulfilment of the incense law, but a lovely one: what was kept for God alone now describes a people who carry Christ.

31.title: The Spirit Equips for God's Work
31.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses,<sup>2</sup>"See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah,<sup>3</sup>and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship,<sup>4</sup>to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze,<sup>5</sup>in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood, to work in every craft.<sup>6</sup>And behold, I have appointed with him Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. And I have given to all able men ability, that they may make all that I have commanded you:<sup>7</sup>the tent of meeting, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is on it, and all the furnishings of the tent,<sup>8</sup>the table and its utensils, and the pure lampstand with all its utensils, and the altar of incense,<sup>9</sup>and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin and its stand,<sup>10</sup>and the finely worked garments, the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments of his sons, for their service as priests,<sup>11</sup>and the anointing oil and the fragrant incense for the Holy Place. According to all that I have commanded you, they shall do."<sup>12</sup>And the LORD said to Moses,<sup>13</sup>"You are to speak to the people of Israel and say, 'Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you.<sup>14</sup>You shall keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you. Everyone who profanes it shall be put to death. Whoever does any work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people.<sup>15</sup>Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day shall be put to death.<sup>16</sup>Therefore the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever.<sup>17</sup>It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.'"<sup>18</sup>And he gave to Moses, when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone, written with the finger of God.
31.overview:
Before the building begins, God provides the builders. Bezalel is the first person Scripture describes as filled with the Spirit of God, and the filling is for craftsmanship: God cares about beauty and skill in his service, and he supplies the ability himself.

Then God seals the instructions with the Sabbath, a sign "that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you." Even the holy work of building must keep the rhythm of rest, because his people's standing rests not on their work but on his grace. The Sabbath is the gospel embedded in the calendar: we rest because God has done, and will do, the saving work.
31.theology:
The Spirit equips for God's work. God gifts those he calls, and every ability used in his work is grace.

The dignity of skilled labour. Skill is not less spiritual than speech; artistry and excellence offered for God's glory are gifts of the Spirit.

The Sabbath as sign of grace. God, not our labour, makes us holy, and the sign points to our rest in Christ's finished work.
31.examples:
Then: God filled Bezalel with his Spirit to build the tabernacle, and gave the Sabbath as a sign that the LORD sanctifies his people.

Now: God still equips by his Spirit those he calls, and every skill used for his glory is his gift. And Christ gives the soul the rest the Sabbath pictured.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-11 — Bezalel and Oholiab, Filled with the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-11: Bezalel is called by name and filled with the Spirit, Oholiab is set beside him, and ability is given to all the skilled workers.
verseByVerse.theology:
The First Man Filled With the Spirit Is a Craftsman

The Spirit's filling is described entirely in terms of skill.
verseByVerse.examples: The whole workforce's competence was credited to God. A Christian whose gifts are practical rather than public need not think them second-class.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability and intelligence, with knowledge and all craftsmanship, to devise artistic designs, to work in gold, silver, and bronze, in cutting stones for setting, and in carving wood, to work in every craft. And behold, I have appointed with him Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan. And I have given to all able men ability, that they may make all that I have commanded you: the tent of meeting, and the ark of the testimony, and the mercy seat that is on it, and all the furnishings of the tent, the table and its utensils, and the pure lampstand with all its utensils, and the altar of incense, and the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the basin and its stand, and the finely worked garments, the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments of his sons, for their service as priests, and the anointing oil and the fragrant incense for the Holy Place. According to all that I have commanded you, they shall do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After six chapters of specification, God names the builder, and what he says about him is the first statement of its kind in the Bible. The first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God is not a prophet, priest or king but a craftsman, and the filling is described entirely as skill: ability, intelligence, knowledge, the capacity to design beautiful things and make them in metal, stone and wood.

That deserves saying plainly, because much Christian thinking quietly assumes that spiritual gifts are the ones exercised on a platform. God lists this man's gifts as specific trades. There is no sacred-secular divide in God's economy: the craftsman working with gold and wood is filled with the same Spirit who would later fill prophets and apostles.

Then the wider provision: every skilled worker in the camp is included. The tabernacle was built not by two geniuses but by a workforce whose competence is credited to God. The same pattern runs on: the ascended Christ gives gifts to his people for building up the body of Christ (Eph. 4:8–12), the house in which God now lives, and the Spirit who fills them is the one who makes the work possible.

Where did these men learn their trade? As slaves in Egypt, a country of extraordinary metalwork and joinery. Skills acquired in captivity, probably under compulsion, now build God's house. Nothing learned in the years that felt wasted is necessarily wasted.
verseByVerse.note: Bezalel was from the tribe of Judah and Oholiab from the tribe of Dan, so the work was not left to one tribe.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-18 — The Sabbath, a Sign Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 12-18: The Sabbath is a sign that the LORD sanctifies Israel; then Moses receives the two tablets, written with the finger of God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not Even Work Commanded by God

The last word before the tablets is rest, the sign of whose people Israel is.
verseByVerse.examples: The tabernacle could wait a day a week. Our holiness is something God does in us, not something we achieve, and the Lord's Day is a weekly gift that says so.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "You are to speak to the people of Israel and say, 'Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you. You shall keep the Sabbath, because it is holy for you. Everyone who profanes it shall be put to death. Whoever does any work on it, that soul shall be cut off from among his people. Six days shall work be done, but the seventh day is a Sabbath of solemn rest, holy to the LORD. Whoever does any work on the Sabbath day shall be put to death. Therefore the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever. It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.'" And he gave to Moses, when he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone, written with the finger of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Immediately after all the building instructions, God returns to the Sabbath, and the placement is the point. Israel has just been handed the most important construction project in its history, and the last word before Moses comes down is Above all, keep the Sabbath. Not even work commanded by God was a reason to skip Israel's rest; the tabernacle could wait a day a week.

And the reason is relational. The Sabbath is a sign: a weekly marker that this people belongs to God, and that their holiness is something he does to them rather than something they achieve. A nation that downs tools every seventh day says, publicly and repeatedly, that the world is not held up by its effort.

The sign rests on creation: in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed. As in 20:11, Israel's week copies God's week, and this commentary takes the six days of Genesis 1 as ordinary days (see on Genesis 1:5), while honouring faithful Christians who read them as long ages or as a framework. Refreshed does not mean God was tired (Isa 40:28); it pictures him taking delight in finished work.

The finger of God is the phrase Egypt's magicians used when they failed (8:19), and the phrase Jesus used of his own authority over demons (Luke 11:20). The same finger that made gnats out of dust and set people free in Galilee wrote the commandments into rock.

Moses now holds tablets inscribed by God himself, containing a covenant Israel has three times sworn to keep. And at the bottom of the mountain, at this exact moment, they are dancing round a golden calf.

Was Sabbath-breaking really punished by death? It was, and once the penalty was carried out (Num 15:32–36). Under the covenant at Sinai the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant itself, so to defy it openly was to reject the covenant. That civil penalty ended with Israel’s theocracy. And the “forever” of verse 16 lasts as long as the covenant it belongs to. Its substance is now Christ, who gives the true rest (Matt 11:28; Heb 4:9–10), so no day binds the Christian conscience (Col 2:16–17).

32.title: The Golden Calf and the Intercessor
32.text: <sup>1</sup>When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron and said to him, "Up, make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him."<sup>2</sup>So Aaron said to them, "Take off the rings of gold that are in the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me."<sup>3</sup>So all the people took off the rings of gold that were in their ears and brought them to Aaron.<sup>4</sup>And he received the gold from their hand and fashioned it with a graving tool and made a golden calf. And they said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!"<sup>5</sup>When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it. And Aaron made a proclamation and said, "Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD."<sup>6</sup>And they rose up early the next day and offered burnt offerings and brought peace offerings. And the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.<sup>7</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves.<sup>8</sup>They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them. They have made for themselves a golden calf and have worshiped it and sacrificed to it and said, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!'"<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people.<sup>10</sup>Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them, in order that I may make a great nation of you."<sup>11</sup>But Moses implored the LORD his God and said, "O LORD, why does your wrath burn hot against your people, whom you have brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand?<sup>12</sup>Why should the Egyptians say, 'With evil intent did he bring them out, to kill them in the mountains and to consume them from the face of the earth'? Turn from your burning anger and relent from this disaster against your people.<sup>13</sup>Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by your own self, and said to them, 'I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven, and all this land that I have promised I will give to your offspring, and they shall inherit it forever.'"<sup>14</sup>And the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people.<sup>15</sup>Then Moses turned and went down from the mountain with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand, tablets that were written on both sides; on the front and on the back they were written.<sup>16</sup>The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets.<sup>17</sup>When Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, "There is a noise of war in the camp."<sup>18</sup>But he said, "It is not the sound of shouting for victory, or the sound of the cry of defeat, but the sound of singing that I hear."<sup>19</sup>And as soon as he came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, Moses' anger burned hot, and he threw the tablets out of his hands and broke them at the foot of the mountain.<sup>20</sup>He took the calf that they had made and burned it with fire and ground it to powder and scattered it on the water and made the people of Israel drink it.<sup>21</sup>And Moses said to Aaron, "What did this people do to you that you have brought such a great sin upon them?"<sup>22</sup>And Aaron said, "Let not the anger of my lord burn hot. You know the people, that they are set on evil.<sup>23</sup>For they said to me, 'Make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.'<sup>24</sup>So I said to them, 'Let any who have gold take it off.' So they gave it to me, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf."<sup>25</sup>And when Moses saw that the people had broken loose (for Aaron had let them break loose, to the derision of their enemies),<sup>26</sup>then Moses stood in the gate of the camp and said, "Who is on the LORD's side? Come to me." And all the sons of Levi gathered around him.<sup>27</sup>And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD God of Israel, 'Put your sword on your side each of you, and go to and fro from gate to gate throughout the camp, and each of you kill his brother and his companion and his neighbor.'"<sup>28</sup>And the sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses. And that day about three thousand men of the people fell.<sup>29</sup>And Moses said, "Today you have been ordained for the service of the LORD, each one at the cost of his son and of his brother, so that he might bestow a blessing upon you this day."<sup>30</sup>The next day Moses said to the people, "You have sinned a great sin. And now I will go up to the LORD; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin."<sup>31</sup>So Moses returned to the LORD and said, "Alas, this people has sinned a great sin. They have made for themselves gods of gold.<sup>32</sup>But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written."<sup>33</sup>But the LORD said to Moses, "Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book.<sup>34</sup>But now go, lead the people to the place about which I have spoken to you; behold, my angel shall go before you. Nevertheless, in the day when I visit, I will visit their sin upon them."<sup>35</sup>Then the LORD sent a plague on the people, because they made the calf, the one that Aaron made.
32.overview:
While Moses receives the law, the people commit the great apostasy. Impatient, they demand gods they can see and make a golden calf, crediting it with the exodus. Within weeks of the most stunning revelation of God's glory, they exchange the living God for an idol.

God's wrath burns, and he threatens to consume the people and start again with Moses. Then the chapter rises to a portrait of mediation. Moses stands in the breach, pleads God's glory and promises, and offers his own life for theirs. He cannot accomplish it, but his offer points to the One who could and did: Jesus, the greater Moses, who did not merely offer to be blotted out but actually bore the curse. Moses' intercession is a shadow; Christ's is the substance. The people are not destroyed, because a mediator stood in the gap. The calf shows the depth of our sin; the intercessor shows the height of God's mercy.
32.theology:
The idolatry of the human heart. As Calvin observed, the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols. A calf made within weeks of Sinai shows that we need not only rescue but a new heart.

The wrath of God against sin. Sin against the holy God is no small thing; justice cannot simply ignore rebellion.

The mediator who stands in the breach. Moses offers his own life, a shadow of Christ, who actually became a curse for us (Gal. 3:13) and was forsaken that we might be forgiven.
32.examples:
Then: the people broke the covenant almost before it was given, and Moses stood in the breach, offering to be blotted out for them.

Now: our hearts still make idols. But we have a greater Mediator, forsaken on the cross in our place, so that those who confess their sin and trust him will never be blotted out of the book of life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-6: Moses is late; the people demand gods; Aaron makes a calf and proclaims a feast to the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Second Commandment Broken While the First Is Intended

Aaron uses the covenant name, the LORD, over a metal animal.
verseByVerse.examples: The trigger was nothing more than a delay. Waiting on God is still where many of our substitutes for him are made.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw that Moses delayed to come down from the mountain, the people gathered themselves together to Aaron and said to him, "Up, make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him." So Aaron said to them, "Take off the rings of gold that are in the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me." So all the people took off the rings of gold that were in their ears and brought them to Aaron. And he received the gold from their hand and fashioned it with a graving tool and made a golden calf. And they said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it. And Aaron made a proclamation and said, "Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD." And they rose up early the next day and offered burnt offerings and brought peace offerings. And the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The trigger is a delay. Not persecution, famine or a rival prophet: Moses is late. Forty days of waiting with the fire still visible on the summit, and the nation decides he is gone and that they need something they can see.

Their phrasing gives them away: Moses is the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt. They have already begun crediting the exodus to a person rather than to God, which makes replacing him seem a manageable administrative problem.

And Aaron does it. He does not refuse or stall or remind them of the voice they all heard from the mountain. He makes a calf, then builds an altar before it and proclaims a feast to the LORD.

That detail makes the chapter frightening rather than merely disappointing. This is not apostasy to a foreign god. Aaron uses the covenant name, running a service for the LORD in front of a statue they watched being cast that morning.

It is the second commandment broken while the first is sincerely intended, which is why the two were given separately. The calf may well have been meant as a pedestal for the invisible God rather than a rival to him. The danger is rarely that we worship something else, but that we worship the true God in a shape we have chosen, and find the shape easier to love than the God.

And the gold came from Egypt: the back wages God gave them, meant for the tabernacle, melted down for this. Whatever is not given to God gets given to something.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-14 — Moses Stands in the Breach
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 7-14: God calls them Moses' people and offers to make a great nation of Moses; Moses intercedes, and the LORD relents.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Art of Intercession

Moses pleads three things: that they are God's people, that God's name is at stake, and that God has sworn an oath.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses found nothing good to say about Israel, so he appealed to what was true about God. Christians pray for others, and for themselves, on the same ground.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Go down, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves. They have turned aside quickly out of the way that I commanded them. They have made for themselves a golden calf and have worshiped it and sacrificed to it and said, 'These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!'" And the LORD said to Moses, "I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people. Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them, in order that I may make a great nation of you." But Moses implored the LORD his God and said, "O LORD, why does your wrath burn hot against your people, whom you have brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and with a mighty hand? Why should the Egyptians say, 'With evil intent did he bring them out, to kill them in the mountains and to consume them from the face of the earth'? Turn from your burning anger and relent from this disaster against your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by your own self, and said to them, 'I will multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven, and all this land that I have promised I will give to your offspring, and they shall inherit it forever.'" And the LORD relented from the disaster that he had spoken of bringing on his people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The language is cold: your people, whom you brought up. Yesterday they were God's people; today he calls them Moses'.

Then Moses is offered what Abraham was promised: to be the father of a new nation once the ungrateful one is gone.

He refuses, and his prayer is a model of intercession. He argues three things, and not one is that Israel deserves rescuing. First, whose people they are: he hands them straight back, your people, whom you have brought out. Second, God's reputation among the Egyptians. Third, and decisively, God's oath to Abraham, Isaac and Israel.

That is the whole art of it. Intercession does not consist in finding something good to say about the guilty, but in appealing to something true about God.

Israel survived that morning because a mediator refused to step aside and held God to his promises. It is a picture of the one who always lives to make intercession (Heb. 7:25), whose plea is better than Moses' because it rests not only on God's promise but on his own finished work.

Did Moses change God’s mind? God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind (Num 23:19). Scripture says God “relented” to show his real response to prayer and repentance; the threat of judgment was real, and the outcome was what God had always purposed, through the prayer he himself invited (cf. Jer 18:7–10). God is not moved like a man, but he is moved by the prayers of his people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-24 — The Tablets Broken and the Calf Destroyed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 15-24: Moses breaks the tablets, destroys the calf and makes Israel drink it; Aaron says the calf came out of the fire.
verseByVerse.theology:
Breaking the Tablets Is a Legal Act

The covenant document is smashed at the foot of the mountain, because the covenant has already been broken.
verseByVerse.examples: Aaron's excuse is worth recognising in ourselves. Honest confession names what I did; it does not say that something happened.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses turned and went down from the mountain with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand, tablets that were written on both sides; on the front and on the back they were written. The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets. When Joshua heard the noise of the people as they shouted, he said to Moses, "There is a noise of war in the camp." But he said, "It is not the sound of shouting for victory, or the sound of the cry of defeat, but the sound of singing that I hear." And as soon as he came near the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, Moses' anger burned hot, and he threw the tablets out of his hands and broke them at the foot of the mountain. He took the calf that they had made and burned it with fire and ground it to powder and scattered it on the water and made the people of Israel drink it. And Moses said to Aaron, "What did this people do to you that you have brought such a great sin upon them?" And Aaron said, "Let not the anger of my lord burn hot. You know the people, that they are set on evil. For they said to me, 'Make us gods who shall go before us. As for this Moses, the man who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has become of him.' So I said to them, 'Let any who have gold take it off.' So they gave it to me, and I threw it into the fire, and out came this calf."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The text lingers three times on the tablets as God's own work and writing, so that we feel what is about to be smashed. Joshua guesses war from the noise; Moses knows it is singing.

It is easy to read the breaking as a loss of temper, and it is more. The tablets were a covenant document, and Israel had already broken the covenant; smashing them at the foot of the mountain declares the agreement void. He is not damaging property. He is announcing a divorce.

He grinds the calf to powder and makes them drink it: every person in the camp swallows their god and discovers it goes down like grit.

Then Aaron's explanation, one of the most human sentences in the Bible: out came this calf. As if he had been standing nearby when it happened. Verse 4 says he fashioned it with a graving tool. Aaron is weak rather than wicked, and under pressure he blames the people, the fire and the metal. It is the oldest reflex there is, running back to the woman whom you gave to be with me, and it survives into every apology that contains the word happened.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25-29 — The Levites Take Their Stand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 25-29: Moses calls, Who is on the LORD's side? The Levites go through the camp, and about three thousand fall.
verseByVerse.theology:
Not to Be Softened, and Not to Be Filed Away

Judgment falls only after a public call to come over to the LORD's side.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: an invitation came first, and anyone could have crossed the line. Now: God takes the corruption of his people seriously in both Testaments (Acts 5:1-11).

verseByVerse.quote: And when Moses saw that the people had broken loose (for Aaron had let them break loose, to the derision of their enemies), then Moses stood in the gate of the camp and said, "Who is on the LORD's side? Come to me." And all the sons of Levi gathered around him. And he said to them, "Thus says the LORD God of Israel, 'Put your sword on your side each of you, and go to and fro from gate to gate throughout the camp, and each of you kill his brother and his companion and his neighbor.'" And the sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses. And that day about three thousand men of the people fell. And Moses said, "Today you have been ordained for the service of the LORD, each one at the cost of his son and of his brother, so that he might bestow a blessing upon you this day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is hard reading and should not be softened or hurried past, though a few observations belong here. The judgment falls on those still engaged after a public call to stop: Moses issues an invitation first, and anyone could have crossed the line and lived. The number is a fraction of a nation of hundreds of thousands, so the great majority were spared. And the alternative on the table an hour earlier had been the destruction of everybody.

It is also the beginning of the Levites' priestly vocation, and what qualified them is not comfortable either: they were willing to act against their own relatives when the covenant was at stake. Many preachers have set beside this day another, at Pentecost, when about three thousand were added to the church (Acts 2:41), for Paul says the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (2 Cor. 3:6).

What must not be done is to file this away as the God of the Old Testament being harsher than the God of the New. It was Jesus who spoke most often about hell, and the New Testament records Ananias and Sapphira dead on the floor of the first church. God takes the corruption of his people with a seriousness we find shocking, and the shock measures how lightly we take it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 30-35: Moses asks God to forgive, or else blot him out of his book. God refuses, and sends a plague.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sentence That Breaks Off

Moses offers himself as a substitute, and God refuses.
verseByVerse.examples: The offer was magnificent, and it was refused because the substitute needed a mediator himself. Only one who had no sin of his own could take the place Moses offered to take.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Moses said to the people, "You have sinned a great sin. And now I will go up to the LORD; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin." So Moses returned to the LORD and said, "Alas, this people has sinned a great sin. They have made for themselves gods of gold. But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written." But the LORD said to Moses, "Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot out of my book. But now go, lead the people to the place about which I have spoken to you; behold, my angel shall go before you. Nevertheless, in the day when I visit, I will visit their sin upon them." Then the LORD sent a plague on the people, because they made the calf, the one that Aaron made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What Moses prays the next day is the high point of his life. The sentence breaks off in the middle. He starts if you will forgive their sin and cannot finish it, because there is nothing to put after it: no merit, no mitigating circumstance, nothing Israel can offer. So he offers himself, and asks to be erased in their place.

That is substitutionary atonement, proposed by a man with no authority to perform it, and God refuses. Moses is a sinner himself; a man in the debt cannot pay it for others.

Paul echoed this prayer about his own countrymen: I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers (Rom. 9:3). He too could not do it. Neither could anyone else.

About fifteen centuries later someone made the same offer and was not refused. He was forsaken and made a curse, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Mark 15:34), and the names stayed in the book. What Moses proposed and could not do, Christ did at Calvary, because the only person who could be cut off in place of sinners was the one man who had never earned it for himself.

What is the book? It is God’s register of his people, the book of the living (Ps 69:28), which the New Testament calls the book of life (Phil 4:3; Rev 20:15). Can a name be erased? Some take this verse to mean a believer can lose salvation. But the book here includes all Israel, the living members of the covenant people, and the sinners blotted out are those who rebelled. Christ promises his own: I will never blot his name out of the book of life (Rev 3:5). Those written there before the foundation of the world (Rev 17:8) are kept.

33.title: If Your Presence Will Not Go
33.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Depart; go up from here, you and the people whom you have brought up out of the land of Egypt, to the land of which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'To your offspring I will give it.'<sup>2</sup>I will send an angel before you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>3</sup>Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey; but I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people."<sup>4</sup>When the people heard this disastrous word, they mourned, and no one put on his ornaments.<sup>5</sup>For the LORD had said to Moses, "Say to the people of Israel, 'You are a stiff-necked people; if for a single moment I should go up among you, I would consume you. So now take off your ornaments, that I may know what to do with you.'"<sup>6</sup>Therefore the people of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments, from Mount Horeb onward.<sup>7</sup>Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, far off from the camp, and he called it the tent of meeting. And everyone who sought the LORD would go out to the tent of meeting, which was outside the camp.<sup>8</sup>Whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people would rise up, and each would stand at his tent door, and watch Moses until he had gone into the tent.<sup>9</sup>When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the entrance of the tent, and the LORD would speak with Moses.<sup>10</sup>And when all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance of the tent, all the people would rise up and worship, each at his tent door.<sup>11</sup>Thus the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. When Moses turned again into the camp, his assistant Joshua the son of Nun, a young man, would not depart from the tent.<sup>12</sup>Moses said to the LORD, "See, you say to me, 'Bring up this people,' but you have not let me know whom you will send with me. Yet you have said, 'I know you by name, and you have also found favor in my sight.'<sup>13</sup>Now therefore, if I have found favor in your sight, please show me now your ways, that I may know you in order to find favor in your sight. Consider too that this nation is your people."<sup>14</sup>And he said, "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest."<sup>15</sup>And he said to him, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here.<sup>16</sup>For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct, I and your people, from every other people on the face of the earth?"<sup>17</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "This very thing that you have spoken I will do, for you have found favor in my sight, and I know you by name."<sup>18</sup>Moses said, "Please show me your glory."<sup>19</sup>And he said, "I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name 'The LORD.' And I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.<sup>20</sup>But," he said, "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live."<sup>21</sup>And the LORD said, "Behold, there is a place by me where you shall stand on the rock,<sup>22</sup>and while my glory passes by I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand until I have passed by.<sup>23</sup>Then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back, but my face shall not be seen."
33.overview:
After the calf, the question is no longer survival but presence. God offers to send Israel to the land with an angel but to withdraw his own presence, lest his holiness consume this stiff-necked people. Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than the promised land without him, and that is the heart of true religion: the believer wants God himself, not merely his gifts. Moses does not want the milk and honey; he wants the God who gives it.

Then Moses dares to ask to see God's glory. God answers with grace and with reserve: his goodness will pass by and his name be proclaimed, but Moses cannot see his face and live, so he is hidden in the rock, covered by God's own hand. Here is both the unapproachable holiness of God and his astonishing condescension.
33.theology:
The supreme value of God's presence. The presence of God is what sets his people apart, and true faith wants him more than anything he gives.

The problem of a holy God dwelling with sinners. God's presence among an unholy people would consume them, a crisis resolved only in Christ, who deals with our sin so that God can dwell with us.

The unseeable glory revealed in Christ. No one can see God's face and live, yet in Christ we behold "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6).
33.examples:
Then: God threatened to send Israel on without his presence, and Moses refused to go without it and asked to see his glory.

Now: the glory Moses could not fully see has drawn near in Christ, and in him God's presence is ours forever.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-6 — 'I Will Not Go Up Among You'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-6: Everything is promised except God's own presence, and the people mourn and strip off their ornaments.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything Except Him

Every gift remains on offer; only the Giver withdraws.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel's repentance came not from the threat of punishment but from the threat of God's absence. Grief at the thought of losing him is itself a sign that he is at work.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Depart; go up from here, you and the people whom you have brought up out of the land of Egypt, to the land of which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, 'To your offspring I will give it.' I will send an angel before you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey; but I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people." When the people heard this disastrous word, they mourned, and no one put on his ornaments. For the LORD had said to Moses, "Say to the people of Israel, 'You are a stiff-necked people; if for a single moment I should go up among you, I would consume you. So now take off your ornaments, that I may know what to do with you.'" Therefore the people of Israel stripped themselves of their ornaments, from Mount Horeb onward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the most chilling offer in the book, and it takes a moment to see why. Everything is still on the table: the land, the promise, an angel to drive out the nations, every material blessing Israel was ever offered. The only thing withdrawn is God himself.

It is presented as mercy, which it partly is. A holy God travelling in the middle of a people like this is dangerous to them; distance would keep them alive.

The people understand at once what has happened, and no one puts on his ornaments. They had worn their gold to make a calf; now they take it off. This is the first genuine repentance in the chapter, produced not by the threat of punishment but by the threat of absence.

Which is the question the chapter puts to every reader: would the land without God have been a good enough offer? Israel had complained about food and water since the sea and never once grieved at the thought of losing God's company. Now everything they asked for, minus him, registers as a disastrous word. Something in them has grown up.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-11 — The Tent of Meeting, and a Friend of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 7-11: The tent of meeting outside the camp, where the LORD speaks with Moses as a friend, and Joshua stays behind.
verseByVerse.theology:
Face to Face

God speaks with Moses directly, the way friends talk.
verseByVerse.examples: The young man stayed where God speaks. Leaders are often formed in places nobody ordered them to stay.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses used to take the tent and pitch it outside the camp, far off from the camp, and he called it the tent of meeting. And everyone who sought the LORD would go out to the tent of meeting, which was outside the camp. Whenever Moses went out to the tent, all the people would rise up, and each would stand at his tent door, and watch Moses until he had gone into the tent. When Moses entered the tent, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand at the entrance of the tent, and the LORD would speak with Moses. And when all the people saw the pillar of cloud standing at the entrance of the tent, all the people would rise up and worship, each at his tent door. Thus the LORD used to speak to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. When Moses turned again into the camp, his assistant Joshua the son of Nun, a young man, would not depart from the tent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Face to face, as a man speaks to his friend sits only a few verses from God saying no one may see his face and live. Moses pitched this tent outside the camp; anyone who sought the LORD went out to it, and when the pillar of cloud stood at its door the people rose and worshipped at their own tent doors. The two are not in conflict: face to face is an idiom for direct, unmediated conversation, not a claim about physical sight. But the phrase is not diminished by that. God spoke to this man the way friends talk.

And a quiet detail at the end: the older man goes back to work; the young Joshua stays behind in the place where God speaks. He is being formed for forty years' time in a tent nobody ordered him to remain in.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — 'If Your Presence Will Not Go'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 12-17: Moses asks to know God's ways and refuses the land without his presence, and God promises to go with them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Presence Is the Distinctive

God's going with them is what makes Israel different from every other nation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the land was never what made Israel special. Now: a church's life depends on the same presence, which God has promised to those who ask.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said to the LORD, "See, you say to me, 'Bring up this people,' but you have not let me know whom you will send with me. Yet you have said, 'I know you by name, and you have also found favor in my sight.' Now therefore, if I have found favor in your sight, please show me now your ways, that I may know you in order to find favor in your sight. Consider too that this nation is your people." And he said, "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." And he said to him, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here. For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct, I and your people, from every other people on the face of the earth?" And the LORD said to Moses, "This very thing that you have spoken I will do, for you have found favor in my sight, and I know you by name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the conversation the chapter exists for. Moses argues like a man with nothing left to lose. He presses God on his own words, and asks not for the route but that I may know you. And he will not let go of God's word about the people: this nation is your people.

God concedes: My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest. And Moses' reply ought to be carved over the whole chapter. He would rather stay in the desert with God than enter the land without him, and his reason is not sentiment. The presence of God is the only thing that makes Israel different from anybody else. Strip that out and they are one more nation with a territory and a flag.

That test still works, on a church or on a life. Take away every distinctive explained by history, culture, effort or good management: what remains that can only be accounted for by God actually being present? If the honest answer is nothing much, the offer of verse 1 has quietly been accepted: all the blessings, and none of him. The remedy is Moses' own: not more effort but asking, on the ground of God's word, for his presence, which he has promised to his people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 18-23: Moses asks, Show me your glory. God's goodness passes by while Moses is hidden in the rock and sees only his back.
verseByVerse.theology:
What God Says His Glory Consists Of

God defines his glory as his goodness and his name, and Moses sees it only from behind.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses was given a glimpse of God's back. The church has been shown his face, in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said, "Please show me your glory." And he said, "I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name 'The LORD.' And I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy. But," he said, "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." And the LORD said, "Behold, there is a place by me where you shall stand on the rock, and while my glory passes by I will put you in a cleft of the rock, and I will cover you with my hand until I have passed by. Then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back, but my face shall not be seen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Emboldened, Moses asks for the thing he has wanted his whole life. He has seen a bush burn, a sea open and a mountain smoke, and it has not been enough. This is the appetite God's presence creates rather than satisfies.

God's answer grants and refuses in one breath. What he equates with his glory is goodness, and a name. And a man hidden in a rock, covered by God's own hand, is permitted to see the afterglow of God going by. That is the most the old covenant could give, even to God's friend.

Which makes John's sentence extraordinary: No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known (John 1:18). And Paul: God, who said, "Let light shine out of darkness," has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor. 4:6).

The face Moses was refused is the face the church has been shown. Ordinary people in Galilee looked at it across a supper table and did not know what they were seeing. Moses was given his answer at last: on another mountain he talked with Jesus while that face shone like the sun (Matt. 17:2–3). And what God said his glory consisted of, goodness and a name, proved exactly right: when the glory stood still long enough to be seen it was a man doing good and bearing the name given because he will save his people from their sins (Matt. 1:21).

Paul cites verse 19 to show that God’s mercy does not depend on human will or exertion (Rom 9:15–16). The objection is that this makes God arbitrary. But it is said as part of his goodness passing by, and to a people who deserved nothing after the calf. Mercy that could be earned would not be mercy.

34.title: The LORD, the LORD, a God Merciful and Gracious
34.text: <sup>1</sup>The LORD said to Moses, "Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke.<sup>2</sup>Be ready by the morning, and come up in the morning to Mount Sinai, and present yourself there to me on the top of the mountain.<sup>3</sup>No one shall come up with you, and let no one be seen throughout all the mountain. Let no flocks or herds graze opposite that mountain."<sup>4</sup>So Moses cut two tablets of stone like the first. And he rose early in the morning and went up on Mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, and took in his hand two tablets of stone.<sup>5</sup>The LORD descended in the cloud and stood with him there, and proclaimed the name of the LORD.<sup>6</sup>The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness,<sup>7</sup>keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children and the children's children, to the third and the fourth generation."<sup>8</sup>And Moses quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped.<sup>9</sup>And he said, "If now I have found favor in your sight, O Lord, please let the Lord go in the midst of us, for it is a stiff-necked people, and pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance."<sup>10</sup>And he said, "Behold, I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will do marvels, such as have not been created in all the earth or in any nation. And all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the LORD, for it is an awesome thing that I will do with you.<sup>11</sup>"Observe what I command you this day. Behold, I will drive out before you the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.<sup>12</sup>Take care, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land to which you go, lest it become a snare in your midst.<sup>13</sup>You shall tear down their altars and break their pillars and cut down their Asherim<sup>14</sup>(for you shall worship no other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God),<sup>15</sup>lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and when they whore after their gods and sacrifice to their gods and you are invited, you eat of his sacrifice,<sup>16</sup>and you take of their daughters for your sons, and their daughters whore after their gods and make your sons whore after their gods.<sup>17</sup>"You shall not make for yourself any gods of cast metal.<sup>18</sup>"You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib, for in the month Abib you came out from Egypt.<sup>19</sup>All that open the womb are mine, all your male livestock, the firstborn of cow and sheep.<sup>20</sup>The firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. And none shall appear before me empty-handed.<sup>21</sup>"Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest. In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest.<sup>22</sup>You shall observe the Feast of Weeks, the firstfruits of wheat harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering at the year's end.<sup>23</sup>Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD, the God of Israel.<sup>24</sup>For I will cast out nations before you and enlarge your borders; no one shall covet your land, when you go up to appear before the LORD your God three times in the year.<sup>25</sup>"You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the sacrifice of the Feast of the Passover remain until the morning.<sup>26</sup>The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk."<sup>27</sup>And the LORD said to Moses, "Write these words, for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel."<sup>28</sup>So he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water. And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments.<sup>29</sup>When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand as he came down from the mountain, Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God.<sup>30</sup>Aaron and all the people of Israel saw Moses, and behold, the skin of his face shone, and they were afraid to come near him.<sup>31</sup>But Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him, and Moses talked with them.<sup>32</sup>Afterward all the people of Israel came near, and he commanded them all that the LORD had spoken with him on Mount Sinai.<sup>33</sup>And when Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face.<sup>34</sup>Whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he would remove the veil, until he came out. And when he came out and told the people of Israel what he was commanded,<sup>35</sup>the people of Israel would see the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face was shining. And Moses would put the veil over his face again, until he went in to speak with him.
34.overview:
This is the high point of God's self-revelation in the Old Testament. Moses asked to see God's glory, and God shows it first not by sight but by proclaiming his name and character. The glory of God is supremely the glory of his grace.

The proclamation becomes Israel's creed about the heart of God (Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Pss. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Nah. 1:3), holding overflowing love and forgiveness together with the warning that God "will by no means clear the guilty." His mercy does not cancel his justice; his justice does not quench his mercy.

The covenant is renewed after the calf, and Moses comes down with his face shining, a glory Paul says is surpassed by the glory now shining in the gospel (2 Cor. 3). The God who is merciful and gracious has, in Christ, drawn infinitely near.
34.theology:
The glory of God is the glory of his grace. God reveals his glory by proclaiming his name, and these verses become among the most-quoted in the rest of the Old Testament.

Mercy and justice held together. God forgives, yet "will by no means clear the guilty." The tension is resolved only at the cross, where God is "just and the justifier" (Rom. 3:26).

Transforming glory. Moses' shining face is surpassed by the glory of the gospel; beholding Christ, we are transformed from one degree of glory to another.
34.examples:
Then: God answered Moses' plea by proclaiming his name, renewing the covenant after the calf and sending Moses down with a shining face.

Now: this is the God we worship: merciful and gracious, yet perfectly just. Beholding his glory in the face of Christ, we are being changed by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — The LORD Proclaims His Name
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 1-9: New tablets, cut by Moses this time, and God descends and proclaims his name.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Proportions of the Name

God gives six words of mercy and only one clause of judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: This time Moses cut the stone and God wrote on it. Restored sinners often carry some of the cost of what they broke, and they are restored all the same.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Moses, "Cut for yourself two tablets of stone like the first, and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the first tablets, which you broke. Be ready by the morning, and come up in the morning to Mount Sinai, and present yourself there to me on the top of the mountain. No one shall come up with you, and let no one be seen throughout all the mountain. Let no flocks or herds graze opposite that mountain." So Moses cut two tablets of stone like the first. And he rose early in the morning and went up on Mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, and took in his hand two tablets of stone. The LORD descended in the cloud and stood with him there, and proclaimed the name of the LORD. The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children and the children's children, to the third and the fourth generation." And Moses quickly bowed his head toward the earth and worshiped. And he said, "If now I have found favor in your sight, O Lord, please let the Lord go in the midst of us, for it is a stiff-necked people, and pardon our iniquity and our sin, and take us for your inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant is remade, with one difference. The first tablets were God's work throughout (32:16); this time Moses cuts the stone and God writes on it. Grace does not always restore a thing in the form it was lost; sometimes the man who broke it carries the quarrying up the hill.

Then the moment Moses has waited for since 33:18: God proclaims his own name, the fullest self-description he ever gives.

Look at the proportions. Asked to show his glory, God announces mercy, grace, patience, steadfast love, faithfulness and forgiveness, six terms, and then one clause of judgment. He is not pretending the judgment away. It stands immediately after the offer of forgiveness, and raises a question this chapter cannot answer: how does a God who forgives iniquity also refuse to clear the guilty? Both cannot be true unless the guilt goes somewhere.

Israel's settled understanding of God's character came from this sentence, spoken to one man on a mountain in the aftermath of a national catastrophe. The psalms return to these words again and again, and Jonah is furious about them because he knew them by heart and knew what they meant for Nineveh.

The question it leaves open is answered at a cross, where God proved himself just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom. 3:26): iniquity genuinely forgiven and the guilty genuinely not cleared, because the guilt was borne by someone else.

Does verse 7 teach generational curses? No guilt is inherited: The son shall not suffer for the iniquity of the father (Ezek 18:20). The second commandment adds of those who hate me (20:5): children who repeat their parents’ sin share their judgment, and the effects of sin run through families. But in Christ no curse remains (Gal 3:13), and the contrast is the point: judgment for generations, steadfast love for thousands.
verseByVerse.note: “Thousands” may mean “the thousandth generation” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 10-17: No covenant or intermarriage with the peoples of the land, their altars torn down, for the LORD's name is Jealous.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jealous Is a Name

The renewed terms guard Israel's worship at exactly the point where it failed.
verseByVerse.examples: God's jealousy is not an insecure rival's but a husband's, and it comes from the God who has just forgiven his bride.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Behold, I am making a covenant. Before all your people I will do marvels, such as have not been created in all the earth or in any nation. And all the people among whom you are shall see the work of the LORD, for it is an awesome thing that I will do with you. "Observe what I command you this day. Behold, I will drive out before you the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. Take care, lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land to which you go, lest it become a snare in your midst. You shall tear down their altars and break their pillars and cut down their Asherim (for you shall worship no other god, for the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God), lest you make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and when they whore after their gods and sacrifice to their gods and you are invited, you eat of his sacrifice, and you take of their daughters for your sons, and their daughters whore after their gods and make your sons whore after their gods. "You shall not make for yourself any gods of cast metal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The covenant terms are restated, and the emphasis falls where the failure was: other gods. Jealousy is given as a name rather than described as a mood, and the terms around it are about company. God's jealousy is not insecurity; it is a husband's response to the one thing a marriage cannot survive.

Was the ban on intermarriage racial? No. It was religious: such wives would make your sons whore after their gods (v. 16). Rahab of Jericho and Ruth the Moabite joined Israel by faith and were ancestors of Christ. The principle carries over: a Christian should marry only in the Lord (1 Cor 7:39; 2 Cor 6:14). The command to drive out the nations belonged to the conquest and is not a pattern for today.
verseByVerse.note: Asherah poles were wooden cult objects of the Canaanite goddess Asherah.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 18-26: Feasts, firstborn and Sabbath are restated, with rest even in ploughing and harvest.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remedy for Failing at the Basics Is the Basics

After the calf, God gives the same rhythms of worship and rest again, unchanged.
verseByVerse.examples: The command to rest names the seasons when it is hardest to obey, and God's rest is still a gift most needed when we feel we cannot stop.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time appointed in the month Abib, for in the month Abib you came out from Egypt. All that open the womb are mine, all your male livestock, the firstborn of cow and sheep. The firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, or if you will not redeem it you shall break its neck. All the firstborn of your sons you shall redeem. And none shall appear before me empty-handed. "Six days you shall work, but on the seventh day you shall rest. In plowing time and in harvest you shall rest. You shall observe the Feast of Weeks, the firstfruits of wheat harvest, and the Feast of Ingathering at the year's end. Three times in the year shall all your males appear before the Lord GOD, the God of Israel. For I will cast out nations before you and enlarge your borders; no one shall covet your land, when you go up to appear before the LORD your God three times in the year. "You shall not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, or let the sacrifice of the Feast of the Passover remain until the morning. The best of the firstfruits of your ground you shall bring to the house of the LORD your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother's milk."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ploughing and harvest are the two seasons when stopping costs most, and they are named.

The repetition is the pastoral point. Israel has just broken this covenant spectacularly, and God's response is to say the same things over: no stricter version, no extra clauses to prevent a recurrence. The remedy for a forgiven people who failed at the basics is the basics, said again.

Why redeem a donkey with a lamb (v. 20)? The firstborn belonged to God because he spared Israel’s firstborn at the Passover (13:11–15). A donkey could not be sacrificed, so a lamb died in its place, or the donkey died. Every redeemed firstborn son was bought back the same way: life for life, a picture of the substitute who redeems us. On the young goat in its mother’s milk (v. 26), cf. 23:19.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27-28 — Forty Days, the Ten Words
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 27-28: Another forty days on the mountain without food or water.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Fasts of the Same Length

The words of the covenant are written again, after a second forty days.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Moses fasted forty days on this mountain, twice. Now: Christ fasted forty days and kept the covenant Israel broke.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Write these words, for in accordance with these words I have made a covenant with you and with Israel." So he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water. And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Commandments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two forty-day fasts on this mountain, either side of a national apostasy. One other man fasted forty days and nights in a wilderness, and when the tempter came he answered out of the book Moses was writing: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God (Matt. 4:4). The second Moses quoted the first, from a fast of the same length, and did not break: he kept, in our place, the covenant Israel had broken.

Who wrote on these tablets? Verse 28's he wrote is most naturally the LORD, as verse 1 promised and Deuteronomy 10:2–4 confirms; Moses wrote the wider words of the covenant (v. 27).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29-35 — The Shining Face of Moses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 29-35: Moses' face shines, the people are afraid, and he veils it except before the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology:
What the Veil Was Hiding

Moses covers his shining face between his meetings with God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: the glory on Moses' face was fading (2 Cor. 3:13). Now: the glory the Spirit works in believers keeps increasing.

verseByVerse.quote: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand as he came down from the mountain, Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had been talking with God. Aaron and all the people of Israel saw Moses, and behold, the skin of his face shone, and they were afraid to come near him. But Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him, and Moses talked with them. Afterward all the people of Israel came near, and he commanded them all that the LORD had spoken with him on Mount Sinai. And when Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil over his face. Whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he would remove the veil, until he came out. And when he came out and told the people of Israel what he was commanded, the people of Israel would see the face of Moses, that the skin of Moses' face was shining. And Moses would put the veil over his face again, until he went in to speak with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He did not notice. A man can spend forty days in God's presence and be the only person in the camp unaware of what it has done to him, which is generally how it works.

Paul read this closely and saw something the Old Testament never says outright: the veil was so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end (2 Cor. 3:13). The glory on Moses' face was fading. The veil concealed a brightness that was going out.
